    print("first 8 byte-level merges:", [vocab[256 + i] for i in range(8)])
    print(f"tokens: {len(encode(text, merges))} for {len(text.encode())} bytes")
    print(f"{len(bw)} distinct words, 60 merges: naive regex {t_naive*1e3:.0f} ms, full recount {t_full*1e3:.0f} ms, incremental {t_inc*1e3:.0f} ms")

Matching tiktoken's educational trainer is a strong test because the two implementations were written independently and agree only if every detail matches: chunking, byte-level start, frequency weighting, the non-overlapping left-to-right merge, and above all the tie-breaking rule. A single difference in tie-breaking changes some merge, and every later merge can then differ.

8. Practical traps

Trap 1: tie-breaking. Equal counts are common, especially early on small corpora. "First counted wins" depends on iteration order, which depends on how the corpus was read; reproducing someone else's tokenizer requires their exact rule, and a sort by count alone, or a set, makes training non-deterministic.

Trap 2: overlapping pairs. In "aaa", the pair (a, a) occurs twice when counting but can be merged only once, left to right, giving [aa, a]. Counting overlapping occurrences while merging non-overlapping ones is the convention everyone follows; deviating changes the merges.

Trap 3: decoding multi-byte characters. In the test, "€" is three bytes and three tokens; decoding each token separately gives three U+FFFD replacement characters. When streaming generated tokens to a user, keep incomplete UTF-8 bytes buffered until the character completes.

Trap 4: encoding speed. The encode_chunk here scans all pairs per merge, quadratic in chunk length. Fine for words; for very long chunks (a megabyte of text with no spaces) production encoders cap chunk length or use a priority queue over pairs with a linked list of symbols, making encoding O(n log n).

Trap 5: whitespace and normalisation. Different handling of leading spaces, Unicode normalisation (NFC versus NFD forms of accented characters) or newline conventions produce different byte sequences and therefore different tokens. A tokenizer is defined by its regex, normalisation and merges together; change any one and the model sees unfamiliar input.

Trap 6: special tokens in user text. If the encoder turns the literal text of a control token into its special ID, user input can forge structure. Encode user text with special tokens disabled.

Adding special tokens

Real tokenizers reserve IDs beyond the merges for control tokens: end of text, start and end of chat turns, tool-call delimiters, padding. They are added after training, with IDs above the last merge, and handled outside BPE: the encoder first splits the input on the literal special-token strings (only when explicitly allowed), encodes the ordinary text between them with BPE, and inserts the reserved IDs; the decoder maps those IDs back to their strings. Because special tokens never come from merges, ordinary text can never accidentally produce one, which is exactly the property that keeps users from forging conversation structure. Adding new special tokens to an existing model means adding rows to its embedding table and fine-tuning so the model learns what they mean.

9. Edge cases worth naming

The empty string encodes to no tokens and decodes back to the empty string. A chunk of one byte cannot merge. A text with no repeated pairs stops training immediately because no pair occurs twice. Invalid UTF-8 cannot come from str.encode, but a model can emit token sequences whose bytes are invalid, which is why decode uses errors="replace". Very large vocabularies can reach a point where the most frequent pair occurs only a handful of times, producing tokens that appear almost nowhere else, an argument for stopping at a minimum count. And case matters: "The" and "the" are different byte sequences and different tokens unless the training text makes them share merges.

10. Complexity

Pre-tokenising and counting the corpus is O(corpus length) once. The full-recount trainer then costs O(M × S) for M merges and S total symbols across distinct chunks, recounting and rewriting everything each round. The incremental trainer costs, per merge, time proportional to the chunks containing the merged pair, usually a small fraction; on the test's 3,718 distinct random words, 60 merges took 56 ms incrementally against 594 ms for a full recount and 455 ms for the regex version, with identical results. Encoding a chunk of length n with the simple scan is O(n²) in the worst case, O(n log n) with a priority queue. Memory is the merge table and vocabulary, a few megabytes for 100,000 tokens.

11. Talking through the design

In the interview: explain BPE as compression by repeated pair merging; work a few merges by hand with counts and the tie rule; write the trainer over chunk frequencies with byte-level base symbols; write encode by merge rank and explain why not longest match; write decode by bytes; test round trips including emoji and the empty string. Then volunteer the senior points: the pre-tokeniser regex and why it matters, incremental training, streaming decode of multi-byte characters, special-token injection, and multilingual fairness. State your tie rule out loud before writing the training loop, since it is the detail most often probed.
deep:
Subword regularisation and BPE-dropout

Deterministic BPE always splits a word the same way, so a model never sees alternative segmentations and can be brittle to small spelling variations. Kudo's subword regularisation samples segmentations from a Unigram model during training; BPE-dropout achieves something similar for BPE by randomly skipping merges while encoding training data, so the same word sometimes appears in smaller pieces. Both act as data augmentation and improve robustness, especially for low-resource translation. At inference, encoding is deterministic again. These methods show that the segmentation is a modelling choice, not a fixed fact about the text.

Encoding efficiently at scale

The simple encoder rescans every adjacent pair after each merge, which is quadratic in chunk length. Production encoders keep the chunk as a doubly linked list of symbols and a priority queue of adjacent pairs keyed by merge rank; merging a pair removes two nodes, inserts one, and updates only the two neighbouring pairs in the queue, so a chunk of n bytes encodes in O(n log n). They also cache the encodings of frequent chunks (most words recur), so the BPE loop runs only for chunks not seen before. tiktoken combines both with a compiled regex, which is why it can encode text at many megabytes per second while this lesson's pure-Python version manages far less.

What the tokenizer is trained on

A tokenizer is trained once, usually on a sample of the model's pre-training mix, and then frozen for the model's lifetime: changing it later invalidates the embedding table. The sample's composition decides which languages, programming languages and formats get efficient merges. Teams balance the sample deliberately (upweighting code or under-represented languages), deduplicate it (a few repeated boilerplate strings can otherwise claim many merges), and check fertility by language before committing, because a tokenizer mistake is one of the few training decisions that cannot be fixed by more training.

Why frequency-based merging works

BPE greedily maximises compression: each merge reduces the total number of symbols in the corpus by the merged pair's count, the largest reduction available at that step. Frequent strings in natural language are disproportionately meaningful (common words, inflectional endings, frequent stems), so a compression objective yields a linguistically plausible vocabulary without any linguistic input. Sennrich et al.'s motivation was open-vocabulary translation: rare words and names can be represented as sequences of subword units instead of a single unknown token, and their translation experiments showed better handling of rare words than back-off dictionaries.

Byte-level BPE and the GPT-2 regex

GPT-2 made the base vocabulary the 256 bytes, so any string is encodable, and added a pre-tokeniser regex so merges stay within categories: contractions ('s, 't, 're), letters with an optional leading space, digits, other symbols, and whitespace. GPT-2's vocabulary has 50,257 tokens: 256 bytes, 50,000 merges and one end-of-text token. Later OpenAI tokenisers refined the regex (for example limiting digit runs to three characters, which makes numbers split more regularly) and grew the vocabulary to about 100,000 (cl100k) and about 200,000 (o200k) tokens. The pattern this lesson uses is a simplified version; matching a real tokenizer requires its exact regex, which is why the test passes the same pattern to tiktoken's trainer.

WordPiece, Unigram and SentencePiece

WordPiece (BERT) builds a vocabulary similarly but chooses merges by a likelihood-based score rather than raw frequency, and encodes with greedy longest-match from the left. The Unigram language-model tokenizer (Kudo) starts with a large candidate vocabulary and prunes it, keeping the pieces that best explain the corpus under a unigram model; it can produce several segmentations with probabilities, which enables subword regularisation (sampling segmentations during training). SentencePiece is a library that implements BPE and Unigram directly on raw text, treating spaces as an ordinary symbol, which makes it language-independent and lossless; many multilingual models use it.

Tokenisation and model behaviour

Because the model sees tokens, anything about characters inside a token must be learned indirectly: spelling, rhyming, counting letters, reversing strings. Numbers split into irregular chunks make arithmetic harder, which is why some tokenisers split digits individually or into fixed groups. Leading-space conventions mean "dog" at the start of a line and " dog" after a space are different tokens, a source of odd prompt sensitivity. "Glitch tokens" are tokens that occurred in the tokenizer's training data but almost never in the model's, so their embeddings are barely trained and the model behaves strangely when it sees them. All of these are tokenizer facts with model consequences.

Multilingual fairness and fertility

Fertility, tokens per word or per character, varies widely across languages for a tokenizer trained mostly on English. Petrov and colleagues measured that the same content can require several times more tokens in some languages, which means proportionally higher API cost, shorter effective context and slower generation for those users. The drill reproduces the effect in miniature: an English-trained tokenizer leaves Hindi at the byte level, one token per byte, three per Devanagari character. Larger vocabularies trained on balanced multilingual data reduce the gap, part of why recent vocabularies grew to 200,000 tokens and more.
prod:
Where tokenizers run

At both ends of every LLM call: on the client or server to count tokens for billing and context limits, before the model to encode prompts, and after it to stream decoded text. Production tokenizers are written in Rust or C++ (tiktoken, Hugging Face tokenizers, SentencePiece) because encoding is on the latency path and training on terabytes must be fast, but they implement exactly the algorithm in this lesson.

Failure modes and symptoms

Tokenizer-model mismatch. A model served with a slightly different tokenizer (another version's regex, a different normalisation, a missing merge) produces coherent but noticeably worse output. Detection: encode a reference text and compare IDs with the tokenizer shipped alongside the checkpoint; any difference is a bug.

Broken characters in streamed output. Users see replacement characters (�) mid-word in non-English or emoji-heavy responses. Cause: decoding each streamed token separately. Fix: buffer incomplete UTF-8 sequences. Python's incremental UTF-8 decoder (codecs.getincrementaldecoder) does exactly this: feed it each token's bytes and it emits only complete characters.

Context limits hit early for some users. Token counts per message are far higher for some languages or for code with unusual formatting. Measure tokens per character by language and content type; budget context accordingly; consider a model with a more efficient tokenizer for those users. Report the numbers per language to product teams, since a context limit that is generous in English can be tight in Hindi, Thai or Amharic, and pricing per token passes that difference straight to users.

Prompt injection through special tokens. User text containing a literal control-token string is encoded as the control token. Encode untrusted text with special tokens disallowed; tiktoken raises an error by default when it sees special-token text unless told otherwise.

Counting mistakes in billing and limits. Client-side estimates that use a different tokenizer from the server (or count characters) disagree with the server's count and cause rejected requests or wrong bills. Use the model's own tokenizer for counting.

Silent tokenizer upgrades. A library update changes a default (a regex, a normalisation step, how whitespace is stripped) and token IDs shift for some inputs. The model still runs, but behaves slightly differently, and cached prompts or stored token counts become wrong. Pin the tokenizer version with the model, store a hash of the merge table and regex, and keep an exact-ID regression test on a reference corpus that includes code, emoji, numbers and several scripts.

Mismatched chat templates. The tokenizer is correct but the conversation is formatted with the wrong role markers or separators, so the model sees an unfamiliar structure and follows instructions poorly. The template that turns messages into text (and therefore tokens) ships with the model just like the merges; apply the model's own template and compare its token IDs with the reference implementation for a sample conversation.

What to monitor

Tokens per request and per character by language and product surface, the rate of replacement characters in outputs, encoding latency at the tail, and, after any tokenizer or model update, an exact-match check of token IDs on a fixed reference corpus.

A cost estimate

A tokenizer with 100,000 tokens and a model dimension of 4,096 has an embedding table of 410 million parameters, and the output layer the same unless tied; doubling the vocabulary adds that much again. On the other side, a better vocabulary that cuts tokens per text by 15% cuts the cost of every forward pass, attention's quadratic term by about 28%, and every API bill by 15%. That trade-off, a bigger table against shorter sequences, is the main lever tokenizer designers pull.

The reference for this problem

Sennrich, Haddow and Birch's "Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units" (ACL 2016, arXiv 1508.07909) adapted byte pair encoding, "a simple data compression technique that iteratively replaces the most frequent pair of bytes in a sequence with a single, unused byte", to word segmentation: initialise the symbol vocabulary with characters plus an end-of-word symbol, "iteratively count all symbol pairs and replace each occurrence of the most frequent pair ('A', 'B') with a new symbol 'AB'", with "the final symbol vocabulary size … equal to the size of the initial vocabulary, plus the number of merge operations". Their Algorithm 1 is a minimal Python implementation over the vocabulary {'l o w </w>': 5, 'l o w e r </w>': 2, 'n e w e s t </w>': 6, 'w i d e s t </w>': 3}, which this lesson reproduces exactly; their Figure 1 shows merges learned from {low, lowest, newer, wider} and the segmentation of the unseen word "lower" into "low er</w>". They note that "for efficiency, we do not consider pairs that cross word boundaries", the role of the pre-tokeniser here, and that "in practice, we increase efficiency by indexing all pairs, and updating data structures incrementally", the incremental trainer here.
myths: BPE picks merges by linguistic meaning.

It picks the most frequent adjacent pair, nothing else. On Sennrich et al.'s toy vocabulary the first merges are e+s, es+t and est+</w> because 'newest' and 'widest' occur 9 times between them, not because 'est' is a suffix. Morpheme-like tokens emerge only because frequent strings tend to be meaningful.
To encode, find the longest vocabulary token at each position.

Greedy longest-match gives different (and inconsistent) segmentations. BPE encoding replays the learned merges in the order they were learned: repeatedly merge the adjacent pair with the lowest merge rank. That is what makes encoding reproduce the training segmentation, which the tests check for every training chunk.
A byte-level tokenizer can still meet unknown characters.

Its base vocabulary is all 256 byte values, and every string is a sequence of UTF-8 bytes, so every input is encodable; there is no unknown token. Emoji and scripts unseen in training simply fall back to more, shorter tokens, which the tests' round trips confirm.
You can decode a stream one token at a time.

A multi-byte character can be split across tokens. '€' is three UTF-8 bytes; if no merge covers them, it is three tokens, and decoding each separately gives three replacement characters. Decode the concatenated bytes, or buffer incomplete UTF-8 sequences when streaming.
Pre-tokenisation is an optional speed-up.

It changes the vocabulary. Without splitting text into word-like chunks first, merges cross word boundaries and frequent phrases become single tokens; in this lesson's test the longest token learned without pre-tokenisation was 'fox jumps over'. GPT-2-style tokenisers split on a regex first so tokens stay within words, numbers or punctuation runs.
Tokenizers treat every language equally.

A tokenizer trained mostly on English merges English byte sequences and leaves other scripts at the byte level. In the drill, an English-trained tokenizer produced one token per byte for Hindi, several times more tokens per character than for English, which means higher cost and shorter effective context for those users.

recap: BPE training starts from single symbols (characters or bytes) and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new symbol, recording each merge in order.
On the vocabulary {low: 5, lower: 2, newest: 6, widest: 3}, the first merges are es, est, est</w>, lo, low, ne, new, newest</w>, low</w> and wi, exactly what the paper's script prints.
Pairs are counted within words (pre-tokenised chunks), weighted by word frequency; ties go to the pair counted first.
Byte-level BPE uses the 256 byte values as the base vocabulary, so any text can be encoded and nothing is unknown.
Encoding applies merges in learned order: repeatedly merge the adjacent pair with the lowest rank until no learned pair remains.
Decoding concatenates each token's bytes and decodes the whole byte string as UTF-8; decoding tokens one at a time can split multi-byte characters.
This lesson's byte-level trainer learns exactly the same tokens and ranks as tiktoken's educational BPE trainer on the same text and regex.
Recounting every pair after every merge is slow; updating counts only for words that contained the merged pair gave identical merges ten times faster here.
glossary: A tokenisation method that builds a vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols.
Randomly skipping merges while encoding training data so the model sees varied segmentations of the same word.
BPE whose base symbols are the 256 byte values of UTF-8 text, as in GPT-2 and later OpenAI tokenisers.
A piece of text produced by the pre-tokeniser regex; merges never cross chunk boundaries.
A symbol such as </w> appended to each word in Sennrich et al.'s version so that word-final pieces differ from word-internal ones.
The average number of tokens per word (or per character) for a language; higher fertility means more tokens for the same text.
The position of a merge in the learned order; lower ranks were learned earlier and are applied first when encoding.
The ordered list of learned pair merges that, with the byte table, defines the tokenizer.
The pattern that splits text into chunks before BPE; part of the tokenizer's definition.
A regex that splits text into word-like chunks before BPE, keeping tokens within words, numbers or punctuation.
U+FFFD, the symbol a decoder emits for bytes that are not valid UTF-8.
A reserved ID such as end-of-text, added outside the BPE merges and never produced by encoding ordinary text.
The integer a token maps to; the row index into the model's embedding table.
Converting text to a canonical form (such as NFC) so that visually identical strings have identical bytes.
The variable-length encoding of Unicode in which ASCII characters take one byte and others take two to four.
The number of distinct tokens: 256 base bytes plus the number of merges plus any special tokens.
BERT's subword method: merges chosen by a likelihood score, encoding by greedy longest match.
drill:
Work it out

Train your tokenizer on English only, then measure characters per token on an English sentence and on a Hindi sentence of similar meaning. What does the difference mean for cost and context length, and what would fix it?

Answer 
english = "the weather is very nice today and we are going to the market together. "
hindi = "आज मौसम बहुत अच्छा है और हम साथ में बाज़ार जा रहे हैं। "
merges_en, _ = train_bpe(english * 30, 80)

def chars_per_token(s, m):
    return len(s) / len(encode(s, m))

en_rate, hi_rate = chars_per_token(english, merges_en), chars_per_token(hindi, merges_en)
assert en_rate > 3 * hi_rate                       # English packs several characters per token
assert len(encode(hindi, merges_en)) == len(hindi.encode("utf-8"))   # Hindi falls back to raw bytes

No merge ever involved Devanagari bytes, so every Hindi character costs its full three UTF-8 bytes as three tokens, while English packs several characters into each token. The same sentence is several times more tokens in Hindi: higher API cost, less text per context window, slower generation. The fix is in the tokenizer's training mix: include the languages you serve, or use a larger multilingual vocabulary, which is why newer models with 200k-token vocabularies show big efficiency gains for Indic languages.
qa: E
Describe BPE training in four steps.

Split the corpus into chunks (words) and each chunk into base symbols (bytes). Count every adjacent pair of symbols, weighted by how often each chunk occurs. Merge the most frequent pair everywhere into a new symbol and record the merge. Repeat until the vocabulary reaches the target size or no pair occurs twice.
E
How do you encode new text with a trained BPE?

Pre-tokenise it into chunks, turn each chunk into bytes, then repeatedly find the adjacent pair with the lowest merge rank (earliest learned) and merge it, until no adjacent pair is in the merge table. Concatenate the chunks' token IDs. This replays training's merge order, so training text is segmented exactly as during training.
E
Why use bytes rather than characters as the base symbols?

There are only 256 byte values and every string is a byte sequence, so the base vocabulary is small and covers every possible input, including emoji, rare scripts and malformed text. Character-level bases need a large alphabet and still meet unseen characters, which then become an unknown token.
M
Run the first three merges of Sennrich et al.'s example by hand: low 5, lower 2, newest 6, widest 3, with </w> at word ends.

Pair counts: e s, s t and t </w> each 9 (newest 6 + widest 3); w e 8; l o and o w 7. The tie at 9 goes to the pair counted first, e s, giving es. Then es t has 9, giving est; then est </w> has 9, giving est</w>. Next come l o (7) and lo w (7). The paper's script prints these ten merges: es, est, est</w>, lo, low, ne, new, newest</w>, low</w>, wi.
Follow-up: why does tie-breaking matter? — Different tie rules give different vocabularies from the same data, so a reimplementation must break ties exactly as the original to reproduce its merges.
M
Encode ' the' with merges [(' ', 't'), ('h', 'e'), (' t', 'he')] in that order.

Start with the bytes ' ', 't', 'h', 'e'. Of the adjacent pairs, (' ', 't') has rank 0 and ('h', 'e') rank 1, so merge ' t' first: [' t', 'h', 'e']. Now ('h', 'e') has rank 1: [' t', 'he']. Now (' t', 'he') has rank 2: [' the']. One token. These are in fact the first three merges this lesson's trainer learns on its test text.
M
Why does GPT-2 pre-tokenise with a regex before BPE?

So merges stay within word-like units: letters with an optional leading space, numbers, punctuation runs and whitespace. Without it, frequent phrases and words glued to punctuation become tokens ('dog.' versus 'dog'), the vocabulary is wasted on combinations, and segmentation of a word depends on its neighbours. The leading-space convention means ' the' and 'the' are different tokens, which encodes word starts.
M
How do you decode token IDs back to text, and what can go wrong?

Map each ID to its bytes (base bytes plus the concatenation recorded for each merge), concatenate all bytes, and decode the result as UTF-8. Decoding token by token fails when a multi-byte character is split across tokens; in streaming, keep incomplete UTF-8 bytes in a buffer until the character completes.
M
What does vocabulary size trade off?

A larger vocabulary means fewer tokens per text (shorter sequences, cheaper attention, more text per context window) but a larger embedding table and output layer, rarer tokens with less training signal each, and slower softmax over the vocabulary. GPT-2 used 50,257 tokens; newer models use 100,000 to 250,000, largely to serve more languages and code efficiently.
H
How would you make BPE training fast on a large corpus?

Count each distinct chunk once with its frequency; keep a pair-count table and an index from each pair to the chunks containing it; after a merge, update counts only for those chunks (subtract their old pairs, add their new ones) instead of recounting everything; use a priority queue for the maximum, with a tie-break that matches the reference. In the test, the incremental version learned identical merges in 56 ms against 594 ms for a full recount.

Follow-up: what is the remaining bottleneck? — Pre-tokenising and counting the corpus once, which parallelises across documents; production trainers (Hugging Face tokenizers, SentencePiece) do this in Rust or C++.
M
Why are merges never counted across chunk boundaries, and what would change if they were?

The pre-tokeniser defines chunks (a word with its leading space, a number, a punctuation run), and pairs are counted only inside them, so a token can never contain the end of one word and the start of the next. Counting across boundaries lets frequent phrases and word-plus-punctuation combinations become tokens; in this lesson's test, training without pre-tokenisation produced a single token for 'fox jumps over'. Segmentation of a word would then depend on its neighbours, which is bad for generalisation.
Follow-up: is that ever desirable? — Some code tokenisers allow merges across certain whitespace patterns to compress indentation, a deliberate, targeted exception.
H
Why do LLMs struggle with spelling and counting letters, and what does the tokenizer have to do with it?

The model sees token IDs, not characters. 'strawberry' may be one or a few tokens whose spelling the model must have memorised from co-occurrence, so questions about individual letters require knowledge it is never directly shown. Similarly, numbers split into arbitrary multi-digit chunks make arithmetic harder; some tokenisers split digits individually for that reason.
H
A multilingual product finds Hindi users hit context limits far sooner than English users. Explain and fix.

The tokenizer's merges were learned mostly from English text, so Devanagari stays close to the byte level: each character is three UTF-8 bytes and often three tokens, against several English characters per token. The same content costs several times more tokens, which means higher cost, shorter effective context and slower generation. Fixes: a tokenizer trained on a balanced multilingual mix or with a larger vocabulary, which is a model-level change; or choosing a model whose tokenizer handles the language efficiently.
H
What are special tokens and what security issue do they create?

Reserved IDs (end-of-text, chat-role markers, tool-call delimiters) added outside the merges. If user text containing the literal string '<|endoftext|>' is encoded as the special token rather than as ordinary text, a user can inject control tokens into the model's input. Tokenizer APIs therefore encode special tokens from text only when explicitly allowed, and production code should treat user text as ordinary bytes.

t: Decoding: temperature, top-k, top-p and beam search
sum: Turn next-token logits into a choice four ways: temperature reshaping worked by hand (0.5 → [0.685, 0.247, 0.062, 0.007]), top-k and top-p truncation, a batched top-p with an argpartition prefilter, and beam search that finds the 0.38 sequence greedy misses, checked against exhaustive search, with length normalisation and log-space scoring.
prereq: lm8
Decoding strategies: greedy, sampling with temperature, top-k, top-p and beam search, and their effects on quality and diversity.
mc10
Softmax of logits, computed stably by subtracting the maximum, and working in log-probabilities.
mc18
Generation produces one token per step from the last position's logits, using the KV cache.
why:
A language model does not write text. At each step it produces a score for every token in its vocabulary, and something else, the decoding strategy, decides which token to emit. The same model can produce crisp, correct answers or bland repetition or incoherent rambling depending only on that decision. Ask a chat model for a story with the wrong settings and it will loop on "I'm sorry, I'm sorry"; ask it for a JSON object with sampling at high temperature and it will occasionally emit a stray comma that breaks your parser. Decoding is the cheapest lever an AI engineer has over output quality: no retraining, just a few lines of code between the logits and the user.

It is also where a lot of misunderstanding lives. Teams raise temperature to fix factual errors (it makes them worse), use beam search for chat (it makes replies bland), or compare models evaluated with different sampling settings and draw conclusions about the models. Knowing exactly what each knob does to the distribution, with numbers, is what lets you make these calls quickly and defend them.

That is why "implement temperature, top-k, top-p and beam search" appears in LLM coding interviews, usually with follow-ups that test judgement. Why does greedy decoding sometimes miss the most likely sentence? (In this lesson's example it settles for probability 0.21 when 0.38 is available.) Why does top-p adapt where top-k does not? Why do beam scores need a length penalty and log-probabilities? And why did Holtzman and colleagues find that beam search, the "best" search, produces the worst open-ended text?

The implementation details matter too. Temperature zero must be special-cased rather than divided by. The top-p cut needs a precise rule (keep tokens while the mass before them is below p, so the top token always survives). Sorting a 128,000-token vocabulary for every row of every step is expensive, and a top-k prefilter with argpartition removes most of that cost without changing the result. Beam search must sum log-probabilities, because multiplying hundreds of probabilities underflows to exactly zero.

This lesson works the four strategies by hand on a four-token distribution, then implements an inverse-CDF sampler with a loop and an exhaustive best-sequence search as references, the vectorised sampler with temperature, top-k and top-p, a batched top-p for many rows, and beam search with length normalisation. The tests check the hand numbers, sampled frequencies, the greedy trap against beam and exhaustive search, the length bias, the underflow trap and the prefilter's equivalence. The drill adds min-p sampling.
primer:
Picture the model at one step of writing: it has just produced "The cat sat on the", and its output is a list of probabilities, one per token in its vocabulary: " mat" 0.5, " floor" 0.3, " sofa" 0.15, " moon" 0.05, and tiny amounts for the other hundred thousand tokens. Decoding answers one question: which token comes next?

The simplest answer is greedy: always take the most likely token, " mat". It is deterministic and often good for short factual answers, but over a long text it tends to repeat itself and, as the lesson shows, it can walk into a dead end: a token that looks best now can lead only to weak continuations.

The opposite answer is sampling: roll a weighted die, so " mat" comes up half the time, " floor" 30% of the time, and so on. That gives varied, natural-sounding text, but every so often the die lands in the long tail of very unlikely tokens, and one bad token can derail everything after it. Three knobs shape the die. Temperature sharpens or flattens it: below 1 the likely tokens become more likely (at 0.5, " mat" rises to 68.5%), above 1 the distribution evens out. Top-k removes all but the k most likely faces. Top-p, or nucleus sampling, removes all but the smallest set of faces whose probabilities add up to p, so the number of faces kept adapts to how confident the model is.

An everyday analogy for the three knobs: temperature is how adventurous the writer feels, top-k is a rule like "only ever consider your five favourite words", and top-p is "only consider the words that together make up 90% of your instinct". The first changes how strongly preferences are held, the other two change which options are on the table at all, and top-p's table grows when the writer is unsure and shrinks when they are certain.

Beam search takes a different approach: instead of choosing one token at a time, it keeps a handful of partial sentences, the most probable few seen so far, extends each by its best next tokens, and keeps the best few extensions. It explores alternatives that greedy would discard, so it finds higher-probability sentences, which suits tasks with one correct output, such as translation or extraction. Its cost is that every hypothesis needs its own forward pass and KV cache, so a beam of four costs about four times as much as greedy decoding.

Where the "most probable is best" intuition breaks: for open-ended writing, the most probable text is often not the best text. Human writing regularly uses less likely, more informative words; the highest-probability continuation tends to be generic and repetitive. That is why chat models sample with moderate temperature and top-p, and reserve greedy and beam search for tasks where there is a right answer.
body:
1. The problem as it is usually asked

"Given a function that returns next-token logits, implement greedy decoding, sampling with temperature, top-k and top-p, and beam search." Clarify: is the input logits or probabilities (logits, usually); how should temperature 0 behave (as greedy); are top-k and top-p combined (yes, top-k first, as Hugging Face does); does beam search need length normalisation and end-of-sequence handling (yes); is batching needed. Then outline: a single sample_next with the three knobs, a batched top-p, beam search over log-probabilities, and tests with known distributions.

2. The maths in plain words

Temperature. Divide each logit by T, then softmax. Because probabilities are exponentials of logits, dividing logits by T raises each probability to the power 1/T before renormalising. T = 0.5 squares them (the gaps widen), T = 2 takes square roots (the gaps shrink).

Top-k. Find the k-th largest logit and set every smaller logit to −∞, so their probability becomes 0; softmax renormalises the rest. Ties at the k-th value all survive, which is a harmless detail worth knowing.

Top-p. Sort the probabilities in decreasing order and add them up. Keep tokens until the running total reaches p; keep that last token too, since it is the one that brings the total to p. Equivalently, keep each token whose probability mass before it in sorted order is below p; that rule always keeps the most likely token. Renormalise the kept probabilities and sample.

Beam search. Keep a list of up to b hypotheses, each a partial sequence with a score equal to the sum of the log-probabilities of its tokens. At each step, extend every live hypothesis by its best b next tokens, pool the extensions, move any that ended with the end-of-sequence token to a finished list, and keep the best b of the rest. At the end, choose the finished hypothesis with the best length-normalised score.

3. The equations

temperature:   p_T(i) = exp(z_i / T) / Σ_j exp(z_j / T)  ∝ p(i)^(1/T);    T = 0 → argmax
top-k:         keep i if z_i ≥ z_(k) (the k-th largest);  renormalise
top-p:         sort p descending: p_(1) ≥ p_(2) ≥ …;  keep (j) while Σ_{m<j} p_(m) < p;  renormalise
sampling:      draw u ~ Uniform[0, 1); return the first i with cumsum(p)_i > u

beam search:   score(y_1..y_t) = Σ_{s≤t} log p(y_s | y_<s)
               keep the b best hypotheses at every step; finished ones leave the beam
               final choice: argmax score(Y) / lp(Y),   lp(Y) = ((5 + |Y|) / 6)^α     (GNMT)

Two remarks. The log-sum form of the beam score is not a nicety: multiplying 400 probabilities of 0.01 gives 10⁻⁸⁰⁰, which underflows to exactly 0 in float64, and every hypothesis would tie (the test shows it). And the length penalty changes which hypothesis wins, not just its score: without it, every extra token adds a negative log-probability, so shorter outputs always look better.

4. A worked example by hand

Take next-token probabilities [0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05] (logits are their logarithms).

  • Temperature 0.5. Square and renormalise: 0.25, 0.09, 0.0225, 0.0025, sum 0.365, giving [0.685, 0.247, 0.062, 0.007]. The top token went from 50% to 68.5%; the last from 5% to under 1%.
  • Temperature 2. Square roots: 0.707, 0.548, 0.387, 0.224, sum 1.866, giving [0.379, 0.294, 0.208, 0.120]. The distribution is much flatter.
  • Top-k = 2. Keep 0.5 and 0.3; renormalise by 0.8: [0.625, 0.375, 0, 0].
  • Top-p = 0.75. Cumulative sums 0.5, 0.8, 0.95, 1.0. The mass before token 0 is 0 and before token 1 is 0.5, both below 0.75; before token 2 it is 0.8, not below. Keep tokens 0 and 1: the same [0.625, 0.375].
  • Top-p = 0.9. The mass before token 2 is 0.8 < 0.9, so it is kept; before token 3 it is 0.95. Keep three tokens.

Now the beam-search example. A toy model starts at BOS. Its first step offers A with 0.6 and B with 0.4. After A, the best options are X or Y at 0.35 each, or stopping (EOS) at 0.3; after B, X has 0.95. After X, the model always stops.

  • Greedy takes A (0.6), then X (0.35, the first of the tied pair), then EOS (1.0): probability 0.6 × 0.35 = 0.21.
  • Beam width 2 keeps both A (log 0.6) and B (log 0.4) after step one. Step two extends A to A-X, A-Y (log 0.21 each) and A-EOS (0.18, finished), and B to B-X (log 0.38) and B-EOS (0.02, finished). The best two live hypotheses are B-X (0.38) and A-X (0.21). Step three ends both with EOS. The best finished sequence is BOS-B-X-EOS with probability 0.4 × 0.95 = 0.38.

Greedy lost because it judged A by its first step alone. Beam search kept B alive one step longer and found that its continuation was far stronger. The first block asserts these numbers.

import itertools
import math
import time
import numpy as np

# The hand-worked example: four tokens with probabilities 0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05.
p = np.array([0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05])
logits = np.log(p)
# Temperature divides the logits, so p_T ∝ p^(1/T).
p_half = p ** 2 / (p ** 2).sum()                        # T = 0.5 sharpens
p_two = p ** 0.5 / (p ** 0.5).sum()                     # T = 2 flattens
assert np.allclose(p_half, [0.6849, 0.2466, 0.0616, 0.0068], atol=1e-4)
assert np.allclose(p_two, [0.3790, 0.2936, 0.2076, 0.1199], atol=1e-4)
# Top-k = 2 keeps tokens 0 and 1 and renormalises: 0.5/0.8, 0.3/0.8.
assert np.allclose(np.r_[p[:2] / p[:2].sum(), 0, 0], [0.625, 0.375, 0, 0])
# Top-p = 0.75: cumulative 0.5, 0.8, ... -> the smallest prefix reaching 0.75 is {0, 1}.
assert np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(p), 0.75) == 1
# Top-p = 0.9 needs three tokens (0.5 + 0.3 + 0.15 = 0.95 >= 0.9).
assert np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(p), 0.9) == 2
# Greedy versus beam on a two-step model: A (0.6) then best 0.35 = 0.21; B (0.4) then 0.95 = 0.38.
assert math.isclose(0.6 * 0.35, 0.21) and math.isclose(0.4 * 0.95, 0.38)

5. The naive implementations

Two references, written for clarity rather than speed. sample_naive draws by walking the cumulative probabilities until they pass a uniform number u, the inverse-CDF method that every sampler implements underneath. best_sequence_exhaustive scores every possible sequence up to a maximum length and returns the most probable one that ends with EOS: correct by construction, and exponential in length, which is exactly why beam search exists.

def sample_naive(probs, u):
    """Inverse-CDF sampling with a loop: walk the cumulative sum until it passes u in [0, 1)."""
    total = 0.0
    for i, pi in enumerate(probs):
        total += pi
        if u < total:
            return i
    return len(probs) - 1                               # guard against rounding at the very end

def best_sequence_exhaustive(next_logprobs, bos, eos, vocab, max_len):
    """Score every sequence up to max_len tokens; the true highest-probability completed sequence."""
    best, best_lp = None, -np.inf
    for L in range(1, max_len + 1):
        for body in itertools.product(range(vocab), repeat=L):
            seq, lp = [bos], 0.0
            for tok in body:
                lp += next_logprobs(seq)[tok]; seq = seq + [tok]
                if tok == eos:
                    break
            if seq[-1] == eos and len(seq) == L + 1 and lp > best_lp:
                best, best_lp = seq, lp
    return best, best_lp

Exhaustive search over a vocabulary of 6 and lengths up to 3 enumerates 6 + 36 + 216 sequences; over a real vocabulary of 100,000 and a sentence of 20 tokens it would be 10¹⁰⁰. It is useful only as ground truth on toy models, which is how the tests use it.

6. The vectorised implementations

def sample_next(logits, temperature=1.0, top_k=0, top_p=1.0, rng=None):
    logits = np.asarray(logits, float)
    if temperature == 0:
        return int(logits.argmax())                          # greedy
    z = logits / temperature
    if top_k:
        kth = np.sort(z)[-top_k]
        z = np.where(z < kth, -np.inf, z)                     # keep the k largest (ties at the edge survive)
    p = np.exp(z - z.max()); p /= p.sum()
    if top_p < 1.0:
        order = np.argsort(-p)
        cum = np.cumsum(p[order])
        keep = order[:np.searchsorted(cum, top_p) + 1]        # smallest prefix with mass >= top_p
        mask = np.zeros(len(p), bool); mask[keep] = True
        p = np.where(mask, p, 0.0); p /= p.sum()
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    return int(rng.choice(len(p), p=p))

def filtered_probs_batch(logits, temperature=1.0, top_p=1.0):
    """Temperature + top-p for a whole batch (B, V) at once: sort each row, cut, scatter back."""
    z = np.asarray(logits, float) / temperature
    p = np.exp(z - z.max(-1, keepdims=True)); p /= p.sum(-1, keepdims=True)
    order = np.argsort(-p, axis=-1)
    sp = np.take_along_axis(p, order, -1)
    cum = np.cumsum(sp, -1)
    keep_sorted = (cum - sp) < top_p                          # keep while the mass before it is < top_p
    keep = np.zeros_like(keep_sorted)
    np.put_along_axis(keep, order, keep_sorted, -1)
    p = np.where(keep, p, 0.0)
    return p / p.sum(-1, keepdims=True)

def beam_search(next_logprobs, bos, eos, beam=3, max_len=10, alpha=0.6):
    """next_logprobs(seq) -> log-probabilities over the vocabulary for the next token."""
    live, finished = [([bos], 0.0)], []
    for _ in range(max_len):
        candidates = []
        for seq, score in live:
            lp = next_logprobs(seq)
            for tok in np.argsort(-lp)[:beam]:               # only the top `beam` extensions can survive
                candidates.append((seq + [int(tok)], score + float(lp[tok])))
        candidates.sort(key=lambda c: -c[1])
        live = []
        for seq, score in candidates:
            if seq[-1] == eos:
                finished.append((seq, score))
            elif len(live) < beam:
                live.append((seq, score))
        if not live:
            break
    finished += live                                          # unfinished beams at max_len still count
    length_penalty = lambda c: ((5 + len(c[0])) / 6) ** alpha
    return max(finished, key=lambda c: c[1] / length_penalty(c))

sample_next handles one row: greedy for T = 0; temperature by division; top-k by masking every logit below the k-th largest to −∞; a stable softmax; top-p by sorting, taking cumulative sums, and keeping the prefix found with searchsorted (the index of the first cumulative sum reaching p, plus one); then a draw with rng.choice, which uses the same inverse-CDF idea as the naive version.

filtered_probs_batch applies temperature and top-p to every row of a (B, V) matrix at once: softmax per row, argsort each row descending, gather the sorted probabilities, compute cumulative sums, mark entries whose preceding mass is below p, and scatter the marks back to vocabulary order with put_along_axis. That is the shape of the operation inside a serving engine, which samples for every sequence in the batch at each decode step.

beam_search keeps live hypotheses as (sequence, summed log-probability). For each, it takes the top b next tokens (no other extension can enter the next beam), pools and sorts the candidates, moves EOS-terminated ones to finished, and keeps the best b others. Unfinished hypotheses at the length limit are added to the finished pool. Without that line, a search that never produces an end token would return nothing; with it, the best partial output is still available, which is the behaviour users expect when a maximum length is reached. The winner maximises score divided by the GNMT length penalty ((5 + |Y|)/6)^α; α = 0 disables it.

Drawing the samples for a batch

Filtering gives a probability matrix; the draw itself is also vectorisable. For each row, take one uniform number u in [0, 1), compute the row's cumulative sums, and pick the first index whose cumulative sum exceeds u: (np.cumsum(P, -1) > u[:, None]).argmax(-1). That is the inverse-CDF method of the naive sampler, done for all rows at once, and the test confirms the loop and searchsorted agree draw for draw on shared uniforms. Two cautions: rounding can leave a row's final cumulative sum a hair below 1, so a uniform very close to 1 must still map to the last non-zero token (clip the index or renormalise first); and each row needs its own uniform, ideally from a per-request generator, so that one user's output does not depend on another's.

Repetition penalties, worked

Serving APIs usually offer penalties that act on the logits before temperature and truncation. A frequency penalty subtracts a constant times the number of times a token has already appeared; a presence penalty subtracts a constant once if it has appeared at all. With logits [2.0, 1.0, 0.5] and token 0 already used twice, a frequency penalty of 0.5 lowers its logit to 1.0, tying it with token 1, so its probability falls from 0.63 to 0.38. The multiplicative "repetition penalty" of the CTRL paper divides positive logits (and multiplies negative ones) by a factor such as 1.2. Penalties reduce loops but also discourage legitimate repetition (a variable name in code, a person's name in a story), so they are tuned per use case and usually left off for code. They are applied before temperature and truncation, so a penalised token can also fall out of the top-k or nucleus entirely, which makes their effect larger than the logit change alone suggests.

Choosing settings per task

A working rule of thumb, to be validated on your own data. Deterministic, factual or structured tasks (classification by prompt, extraction, SQL, tool arguments, short factual answers): temperature 0 or near it, with constrained decoding where a schema exists. Code generation: low temperature (0 to 0.3) for a single answer, higher (0.6 to 0.8) when generating several candidates to test and rank. Conversational answers: temperature around 0.7 with top-p 0.9 to 0.95, or min-p around 0.05 to 0.1. Creative writing: higher temperature with min-p to keep the tail in check. Translation and speech recognition: beam search with a small width (4 to 5) and a tuned length penalty. These are starting points; the right values depend on the model, because models differ in how peaked their distributions are, and a setting copied from one model to another can behave quite differently.

Decoding for evaluation

Benchmark numbers depend on decoding as much as on the model. The same model can score several points apart with greedy decoding versus sampling at temperature 0.7, and the "pass@k" metric for code generation is defined in terms of k sampled attempts. A fair comparison fixes the decoding settings, reports them, and when sampling, repeats with several seeds and reports the spread. Self-consistency, majority voting over several sampled answers, is itself a decoding strategy that trades extra samples for accuracy on reasoning tasks.

7. Testing it

The tests check: temperature 0 and top-k = 1 always return the argmax; 20,000 samples with top-p = 0.75 contain only tokens 0 and 1, with token 0 about 62.5% of the time; 20,000 samples at T = 0.5 match the hand-computed distribution to within 1.5 percentage points; the loop sampler gives exactly the same draws as searchsorted on the cumulative sums for 1,000 shared uniforms; the batched top-p keeps two tokens for the hand row, three for the uniform row and one for the confident row; entropy rises with temperature; greedy returns the 0.21 sequence while beam width 2 returns the 0.38 one, and exhaustive search confirms 0.38 is optimal; beam width 1 equals greedy; raw beam scores choose stopping immediately (0.5) over a longer answer (0.451), while α = 1 chooses the longer one; the product of 400 probabilities underflows while the log sum does not; and, on 128 peaked rows of 32,000 logits, a top-64 prefilter finds exactly the same nuclei as sorting everything.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# 1. Greedy, top-k = 1 and the hand-worked top-p frequencies.
assert sample_next(logits, temperature=0) == 0
assert all(sample_next(logits, top_k=1, rng=rng) == 0 for _ in range(50))
draws = np.array([sample_next(logits, top_p=0.75, rng=rng) for _ in range(20_000)])
assert set(np.unique(draws)) == {0, 1} and abs((draws == 0).mean() - 0.625) < 0.015
draws = np.array([sample_next(logits, temperature=0.5, rng=rng) for _ in range(20_000)])
assert np.allclose(np.bincount(draws, minlength=4) / len(draws), p_half, atol=0.015)

# 2. The loop sampler gives exactly the same draws as NumPy's choice from the same uniforms.
us = rng.random(1000)
assert [sample_naive(p_two, u) for u in us] == list(np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(p_two), us, side="right"))

# 3. The batched top-p equals the per-row rule, including ties and a confident row.
L = np.log(np.array([[0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05], [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25], [0.97, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01]]))
P = filtered_probs_batch(L, top_p=0.75)
assert np.allclose(P[0], [0.625, 0.375, 0, 0]) and (P[1] > 0).sum() == 3 and np.allclose(P[2], [1, 0, 0, 0])

# 4. Temperature changes entropy in the expected direction.
def entropy(T):
    q = np.exp(logits / T); q /= q.sum()
    return -(q * np.log(q)).sum()
assert entropy(0.5) < entropy(1.0) < entropy(2.0)

# 5. A model where greedy is a trap: 'A' looks best (0.6) but every continuation after it is weak.
BOS, A, B, X, Y, EOS = range(6)
table = {(BOS,): {A: 0.6, B: 0.4}, (BOS, A): {X: 0.35, Y: 0.35, EOS: 0.3}, (BOS, B): {X: 0.95, EOS: 0.05}}
def next_logprobs(seq):
    dist = table.get(tuple(seq), {EOS: 1.0})
    lp = np.full(6, -1e9)
    for tok, prob in dist.items():
        lp[tok] = np.log(prob)
    return lp
greedy = [BOS]
while greedy[-1] != EOS and len(greedy) < 5:
    greedy.append(int(next_logprobs(greedy).argmax()))
best_seq, best_score = beam_search(next_logprobs, BOS, EOS, beam=2, alpha=0.0)
assert greedy == [BOS, A, X, EOS] and np.isclose(np.exp(best_score), 0.4 * 0.95)
assert best_seq == [BOS, B, X, EOS]                           # 0.38 beats greedy's 0.6 * 0.35 = 0.21
# Reference: exhaustive search over every sequence agrees on the optimum.
ex_seq, ex_lp = best_sequence_exhaustive(next_logprobs, BOS, EOS, 6, 3)
assert ex_seq == best_seq and np.isclose(ex_lp, best_score)

# 6. Beam width 1 is greedy; without length normalisation beam search prefers short outputs.
assert beam_search(next_logprobs, BOS, EOS, beam=1, alpha=0.0)[0] == greedy
short = {(BOS,): {EOS: 0.5, A: 0.5}, (BOS, A): {B: 0.95, EOS: 0.05}, (BOS, A, B): {EOS: 0.95, X: 0.05}}
def lp_short(seq):
    dist = short.get(tuple(seq), {EOS: 1.0}); lp = np.full(6, -1e9)
    for t, q in dist.items():
        lp[t] = np.log(q)
    return lp
# raw log-probability: stopping at once (0.5) beats the longer answer (0.5 * 0.95 * 0.95 = 0.451) ...
assert beam_search(lp_short, BOS, EOS, beam=3, alpha=0.0)[0] == [BOS, EOS]
# ... but with the GNMT length penalty (alpha = 1) the longer answer wins
assert beam_search(lp_short, BOS, EOS, beam=3, alpha=1.0)[0] == [BOS, A, B, EOS]

# 7. Precision trap: multiplying probabilities underflows; summing log-probabilities does not.
probs = np.full(400, 0.01)
assert np.prod(probs) == 0.0 and np.isclose(np.log(probs).sum(), 400 * math.log(0.01))

# 8. Timing: both paths are dominated by sorting 32,000 probabilities per row; a top-k prefilter
#    with argpartition (keep the 64 largest, then sort only those) removes most of that cost.
big = rng.normal(size=(128, 32_000)) * 6                     # peaked, like a trained model's logits
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for row in big:
    sample_next(row, temperature=0.8, top_p=0.9, rng=rng)
t_loop = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter(); full = filtered_probs_batch(big, 0.8, 0.9); t_vec = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter()
idx = np.argpartition(-big, 64, axis=-1)[:, :64]                 # candidates: the 64 largest logits
z = big / 0.8
lse = z.max(-1, keepdims=True) + np.log(np.exp(z - z.max(-1, keepdims=True)).sum(-1, keepdims=True))
psub = np.exp(np.take_along_axis(z, idx, -1) - lse)              # true probabilities, full normaliser
ps = -np.sort(-psub, -1)
kept_pre = ((np.cumsum(ps, -1) - ps) < 0.9).sum(-1)
t_pre = time.perf_counter() - t0
kept_full = (full > 0).sum(-1)
assert (kept_full <= 64).all()                                    # here the nucleus fits in 64 tokens,
assert (kept_pre == kept_full).all()                              # so the prefilter changes nothing
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("T=0.5:", p_half.round(4), "T=2:", p_two.round(4))
    print(f"top-p for 128 x 32k: per-row {t_loop*1e3:.0f} ms, batched {t_vec*1e3:.0f} ms, top-64 prefilter {t_pre*1e3:.0f} ms; nucleus sizes {kept_full.min()}-{kept_full.max()}")

Testing a random sampler needs statistical tolerance: with 20,000 draws, a frequency of 0.625 has a standard error of about 0.0034, so a tolerance of 0.015 is more than four standard errors, which makes a false failure vanishingly rare while still catching any real bug (a wrong renormalisation changes the frequency by far more). Fixing the generator's seed makes the test deterministic as well.

8. Numerical and practical traps

Trap 1: temperature zero. Dividing by zero gives inf and NaN. Special-case T = 0 as argmax, and clamp tiny temperatures if the API allows them.

Trap 2: the top-p boundary. Keeping tokens while cumulative mass is ≤ p (instead of the mass before them being < p) can drop the token that crosses the threshold, and when p is smaller than the top token's probability it keeps nothing at all. The "mass before" rule always keeps at least the top token.

Trap 3: products of probabilities. Underflow, as shown. Sum log-probabilities, and compute them with a stable log-softmax (mc10).

Trap 4: order of filters. Applying temperature after top-p changes which tokens are in the nucleus; applying top-k after top-p is different from before. Libraries apply temperature, then top-k, then top-p; document whatever order you use.

Trap 5: sorting the whole vocabulary. A full sort of 128,000 logits per sequence per step is a noticeable cost at high throughput. Prefilter the top few hundred with argpartition, compute their true probabilities with the full log-sum-exp, and sort only those; the test confirms identical nuclei whenever the nucleus fits in the prefilter. (Renormalising within the prefilter before applying top-p would change the nucleus, which is a subtle bug.)

Trap 6: randomness per sequence. In a batch, each sequence needs its own random draws; reusing one uniform for every row correlates outputs across users.

9. Edge cases worth naming

Top-k larger than the vocabulary should keep everything; top-k of 0 conventionally means "off". Top-p of 1.0 keeps everything, but cumulative sums in float32 may end at 0.99999994, so the boundary logic must not drop the last token because of rounding; the "mass before" rule handles it. Logits containing −∞ (masked tokens, constrained decoding) are fine for softmax as long as at least one token is finite. Beam search with all hypotheses finished early stops before the length limit. A beam width larger than the number of possible continuations simply keeps fewer hypotheses, which the code handles because it slices at most b candidates per hypothesis. And an EOS token that is never produced leaves only unfinished hypotheses, which the code still ranks rather than returning nothing.

10. Complexity

Greedy is O(V) per step (an argmax). Sampling with top-k is O(V) with argpartition; top-p with a full sort is O(V log V), or O(V + K log K) with a K-candidate prefilter. Beam search with width b costs b model evaluations per step (batched as one forward pass of b sequences with b caches) plus O(b·V) to select candidates, and b times the KV-cache memory. In the test on 128 rows of 32,000 logits, per-row sorting took 212 ms, the batched sort 293 ms (the sort dominates either way on a CPU) and the top-64 prefilter 87 ms.

11. Talking through the design

In the interview: start with greedy and sampling; write temperature as division of logits with the p^(1/T) interpretation; write top-k and top-p with the precise boundary rule; then beam search over summed log-probabilities with EOS handling and a length penalty; then test with fixed distributions and the greedy-trap example. Finish with judgement: which tasks want which strategy, why beam search degenerates on open-ended text, and how decoding interacts with batching, caches and constrained output.

If the interviewer asks you to extend the code, the natural next steps are a batched sampler (filter all rows, then one inverse-CDF draw per row), a repetition penalty applied to the logits before temperature, constrained decoding through a mask, and beam search that batches its hypotheses into a single forward pass with per-hypothesis caches. Each is a small change to the functions here, and naming them shows you see decoding as part of a serving system rather than a standalone function.
deep:
Why high-probability text degenerates

Holtzman and colleagues' key observation is that natural text is not the most probable text under the model. Their Figure 2 shows the per-token probabilities of human text varying widely and often dipping low, while beam search text stays in a narrow, high-probability band and falls into repetition. Repetition is self-reinforcing: once a phrase has appeared, the model assigns higher probability to it appearing again, so maximising probability locks into loops. Their Figure 1 shows beam search (size 32) on GPT-2 Large repeating a phrase, and pure sampling producing incoherent text from the unreliable tail. Nucleus sampling cuts the tail dynamically, keeping the "nucleus" that they note ranges between one and a thousand candidates depending on the step, and they compare it with top-k = 40 and with top-k = 40 at temperature 0.7.

Length normalisation and its alternatives

Google's neural machine translation system (Wu et al., 2016) divides the log-probability by lp(Y) = (5 + |Y|)^α / (5 + 1)^α, with α around 0.6 to 0.7 tuned on development data, and adds a coverage penalty that favours translations attending to every source word. Simpler variants divide by length (α = 1) or add a per-token bonus. The point is the same: beam search optimises a score that, unnormalised, prefers short outputs, and translation quality improves when that bias is removed. Exact search with very large beams (Stahlberg and Byrne) famously finds that the single most probable translation under many models is the empty one, the extreme form of this bias.

Combining filters, and min-p

Practical samplers chain operations: repetition penalties on logits, temperature, top-k, then top-p or min-p. Min-p (the drill) keeps tokens with probability at least a fraction of the top token's probability, so its threshold scales with the model's confidence: one token survives when the top is 0.9 and the rest small, all survive when the top five are near 0.2. At high temperatures, where the flattened tail can hold enough mass to fill a top-p nucleus with junk, min-p still rejects tokens far below the top one, which is why it has become popular for creative sampling.

Constrained decoding

For structured outputs (JSON matching a schema, a function call, a regular expression), constrained decoding sets the logits of every token that would make the output invalid to −∞ before sampling. A grammar compiled into a state machine tells, at each step, which tokens are allowed; the decoder intersects that set with the model's distribution. The result always parses, and the model's preferences decide only among valid continuations. The mask is applied before temperature and truncation, using the same masking machinery as top-k.

One subtlety: masking changes the distribution the model would have chosen from, and if the grammar forces an unlikely token early, the rest of the output can suffer, because the model is now continuing text it would not have written. Good schemas leave the model room (allowing whitespace, ordering fields the way the model naturally writes them), and some systems let the model think in free text first and then produce the constrained output.

Temperature as a calibration knob

Temperature also has a statistical reading: a model's probabilities may be over- or under-confident, and dividing logits by a single fitted temperature (temperature scaling) is the standard post-hoc calibration method for classifiers. For generation it is usually treated as a creativity dial rather than fitted, but the same mathematics applies: T changes the entropy of every step's distribution without changing the ranking of tokens, which is why top-k with T is equivalent to top-k without it in which tokens are kept, but not in how often each is chosen.

Best-of-n and other sequence-level strategies

Several strategies work at the level of whole outputs instead of tokens. Best-of-n samples n completions and keeps the one a scorer prefers (a reward model, a test suite for code, or the model's own log-probability); self-consistency samples n reasoning chains and returns the most common final answer. Both cost n times the generation and often beat a single greedy answer by a wide margin on reasoning and coding tasks, which is why sampling diversity matters even when the user sees only one output. Locally typical sampling is another token-level alternative: it keeps tokens whose surprisal is close to the distribution's entropy, avoiding both the bland most-likely tokens and the incoherent tail.

Speculative decoding

Decoding is memory-bound (mc18), so a cheap draft model proposing several tokens, verified by the large model in one batched forward pass, can produce multiple tokens per expensive step. Leviathan and colleagues' acceptance rule, accept a drafted token with probability min(1, p_large/p_draft) and otherwise resample from the normalised positive part of p_large − p_draft, guarantees the output is distributed exactly as if sampled from the large model alone. It composes with temperature and top-p, applied consistently to both models' distributions.
prod:
Where decoding runs

In every generation call: the API's temperature, top_p, top_k and max_tokens parameters map directly onto this lesson's code, applied per sequence at every decode step inside the serving engine, after the logits and before the token is appended to the KV cache. Beam search runs mainly in translation, speech recognition and some extraction systems; chat and code assistants sample.

Failure modes and symptoms

Loops and repetition. Greedy or near-zero temperature on open-ended prompts, or a model that has slipped into a repetitive pattern. Fixes: sampling with top-p or min-p, frequency or presence penalties, n-gram blocking. Measure the repetition rate before and after any change. It is cheap to compute.

Incoherent or off-topic output. Temperature too high or no truncation, so tail tokens get sampled. Lower the temperature or tighten top-p; check for a bug that applies temperature twice. Also check that the logits are not being divided by temperature both in the client library and on the server.

Invalid structured output. Sampling produced JSON that does not parse. Use greedy decoding or constrained decoding for structured fields, and validate with a schema before use.

Truncated beam outputs. Translations that stop early or drop clauses: no or weak length normalisation. Tune α on held-out data.

Inconsistent evaluations. Benchmark scores vary between runs because evaluation used sampling. Evaluate with greedy decoding, or report the mean and spread over several seeds. A two-point difference between models evaluated once each at temperature 0.7 may be nothing but sampling noise.

Sampling throughput bottleneck. At very high batch sizes with large vocabularies, the sort for top-p shows up in profiles. Use a candidate prefilter or fused sampling kernels.

Safety filters bypassed by sampling. A model refuses a harmful request under greedy decoding but occasionally complies when sampled at high temperature, because the compliant continuation has small but non-zero probability. Safety evaluations should sample many times at the production settings, not test a single greedy output, and output-side classifiers should not assume the decoding is deterministic.

Parameter drift between environments. A prompt tested in a playground at temperature 0.7 is deployed with the API default of 1.0, or a client library silently applies its own top-p, and output quality changes. Make decoding parameters explicit in every call and log them with each request. Include them in the cache key for any cached responses, too.

What to monitor

Per-request decoding parameters (so quality changes can be traced to configuration), output length distribution, repetition rate (fraction of outputs with repeated n-grams), structured-output parse failure rate, and, for evaluation, the decoding settings next to every reported score.

A cost estimate

For a 128,000-token vocabulary, a softmax and full sort per sequence per step is about 128,000 × log₂(128,000) ≈ 2.2 million comparisons, against roughly 14 billion floating-point operations for the model's forward pass on one token for a 7-billion-parameter model: negligible per token, but at a batch of 256 sequences it is half a billion comparisons per step on the host or in a separate kernel, which is why serving engines fuse sampling on the GPU and prefilter candidates. Beam search with width 4 multiplies the forward-pass work and the KV cache by 4 for the same output length.

The reference for this problem

Holtzman, Buys, Du, Forbes and Choi's "The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration" (arXiv 1904.09751) is the reference for this lesson's view of decoding. It reports that "maximization-based decoding methods such as beam search lead to degeneration: output text that is bland, incoherent, or gets stuck in repetitive loops", illustrated with GPT-2 Large and beam size 32, and proposes Nucleus Sampling, defining the top-p vocabulary as the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p, so that "the size of the sampling set will adjust dynamically based on the shape of the probability distribution at each time step". Its experiments compare greedy decoding, beam search with b = 16, pure sampling, temperature 0.9, top-k = 40 and 640, top-k = 40 with temperature 0.7, and nucleus sampling with p = 0.95, using measures such as Self-BLEU and perplexity against human text. This lesson's batched top-p uses exactly that smallest-set definition, implemented as "keep while the mass before the token is below p".
myths: Temperature 0 means sampling with a very cold distribution.

Dividing by zero is undefined; implementations treat temperature 0 as greedy argmax. As T approaches 0 the softmax does approach a one-hot on the largest logit, but the code must special-case it rather than divide.
Beam search always gives better text than sampling.

Beam search finds higher-probability sequences, which for open-ended generation are often generic and repetitive. Holtzman et al. showed beam search with GPT-2 Large degenerating into repetition, and that natural text has lower per-token probability than beam output. Beam search suits tasks with one right answer (translation, extraction); sampling suits open-ended writing.
Top-k and top-p are interchangeable knobs.

Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens whatever the distribution's shape: too many when the model is sure, too few when it is unsure. Top-p keeps the smallest set whose probability reaches p, so it adapts: one token when the top token has probability 0.97, three when the probabilities are equal (the test checks both).
Greedy decoding returns the most likely sequence.

It returns a sequence of locally most likely tokens. In this lesson's example greedy picks A (0.6) and ends with probability 0.21, while B (0.4) leads to a sequence with probability 0.38, which beam search with width 2 finds and exhaustive search confirms.
Beam scores can be computed by multiplying probabilities.
The product of 400 probabilities of 0.01 is 10⁻⁸⁰⁰, which is exactly 0 in float64, so every long hypothesis ties. Beam search sums log-probabilities, which stay finite and preserve order.
Without length normalisation, beam search treats all lengths fairly.

Every extra token multiplies in a probability below 1, so raw scores always favour shorter outputs. In the test, stopping immediately (0.5) beats a longer answer (0.451) on raw score; with the GNMT length penalty the longer answer wins.

drill:
Work it out

Implement min-p sampling: keep only tokens whose probability is at least min_p times the top token's probability. Show how the kept set adapts between a confident and an uncertain distribution, compared with top-k = 3.

Answer 
def min_p_filter(logits, min_p=0.1, temperature=1.0):
    z = np.asarray(logits, float) / temperature
    p = np.exp(z - z.max()); p /= p.sum()
    keep = p >= min_p * p.max()
    p = np.where(keep, p, 0.0)
    return p / p.sum()

confident = np.log(np.array([0.90, 0.04, 0.03, 0.02, 0.01]))
uncertain = np.log(np.array([0.22, 0.21, 0.20, 0.19, 0.18]))
assert (min_p_filter(confident) > 0).sum() == 1             # only the obvious token survives
assert (min_p_filter(uncertain) > 0).sum() == 5             # every plausible option survives
# top-k = 3 keeps three either way: two junk tokens when confident, drops two good ones when unsure

Min-p's threshold is relative to the model's own confidence, so the candidate set shrinks to one when the model is sure and stays wide when it is not. Top-k keeps a fixed count regardless. Top-p also adapts, but at high temperature it admits a long tail of junk because the tail's cumulative mass grows; min-p's rule keeps rejecting tokens far below the top one, which is why it holds up better for creative high-temperature sampling.
qa: E
What does temperature do, mathematically?

It divides the logits by T before the softmax, so each probability becomes proportional to p^(1/T). T below 1 exaggerates differences (the top token gains mass), T above 1 shrinks them (the distribution flattens), and T = 0 is implemented as argmax. On [0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05], T = 0.5 gives [0.685, 0.247, 0.062, 0.007].
E
Explain top-k and top-p sampling.

Top-k sorts by probability, keeps the k highest, renormalises and samples. Top-p sorts, takes the shortest prefix whose cumulative probability reaches p, renormalises and samples. With probabilities [0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05], top-k = 2 and top-p = 0.75 both keep the first two, renormalised to [0.625, 0.375]; top-p = 0.9 keeps three.
E
When would you use greedy decoding?

When you want the single most likely answer and determinism: classification-style prompts, short factual answers, extraction, tool-call arguments, evaluation runs that must be reproducible. It is fast and needs no randomness, but in long open-ended text it tends to repeat itself.
M
Why does top-p adapt better than top-k?

Top-k uses a fixed count. When the model is confident (0.97 on one token), top-k = 3 still admits two junk tokens; when it is uncertain (four tokens at 0.25), it may cut plausible options. Top-p's set grows and shrinks with the distribution: one token in the confident case, three or four in the uncertain one.

Follow-up: what problem does top-p have at high temperature? — Flattening grows the tail's cumulative mass, so the nucleus admits many unlikely tokens; min-p, which keeps tokens above a fraction of the top probability, holds up better.
M
Walk through the greedy trap in this lesson's toy model.

From BOS, A has probability 0.6 and B 0.4, so greedy takes A. After A, the best continuation has 0.35 and the path ends with total 0.6 × 0.35 = 0.21. After B, X has 0.95, so BOS-B-X-EOS has 0.4 × 0.95 = 0.38. Beam search with width 2 keeps B alive after step one and finds 0.38; exhaustive search over every sequence confirms it is optimal.
M
Implement top-p for a batch of logits without a Python loop over rows.

Softmax each row, argsort descending, gather the sorted probabilities, take cumulative sums, keep entries where the cumulative mass before them is below p (that always keeps the top token), scatter the boolean mask back with put_along_axis, zero the rest and renormalise. Then sample each row, for example by comparing uniforms with each row's cumulative sum.

Follow-up: how do you avoid sorting 128,000 logits per row? — Pre-select candidates with argpartition (top 64 or so), compute their true probabilities with the full log-sum-exp, and sort only those; the test confirms identical nuclei when the nucleus fits.
M
Why does beam search need length normalisation?

Each token adds a negative log-probability, so longer hypotheses always score lower, and the search stops early. Dividing by a length penalty such as ((5 + |Y|)/6)^α (Google's GNMT, α around 0.6-0.7) removes most of that bias. In the test, raw scores pick stopping immediately (0.5 over 0.451) and α = 1 picks the longer answer.
M
How do you make sampled generation reproducible?

Fix the random seed per request, use the same filtering parameters and the same numerical precision, and avoid batch-dependent kernels; even then, GPU non-determinism in matrix multiplication can change logits slightly and flip a sample. For strict reproducibility in evaluation, use greedy decoding or log the sampled tokens.
H
Why does maximum-likelihood decoding degenerate on open-ended text?

Holtzman et al. show that human text is not the highest-probability text under the model: its per-token probability varies and is often low, while beam search output sits in a narrow high-probability band and falls into repetition loops, because once a phrase repeats the model assigns high probability to repeating it again. Truncated sampling avoids both the bland mode and the incoherent tail.
H
How do beam search and the KV cache interact?

Each hypothesis needs its own cache. When beams are pruned and re-ranked, the surviving hypotheses' caches must be reordered (gathered by index), and when two beams share a prefix, their caches share those blocks. Paged caches make this cheap: forking a beam copies a block table, not the cache itself (copy-on-write).
H
What decoding settings would you use for code generation, chat and structured JSON output?

Code: low temperature (0-0.3), possibly several samples ranked by tests. Chat: moderate temperature (0.7-1.0) with top-p 0.9-0.95 or min-p. JSON or tool arguments: greedy or very low temperature plus constrained decoding, which masks every token that would make the output invalid according to a grammar, so the result always parses.
H
What is speculative decoding and does it change the output distribution?

A small draft model proposes several tokens; the large model scores them all in one forward pass and accepts each with probability min(1, p_large/p_draft), resampling from an adjusted distribution at the first rejection. The accepted tokens are distributed exactly as if sampled from the large model, so quality is unchanged while several tokens can be produced per large-model step.
H
Your chat model loops ('I'm sorry, I'm sorry, ...') in production. What decoding-side fixes would you try?

Check the temperature is not near zero and top-p not tiny for chat; add a repetition or frequency penalty that lowers the logits of recent tokens; use min-p or nucleus sampling instead of greedy; cap n-gram repeats; and examine whether the loop starts after a long context or a specific prompt pattern, which points to a model or prompt issue rather than decoding.
refs: Holtzman et al. (2019), The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration

The reference for this problem: beam search (size 32) degenerates into repetition with GPT-2 Large, natural text has lower per-token probability than beam output, and nucleus sampling picks the smallest top-p set; the comparison includes top-k = 40 and nucleus p = 0.95.
Greedy, beam search, sampling with temperature, top-k and top-p, and their parameters in practice.
Wu et al. (2016), Google's Neural Machine Translation System
Beam search with the length penalty lp(Y) = (5 + |Y|)^α / (5 + 1)^α and a coverage penalty.
Truncation relative to the top token's probability, robust at high temperature.
Leviathan, Kalman & Matias (2022), Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
