mc20
A sequence's log-probability is the sum of its tokens' log-probabilities under the model.
why:
A supervised fine-tuned model writes reasonable answers, but people prefer some answers over others: clearer, safer, more helpful. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) turns those preferences into training: fit a reward model to pairs of responses where a person picked one over the other, then optimise the language model to maximise that reward while staying close to the original model, using a reinforcement learning algorithm such as PPO. It works, and it is complicated: a second model to train, sampling from the policy during training, a value function, many hyperparameters, and instabilities.

Direct preference optimisation, published by Rafailov and colleagues in 2023, removes most of that machinery. It shows that the optimum of the KL-regularised RLHF objective defines a reward implicitly in terms of the policy itself — β times the log-ratio of the policy's and the reference model's probabilities — so the preference likelihood can be written and maximised directly. The result is a loss you could explain on one line: for each pair, compute how much the policy has raised the chosen response's log-probability relative to the reference, minus the same for the rejected response, scale by β, and take −log σ of that. Training looks like supervised learning on pairs.

The interview version asks you to implement that loss and its gradient from scratch and to show it behaves as claimed. That tests sequence log-probabilities, numerical stability (log σ of a large negative number overflows if written naively), deriving a gradient through a sigmoid and a softmax, and checking it. This lesson works the loss and a gradient step by hand on a three-token policy; implements a loop version and a vectorised version on a toy policy over 8 prompts and 5-token responses; checks them against each other, finite differences and PyTorch autograd; and trains for 300 steps to show the loss falling from log 2 to 0.15, the margin growing from 0 to 1.9, preference accuracy reaching 100%, and a larger β keeping the policy measurably closer to the reference.
primer:
The analogy: a tutor adjusting a student's habits relative to a baseline

A writing tutor has a student who already writes competently — the baseline. The tutor is shown pairs of the student's drafts for the same assignment and told which one readers preferred. The tutor does not grade drafts on an absolute scale. Instead, for each pair, the tutor asks: compared with the student's old habits, has the student become more inclined to write the preferred draft and less inclined to write the other? If yes, little to do. If the student has drifted the wrong way, a strong correction. And the tutor is cautious about changing the student too much at once — a student who abandons all their old habits to chase reader preferences tends to start writing oddly.

The student's current habits are the policy πθ; the old habits are the frozen reference πref; "more inclined than before" is the log-ratio log πθ(y) − log πref(y); comparing the preferred draft's change with the other's is the margin; "strong correction when wrong, little when right" is the gradient weight σ(−z); and the caution about changing too much is β.

The analogy breaks in one technical way: the student's "inclination" to write a draft is a product of word-by-word probabilities, so the log-ratio is a sum over every token of the response. That is why sequence log-probabilities, not single-token ones, sit at the centre of the implementation.

Where DPO sits in the training pipeline

A modern assistant model is typically built in stages: pre-training on large text corpora, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on demonstrations of good responses, and then preference tuning on pairs where one response was judged better. Preference tuning is where RLHF — reinforcement learning from human feedback, usually with the PPO (proximal policy optimisation) algorithm — or DPO comes in. The SFT model plays two roles in DPO: it is the starting point of the policy and, frozen, the reference. Everything DPO learns is expressed relative to it, which is why the reference is not an implementation detail but part of the objective.

From the loss to the gradient, in one picture

Everything in DPO flows from one scalar per pair, the margin z. The loss is a fixed function of z; the gradient with respect to z is σ(z) − 1; and z depends on the policy only through the two sequence log-probabilities. So the implementation has three layers — sequence log-probabilities, the margin, the sigmoid — and the gradient runs back through them in reverse. The figure shows the chain, and where the reference enters as constants.
body:
1. The problem as it is usually asked

"Implement the DPO loss in NumPy for a batch of preference pairs, given a policy and a reference model. Derive and implement its gradient, verify it, and show a few training steps improve the preference margin." Clarify: what the model is (here a toy policy whose logits are a table indexed by prompt and position, so the gradient is easy to state; with a real transformer the same loss sits on top of autograd); how sequence log-probabilities are formed (sum over response tokens); β (0.1 by default); averaging (mean over pairs). Outline: hand example, stable log-sigmoid, loop implementation, vectorised implementation, tests and a short training run.

2. The maths in plain words

For each response, ask how much more (or less) likely the policy makes it than the reference does, in log terms: the log-ratio. Multiply by β to get the response's implicit reward. The margin is the chosen response's implicit reward minus the rejected response's. Pass the margin through a sigmoid to get the probability that the chosen response is preferred under the Bradley-Terry model, and take the negative log: that is the loss. It is zero only in the limit of an infinitely large margin and equals log 2 when the margin is zero.

The gradient falls out of the chain rule. The loss's slope with respect to the margin is σ(z) − 1: close to −1 when the margin is very negative (the pair is badly misordered), close to 0 when it is large and positive (already right). The margin rises one-for-one (times β) with the chosen response's log-probability and falls with the rejected's. And a response's log-probability, for a softmax model, has the familiar gradient at each position: one-hot of the actual token minus the probabilities.

3. The equations

sequence log-prob:  log π(y | x) = Σ_t log softmax(logits_t)[y_t]           (sum over response tokens)
log-ratios:         ρ_w = log π_θ(y_w|x) − log π_ref(y_w|x),   ρ_l = log π_θ(y_l|x) − log π_ref(y_l|x)
implicit rewards:   r̂_w = β·ρ_w,   r̂_l = β·ρ_l
margin:             z = r̂_w − r̂_l = β·(ρ_w − ρ_l)
loss:               L = −log σ(z) = softplus(−z)        (mean over pairs)
stable:             log σ(z) = min(z, 0) − log1p(exp(−|z|))

gradient:           dL/dz = σ(z) − 1 = −σ(−z)
                    ∇_θ L = −β·σ(−z)·(∇_θ log π_θ(y_w|x) − ∇_θ log π_θ(y_l|x))
softmax policy:     ∂ log π(y|x) / ∂ logits_t = onehot(y_t) − softmax(logits_t)
toy policy here:    logits_t = θ[x, t]   ⇒   ∂z/∂θ[x, t] = β·(onehot(y_w,t) − onehot(y_l,t))   (softmax terms cancel)

4. A worked example by hand

The loss. β = 0.1. A pair whose chosen response has log-probability −5.0 and rejected −4.0 under the reference (the rejected one was more likely to begin with). At the start the policy equals the reference: both log-ratios are 0, z = 0, σ(0) = 0.5, and L = −log 0.5 = 0.6931 = log 2. After some training, suppose the policy gives the chosen response −4.5 (up 0.5 nats) and the rejected one −4.5 (down 0.5 nats): ρw = +0.5, ρl = −0.5, implicit rewards +0.05 and −0.05, z = 0.1 × (0.5 − (−0.5)) = 0.1, and L = log(1 + e−0.1) = 0.6444. Notice that the rejected response is still exactly as likely as the chosen one in absolute terms; the loss rewards the change relative to the reference, not absolute probability.

A gradient step. A one-position policy over 3 tokens with logits θ = [0, 0, 0], so π = [1/3, 1/3, 1/3]; the reference is the same. Chosen token 0, rejected token 1. The gradient of log π(0) with respect to θ is e0 − π = [2/3, −1/3, −1/3]; of log π(1), [−1/3, 2/3, −1/3]. Their difference is [1, −1, 0] — the probabilities cancel. At z = 0, dL/dz = σ(0) − 1 = −0.5, so ∇L = −0.5 × 0.1 × [1, −1, 0] = [−0.05, 0.05, 0]. A gradient-descent step with learning rate 1 gives θ = [0.05, −0.05, 0]. Now log π(0) − log π(1) = θ0 − θ1 = 0.1 (the normaliser cancels), and since the reference difference is 0, z = 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01; the loss falls to log(1 + e−0.01) = 0.68816. Token 2, not involved in the pair, was untouched.

import math
import numpy as np

# The hand-worked example. Sequence log-probabilities under the policy and the frozen reference.
beta = 0.1
def dpo_from_logps(pw, pl, rw, rl, beta):
    z = beta * ((pw - rw) - (pl - rl))                      # margin of implicit rewards
    return z, math.log1p(math.exp(-z))                       # loss = -log sigmoid(z) = softplus(-z)
z0, L0 = dpo_from_logps(-5.0, -4.0, -5.0, -4.0, beta)        # policy == reference
assert z0 == 0.0 and abs(L0 - math.log(2)) < 1e-12           # 0.6931: the loss starts at log 2
z1, L1 = dpo_from_logps(-4.5, -4.5, -5.0, -4.0, beta)        # chosen up 0.5 nats, rejected down 0.5
assert abs(z1 - 0.1) < 1e-12 and round(L1, 4) == 0.6444
r_w, r_l = beta * (-4.5 + 5.0), beta * (-4.5 + 4.0)          # implicit rewards beta * log(pi / pi_ref)
assert np.allclose([r_w, r_l], [0.05, -0.05])

# Gradient by hand for a one-position policy over 3 tokens, logits theta = [0, 0, 0], y_w = 0, y_l = 1.
theta = np.zeros(3); pi = np.exp(theta) / np.exp(theta).sum()  # [1/3, 1/3, 1/3]
g_w = np.eye(3)[0] - pi                                       # d log pi(y_w) / d theta = onehot - softmax
g_l = np.eye(3)[1] - pi
sig = lambda t: 1 / (1 + math.exp(-t))
dL = (sig(0.0) - 1) * beta * (g_w - g_l)                      # dL/dz = sigma(z) - 1 = -0.5 at z = 0
assert np.allclose(g_w - g_l, [1, -1, 0]) and np.allclose(dL, [-0.05, 0.05, 0])
theta = theta - 1.0 * dL                                      # one step, learning rate 1
z2 = beta * (theta[0] - theta[1])                             # log pi(y_w) - log pi(y_l) = theta0 - theta1
assert np.isclose(z2, 0.01) and round(math.log1p(math.exp(-z2)), 5) == 0.68816

5. The naive implementation

The toy policy has a logit table θ of shape (prompts, positions, vocabulary): the probability of token v at position t of a response to prompt x is softmax(θ[x, t])[v], independent of earlier tokens. That keeps the gradient readable while preserving the two things that matter — sequence log-probabilities are sums over positions, and gradients are one-hot minus softmax. The reference is a frozen copy. The naive version computes each sequence log-probability with an explicit loop and a log-sum-exp written the risky way, then for each pair computes z, the loss with the stable log-sigmoid, and the gradient position by position.

def log_sigmoid(z):
    """Stable log(sigmoid(z)) = -softplus(-z): never exponentiates a large positive number."""
    z = np.asarray(z, dtype=float)
    return np.minimum(z, 0) - np.log1p(np.exp(-np.abs(z)))

def log_softmax(a, axis=-1):
    a = a - a.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    return a - np.log(np.exp(a).sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True))

def seq_logp_naive(theta, x, y):
    """log pi(y | x) for a toy policy: independent softmax over V tokens at each of L positions,
    with logits theta[x, t]. Summed over positions, as for a real sequence."""
    total = 0.0
    for t, tok in enumerate(y):
        logits = theta[x, t]
        total += logits[tok] - math.log(sum(math.exp(v) for v in logits))   # unstable on purpose
    return total

def dpo_naive(theta, ref, batch, beta):
    """Mean DPO loss and its gradient, one pair at a time."""
    loss, grad = 0.0, np.zeros_like(theta)
    for x, yw, yl in batch:
        z = beta * ((seq_logp_naive(theta, x, yw) - seq_logp_naive(ref, x, yw))
                    - (seq_logp_naive(theta, x, yl) - seq_logp_naive(ref, x, yl)))
        loss += -float(log_sigmoid(z))
        coef = (1 / (1 + math.exp(-z)) - 1) * beta            # dL/dz * dz/d(logp_w - logp_l)
        for t in range(len(yw)):
            p = np.exp(log_softmax(theta[x, t]))
            grad[x, t] += coef * ((np.eye(len(p))[yw[t]] - p) - (np.eye(len(p))[yl[t]] - p))
    return loss / len(batch), grad / len(batch)

6. The vectorised implementation

seq_logp indexes the logit table by each pair's prompt to get a (B, L, V) block, applies a stable log-softmax along the vocabulary, gathers each actual token's log-probability with take_along_axis, and sums over positions: one array expression per batch. dpo_loss_and_grad computes the margins for all pairs, the mean loss with the stable log-sigmoid, and the per-pair coefficient β·(σ(z) − 1)/B — computing σ(z) as exp(log σ(z)) so it inherits the stable form. The per-position gradient is (one-hot(yw) − p) − (one-hot(yl) − p), which the code writes out to mirror the derivation even though the p terms cancel. Several pairs can share a prompt, so gradients are accumulated into θ with np.add.at. The function also returns the margins, preference accuracy and the chosen and rejected implicit rewards — the quantities worth logging. kl_to_ref measures the average KL divergence between policy and reference per position.

def seq_logp(theta, X, Y):
    """Vectorised: X (B,), Y (B, L) -> (B,) sequence log-probabilities."""
    lp = log_softmax(theta[X])                                 # (B, L, V)
    return np.take_along_axis(lp, Y[..., None], axis=-1)[..., 0].sum(axis=1)

def dpo_loss_and_grad(theta, ref, X, YW, YL, beta):
    """DPO loss  -mean log sigmoid(beta * [(lp_w - ref_w) - (lp_l - ref_l)])  and d loss / d theta."""
    B, L = YW.shape
    V = theta.shape[-1]
    z = beta * ((seq_logp(theta, X, YW) - seq_logp(ref, X, YW))
                - (seq_logp(theta, X, YL) - seq_logp(ref, X, YL)))
    loss = -log_sigmoid(z).mean()
    coef = beta * (np.exp(log_sigmoid(z)) - 1) / B             # (B,) = beta * (sigma(z) - 1) / B
    p = np.exp(log_softmax(theta[X]))                          # (B, L, V)
    oh_w, oh_l = np.eye(V)[YW], np.eye(V)[YL]                  # (B, L, V)
    per_pair = coef[:, None, None] * ((oh_w - p) - (oh_l - p))   # the softmax terms cancel: oh_w - oh_l
    grad = np.zeros_like(theta)
    np.add.at(grad, X, per_pair)                               # several pairs may share a prompt
    stats = {"z": z, "acc": float((z > 0).mean()),
             "chosen_reward": beta * (seq_logp(theta, X, YW) - seq_logp(ref, X, YW)),
             "rejected_reward": beta * (seq_logp(theta, X, YL) - seq_logp(ref, X, YL))}
    return float(loss), grad, stats

def kl_to_ref(theta, ref):
    """Mean over prompts and positions of KL(pi || pi_ref) for the per-position softmaxes."""
    lp, lr = log_softmax(theta), log_softmax(ref)
    return float((np.exp(lp) * (lp - lr)).sum(axis=-1).mean())

7. Testing it

Seven checks on a batch of 64 random pairs over 8 prompts, 5 positions and 6 tokens. (1) The stable log-sigmoid equals the naive formula from −30 to 1000, returns exactly −1000 at z = −1000 where the naive one returns −inf, and exactly 0 at z = 1000. (2) At θ = reference every margin is 0 and the loss is log 2, whatever the data. (3) Away from the reference, the vectorised and naive implementations agree on loss and gradient. (4) Central finite differences at three coordinates match the analytic gradient to 10−8. (5) Gradient descent for 300 steps at β = 0.1 lowers the loss from 0.693 to about 0.152 — monotonically in this run — raises the mean margin from 0 to about 1.9, and brings preference accuracy from 0 (no margin is strictly positive at the start) to 100%. (6) The same training at β = 0.5 ends with a mean per-position KL to the reference of about 0.80 against 1.25 for β = 0.1: β is the leash. (7) If PyTorch is installed, the same loss built with torch.log_softmax, gather and logsigmoid, differentiated by autograd, matches the loss and the gradient to 10−12.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
NP, L, V, B = 8, 5, 6, 64                                      # prompts, positions, vocabulary, pairs
ref = rng.normal(scale=1.0, size=(NP, L, V))                   # the frozen SFT reference
X = rng.integers(0, NP, size=B)
YW = rng.integers(0, V, size=(B, L)); YL = rng.integers(0, V, size=(B, L))
batch = list(zip(X.tolist(), YW.tolist(), YL.tolist()))

# 1. The stable log-sigmoid matches the naive formula where that works and survives where it fails.
zs = np.array([-1000.0, -30.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 30.0, 1000.0])
with np.errstate(over="ignore", divide="ignore"):
    naive = np.log(1 / (1 + np.exp(-zs)))                       # -inf at -1000 (exp overflows)
assert np.isneginf(naive[0]) and np.allclose(log_sigmoid(zs)[1:], naive[1:])
assert log_sigmoid(-1000.0) == -1000.0 and log_sigmoid(1000.0) == 0.0

# 2. At theta = ref every margin is 0 and the loss is log 2, whatever the data.
loss0, g0, st0 = dpo_loss_and_grad(ref.copy(), ref, X, YW, YL, beta=0.1)
assert np.isclose(loss0, math.log(2)) and np.all(st0["z"] == 0)

# 3. Vectorised and naive agree (loss and gradient) away from the reference.
theta = ref + rng.normal(scale=0.3, size=ref.shape)
lv, gv, _ = dpo_loss_and_grad(theta, ref, X, YW, YL, beta=0.1)
ln, gn = dpo_naive(theta, ref, batch, beta=0.1)
assert np.isclose(lv, ln) and np.allclose(gv, gn)

# 4. Finite-difference check of the analytic gradient.
for idx in [(0, 0, 0), (3, 2, 5), (7, 4, 1)]:
    tp, tm = theta.copy(), theta.copy(); tp[idx] += 1e-6; tm[idx] -= 1e-6
    num = (dpo_loss_and_grad(tp, ref, X, YW, YL, 0.1)[0] - dpo_loss_and_grad(tm, ref, X, YW, YL, 0.1)[0]) / 2e-6
    assert abs(num - gv[idx]) < 1e-8

# 5. A few gradient steps: loss falls, the reward margin grows, preference accuracy rises.
def train(beta, steps=300, lr=20.0):
    th, hist = ref.copy(), []
    for _ in range(steps):
        loss, g, st = dpo_loss_and_grad(th, ref, X, YW, YL, beta)
        hist.append((loss, float(st["z"].mean()), st["acc"]))
        th -= lr * g
    return th, hist
th01, h01 = train(0.1)
assert h01[-1][0] < h01[0][0] - 0.2 and h01[-1][1] > h01[0][1] + 0.5 and h01[-1][2] > 0.9
assert all(a >= b - 1e-12 for a, b in zip([h[0] for h in h01], [h[0] for h in h01[1:]]))  # monotone here

# 6. beta is the leash: for the same number of steps, a larger beta stays closer to the reference.
th05, h05 = train(0.5)
assert kl_to_ref(th05, ref) < kl_to_ref(th01, ref)

# 7. Cross-check loss and gradient with PyTorch autograd, if available.
try:
    import torch
    T = torch.tensor(theta, requires_grad=True); R = torch.tensor(ref)
    Xt, Wt, Lt = torch.tensor(X), torch.tensor(YW), torch.tensor(YL)
    def lp(P, Yt):
        return torch.log_softmax(P[Xt], -1).gather(-1, Yt[..., None])[..., 0].sum(1)
    zt = 0.1 * ((lp(T, Wt) - lp(R, Wt)) - (lp(T, Lt) - lp(R, Lt)))
    lt = -torch.nn.functional.logsigmoid(zt).mean()
    lt.backward()
    assert np.isclose(lt.item(), lv) and np.allclose(T.grad.numpy(), gv, atol=1e-12)
except ImportError:
    pass
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("beta 0.1: loss %.3f -> %.3f, margin %.3f -> %.3f, acc %.2f -> %.2f" % (h01[0][0], h01[-1][0], h01[0][1], h01[-1][1], h01[0][2], h01[-1][2]))
    print("KL to reference after 300 steps: beta 0.1 -> %.3f, beta 0.5 -> %.3f" % (kl_to_ref(th01, ref), kl_to_ref(th05, ref)))

8. Numerical and practical traps

Log-sigmoid overflow. Covered above; use the stable form, also for σ(z) itself in the gradient. Summing versus averaging token log-probabilities. DPO uses the sum; averaging per token changes the objective and biases it toward length. Either way, mask prompt and padding tokens so only response tokens count. Recomputing the reference. Computing reference log-probabilities in a different precision, with a different dropout state, or after accidentally updating the reference makes the step-zero loss differ from log 2 — the first sanity check. Gradient flowing into the reference. In autograd frameworks, wrap the reference forward in a no-gradient context; otherwise memory doubles and the "frozen" model may be updated. Large margins late in training. σ(−z) → 0 so learning stalls, and in low precision z itself can be large enough to overflow naive code.

9. Edge cases worth naming

Identical chosen and rejected responses: the margin is always 0 and the gradient is 0 — such pairs only add log 2 to the loss and should be filtered. Responses of very different lengths: summed log-probabilities scale with length, so length differences dominate margins; some variants normalise by length. Ties in human labels: drop them or use a variant that models ties. Label noise: a misordered pair keeps pushing with weight near 1; robust variants smooth the target (conservative DPO).

10. Complexity

Per pair, two policy forward passes (chosen and rejected) and two reference passes, which can be precomputed once. With a transformer, cost is dominated by the forward and backward passes: about four times the forward FLOPs of SFT on the same tokens for the policy (two responses, forward and backward), plus the reference forwards, and memory for two models unless the reference log-probabilities are cached. In the toy, the loss and gradient are O(B·L·V).

11. Talking through the design

Lead with the loss on one line, explain each term (log-ratios, β, Bradley-Terry), state the step-zero value of log 2, then derive the gradient through σ and the softmax and point out the σ(−z) weighting. Implement with a stable log-sigmoid and summed, masked sequence log-probabilities; verify against finite differences and autograd; show a few steps with the margin and accuracy improving; and name what to monitor beyond the loss.
deep:
Where the loss comes from

RLHF optimises maxπ Ex, y∼π[r(x, y)] − β·KL(π(·|x) || πref(·|x)). For a fixed reward, the maximiser has a closed form: π*(y|x) = πref(y|x)·exp(r(x, y)/β)/Z(x), a reweighting of the reference by exponentiated reward. Solve for the reward: r(x, y) = β·log(π*(y|x)/πref(y|x)) + β·log Z(x). Preference data are modelled with Bradley-Terry, P(yw ≻ yl | x) = σ(r(x, yw) − r(x, yl)). Substituting, the partition function Z(x) — impossible to compute, since it sums over every possible response — appears in both rewards and cancels in the difference. What remains is σ(β·log-ratiow − β·log-ratiol), a likelihood that depends only on the policy and the reference. Maximum likelihood on the preference data, with the policy as the parameterisation, is the DPO loss.

What the margin can hide

Because only the difference of log-ratios matters, the loss is indifferent to moving both log-probabilities down together. In practice, DPO-trained models often lower the absolute likelihood of chosen responses while lowering rejected ones faster, shifting probability mass to responses outside the dataset. Sometimes that is benign; sometimes it produces verbose or off-distribution outputs. Remedies studied in the literature include adding a supervised loss on chosen responses, constraining the chosen log-probability not to fall, or alternative objectives. The practical lesson for the implementer is to log chosen and rejected log-probabilities separately from day one.

The role of β, made concrete

In the RLHF objective β weights the KL penalty: large β means "stay close to the reference". DPO inherits it: margins are β times log-ratio differences, so with larger β a given margin — and therefore a given loss — is reached with smaller changes in log-probability, after which σ(−z) is small and the gradient fades. The toy run shows the effect directly: after the same 300 steps, β = 0.5 sits at a KL of about 0.80 from the reference against 1.25 for β = 0.1. Choosing β is a trade between fitting preferences and preserving the reference's general behaviour, and it interacts with the learning rate and the number of epochs.

Variants built on the same skeleton

Many later methods change one piece of the formula while keeping the implementation shape of this lesson. IPO replaces −log σ(z) with a squared loss on the margin around a target, avoiding unbounded margins. Conservative or label-smoothed DPO mixes in the loss for the flipped label to tolerate noisy preferences. Length-normalised variants average rather than sum log-probabilities. Reference-free variants such as SimPO drop πref and use average log-probability with a target margin. lm23 compares them; implementing any of them is a small edit to dpo_loss_and_grad.

Why the softmax terms cancel, and when they do not

For the toy policy, the gradient of log π(yw) − log π(yl) with respect to position t's logits is (onehot(yw,t) − pt) − (onehot(yl,t) − pt) = onehot(yw,t) − onehot(yl,t): the probabilities cancel because both responses are scored with the same logits at that position. In a real transformer the logits at position t depend on the tokens before t, so once the two responses diverge, their contexts differ and the cancellation no longer holds exactly. The shared prefix still gets zero net gradient — identical tokens in identical contexts — which is one reason pairs that differ only in a short span produce focused, efficient updates, and pairs that differ everywhere produce diffuse ones.

Offline data and distribution shift

DPO trains on a fixed set of pairs, usually sampled from the reference or another model. As the policy changes, its own outputs drift away from the responses in the data, and the loss says nothing about responses it never sees. Online and iterative variants periodically sample new responses from the current policy, label them (with people or a judge model) and continue training, which keeps the data on the policy's distribution — at the cost of reintroducing some of RLHF's sampling machinery.
prod:
Where DPO runs

DPO and its variants are widely used for preference tuning of open models because they need only a preference dataset, a reference model and a standard training loop; libraries for fine-tuning language models provide DPO trainers built on exactly the loss in this lesson, with the reference log-probabilities computed under no-gradient or precomputed. Typical runs start from an SFT checkpoint, use β around 0.1, and train for one to a few epochs over the pairs.

Failure modes and symptoms

Loss not starting at 0.693. Cause: the reference is not the policy's initial weights, or log-probabilities are computed differently (masking, dropout, precision). Fix before anything else.

Loss falls, quality falls. Cause: both chosen and rejected log-probabilities dropping, over-fitting a small dataset, or β too small. Diagnose with separate chosen/rejected curves and KL to the reference; remedy with a larger β, fewer epochs or an SFT term.

Verbosity creep. Cause: annotators preferring longer answers, and summed log-probabilities making length a strong signal. Remedies: length-controlled data, length-normalised variants, evaluation that controls for length.

NaN losses. Cause: naive log-sigmoid or σ overflow at large margins, often in low precision. Fix: stable formulations, compute the loss in float32.

Memory blow-up. Cause: two models in memory plus two responses per example. Fix: precompute reference log-probabilities, use parameter-efficient fine-tuning (mc21) with the base as the reference.

Silent data problems. Cause: chosen and rejected swapped for a slice of the data, or duplicated pairs with opposite labels. Symptom: preference accuracy plateaus well below 100% on training data even as other pairs saturate. Fix: inspect the pairs with the most negative margins late in training; they are often mislabelled.

What to monitor and tune

Loss, mean margin, preference accuracy on training and held-out pairs, chosen and rejected implicit rewards and log-probabilities, KL to the reference on held-out prompts, response length, and periodic samples rated by a judge or people. Tune β, learning rate, epochs and data mixture; consider an SFT term when chosen log-probabilities fall.

A cost estimate

For a 7B policy and 100,000 pairs with 300-token responses and 200-token prompts: each pair needs two policy forward-and-backward passes over 500 tokens (about 6 × 7×109 × 1,000 ≈ 4.2 × 1013 FLOPs) plus two reference forwards (about 2 × 7×109 × 1,000 ≈ 1.4 × 1013), roughly 5.6 × 1013 FLOPs per pair and 5.6 × 1018 for an epoch — under an hour on eight modern accelerators at realistic utilisation. Precomputing reference log-probabilities saves a quarter of that and half the model memory.

The reference for this problem

Rafailov, Sharma, Mitchell, Ermon, Manning and Finn, "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model" (NeurIPS 2023), derive the loss from the KL-regularised objective and the Bradley-Terry model, define the implicit reward r̂θ(x, y) = β·log(πθ(y|x)/πref(y|x)), and write the gradient as −β·E[σ(r̂θ(x, yl) − r̂θ(x, yw))·(∇log π(yw|x) − ∇log π(yl|x))], noting that examples are weighted by how incorrectly the implicit reward orders them and that a naive version without this weighting can make the model degenerate. In this lesson's notation σ(r̂l − r̂w) = σ(−z).
myths: DPO needs a reward model.

DPO's point is that the optimal policy for the KL-regularised RLHF objective defines a reward implicitly — r(x, y) = β·log(π(y|x)/π_ref(y|x)) up to a term that cancels in comparisons — so the preference likelihood can be written directly in terms of the policy. Training is supervised-style: no reward model, no sampling, no reinforcement learning loop.
The reference model is optional.

The reference appears in every term: the loss compares how much the policy has moved each response's probability relative to the reference, not the raw probabilities. Removing it turns DPO into a different objective with no KL anchor, which can drift into degenerate text. The reference is frozen and its log-probabilities can be precomputed once per pair.
A lower DPO loss means the chosen responses got more likely.

The loss depends only on the margin: chosen log-ratio minus rejected log-ratio. It can fall while both log-probabilities decrease, as long as the rejected one decreases faster — an often-reported behaviour in practice. Monitor chosen and rejected log-probabilities (or implicit rewards) separately, not just the loss.
log(sigmoid(z)) is safe to compute directly.

For z = −1000, exp(1000) overflows and the result becomes −inf; in low precision this happens far earlier. The stable form min(z, 0) − log1p(exp(−|z|)) never exponentiates a large positive number, and libraries provide it (PyTorch's logsigmoid). DPO margins can reach large magnitudes late in training, so this is not academic.
β controls the learning rate.

β sets how strongly the policy is tied to the reference. In the loss, β scales the log-ratio margin; a larger β makes the sigmoid saturate after smaller changes in log-probability, so the policy stops moving sooner and stays closer to the reference. In the toy run, β = 0.5 ends at about two-thirds of β = 0.1's KL divergence from the reference.
lab:
Goal: run the solution, then vary it, break it and measure it. Python 3.12 with NumPy (the gpt_env venv); PyTorch only for the optional cross-check.

  1. Run the four blocks as one script. All assertions pass and it prints the loss, margin and accuracy before and after training, and the KL at two values of β.
  2. Vary by hand. Redo section 4's step with chosen token 2 and rejected token 0 and β = 0.5: compute the gradient and the new margin, then check with three lines of code.
  3. Break the stability. Replace log_sigmoid with the naive formula and train with β = 5 and a large learning rate until margins exceed 700. When does the loss become NaN or infinite?
  4. Remove the weighting. Replace σ(−z) in the gradient with 1 (always push chosen up, rejected down equally). Train and plot the KL to the reference: what happens?
  5. Watch the hidden quantity. Log the mean chosen and rejected log-probabilities over training. Does the chosen log-probability ever fall while the loss falls?
  6. Try IPO. Replace the loss with (z/β − 1/(2β))² (IPO's form with τ = β) and its gradient; compare margins after 300 steps.

Each run takes a second or two, so it is practical to sweep β and the learning rate and plot loss, margin and KL together. What to look for: stability matters once margins are large; without the σ(−z) weighting the policy drifts much further from the reference; and the chosen log-probability is a separate signal the loss does not protect.
recap: DPO trains a policy directly on preference pairs (prompt, chosen, rejected) without a reward model or reinforcement learning.
For each response, the log-ratio log π_θ(y|x) − log π_ref(y|x) measures how far the policy moved its probability from the frozen reference.
The implicit reward is β times that log-ratio; the margin z is the chosen implicit reward minus the rejected one.
The loss is −log σ(z), the Bradley-Terry negative log-likelihood that the chosen response is preferred; it equals log 2 ≈ 0.693 when the policy equals the reference.
log σ(z) must be computed stably as min(z, 0) − log1p(exp(−|z|)).
dL/dz = σ(z) − 1, so each pair's gradient is −β·σ(−z)·(∇log π(y_w) − ∇log π(y_l)): pairs the model already orders correctly contribute little.
For a softmax policy, ∇log π(y) with respect to logits is one-hot minus probabilities at each position; in the difference of chosen and rejected the probabilities cancel per position.
Sequence log-probabilities sum over tokens, so the gradient touches every position where the two responses differ.
Training lowers the loss and raises the margin; a larger β keeps the policy closer to the reference.
Monitor chosen and rejected log-probabilities, implicit rewards and preference accuracy, not only the loss.
glossary: The coefficient that scales the log-ratios in the DPO loss; it plays the role of the KL penalty strength in the RLHF objective.
A model of pairwise preference in which P(a preferred to b) = σ(r(a) − r(b)) for scores r.
The preferred (y_w) and dispreferred (y_l) responses in a preference pair for the same prompt.
Direct preference optimisation: training a policy on preference pairs with a classification-style loss derived from the KL-regularised RLHF objective.
Identity preference optimisation: a DPO variant that regresses the log-ratio margin towards a fixed target with a squared loss instead of using −log σ.
β·log(π_θ(y|x)/π_ref(y|x)): the reward the trained policy implicitly assigns to a response.
A measure of how one probability distribution differs from another; here, how far the policy has moved from the reference.
log π_θ(y|x) − log π_ref(y|x): the change in a response's log-probability relative to the reference.
log σ(z) = −log(1 + e^(−z)), computed stably as min(z, 0) − log1p(e^(−|z|)).
The chosen implicit reward minus the rejected one; the loss decreases as it grows.
The model being trained, π_θ, which assigns probabilities to responses.
The fraction of pairs whose margin is positive, i.e. where the policy's implicit reward orders chosen above rejected.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: fitting a reward model to preferences and optimising the policy against it with a KL penalty, usually with PPO.
The frozen model, usually the SFT checkpoint, that the policy's probabilities are compared against.
Supervised fine-tuning on demonstration responses; the SFT model is the usual starting point and reference for DPO.
log(1 + e^x); the DPO loss is softplus(−z).
drill:
Work it out

A pair has reference log-probabilities −20 (chosen) and −18 (rejected). After training, the policy gives −21 and −24. With β = 0.1: (a) compute the implicit rewards, margin, loss and dL/dz; (b) the chosen response became less likely — is this a problem for the loss, and what would you check?

Answer 
rw_d, rl_d = 0.1 * (-21 - (-20)), 0.1 * (-24 - (-18))
z_d = rw_d - rl_d
loss_d = -float(log_sigmoid(z_d))
dz_d = 1 / (1 + math.exp(-z_d)) - 1
assert np.isclose(rw_d, -0.1) and np.isclose(rl_d, -0.6) and np.isclose(z_d, 0.5)
assert round(loss_d, 4) == 0.4741 and round(dz_d, 4) == -0.3775

(a) Implicit rewards: chosen 0.1 × (−21 + 20) = −0.1, rejected 0.1 × (−24 + 18) = −0.6. Margin z = −0.1 − (−0.6) = 0.5. Loss = log(1 + e−0.5) = 0.4741, below log 2. dL/dz = σ(0.5) − 1 = −0.3775, so this pair still pushes, but with about three-quarters of the weight of a pair at z = 0. (b) The loss is satisfied — the chosen response gained relative to the rejected one — even though its own probability fell by a factor of e. That is the behaviour the margin can hide. Check the chosen log-probability trend across the dataset, the KL to the reference, and samples: if probability mass is leaving both responses for something else, add an SFT term on chosen responses, raise β, or stop earlier.
qa: E
Write the DPO loss.

For a prompt x with chosen y_w and rejected y_l: z = β·[(log π_θ(y_w|x) − log π_ref(y_w|x)) − (log π_θ(y_l|x) − log π_ref(y_l|x))] and L = −log σ(z), averaged over pairs. π_ref is frozen; log-probabilities are summed over each response's tokens.
E
What is the loss at the start of training and why?

log 2 ≈ 0.693. The policy is initialised from the reference, so every log-ratio is zero, z = 0, σ(0) = 0.5 and −log 0.5 = log 2. A loss far from 0.693 at step zero means the reference and policy are not the same model or the log-probabilities are computed differently.
E
Why compute log σ(z) stably, and how?

Directly, log(1/(1 + exp(−z))) overflows for large negative z (exp(1000) is inf) and loses precision near 0 and 1. Use log σ(z) = min(z, 0) − log1p(exp(−|z|)), which only exponentiates non-positive numbers. It returns −1000 for z = −1000 and 0 for z = 1000.
M
Derive the gradient of the DPO loss.

dL/dz = −(1 − σ(z)) = σ(z) − 1 = −σ(−z). dz/dθ = β·(∇log π_θ(y_w) − ∇log π_θ(y_l)) because the reference terms are constants. So ∇L = −β·σ(−z)·(∇log π(y_w) − ∇log π(y_l)). The weight σ(−z) is large when the policy ranks the pair wrongly (z negative) and small when it already ranks it right — the paper describes it as weighting examples by how incorrectly the implicit reward orders them.
Follow-up: What is ∇log π(y) for a softmax policy? — At each position, one-hot(y_t) minus the softmax probabilities, with respect to that position's logits; summed over positions for a sequence.
M
Work a one-step example by hand.

One position, three tokens, logits [0, 0, 0] (so π = 1/3 each), chosen token 0, rejected token 1, β = 0.1, policy = reference. z = 0, so dL/dz = −0.5. ∇log π(0) − ∇log π(1) = (e0 − π) − (e1 − π) = [1, −1, 0]. Gradient = −0.5 × 0.1 × [1, −1, 0] = [−0.05, 0.05, 0]. A step with learning rate 1 moves the logits to [0.05, −0.05, 0]; the new margin is 0.1 × (0.05 − (−0.05)) = 0.01 and the loss drops from 0.6931 to 0.6882.
M
What does β do?

It scales every log-ratio in the margin. With larger β, a smaller change in log-probabilities produces the same margin and the sigmoid saturates sooner, so gradients shrink and the policy stays closer to the reference — β plays the role of the KL penalty coefficient in RLHF. Smaller β lets the policy move further to fit preferences, with more risk of drifting into degenerate text. Values around 0.1 are a common starting point.
M
What should you log during DPO training?

The loss; the mean margin; preference accuracy (fraction of pairs with z > 0); the chosen and rejected implicit rewards (β·log-ratio) separately; the chosen and rejected log-probabilities; and some measure of distance from the reference such as the KL on held-out prompts. The separate chosen/rejected curves catch the case where the loss falls because both responses become less likely.
M
How do you compute sequence log-probabilities efficiently?

One forward pass over prompt plus response, log-softmax over the vocabulary, gather the log-probability of each actual next token, mask out prompt tokens and padding, and sum over response positions. The reference model's values are computed the same way once (they never change) and can be cached per pair.
H
Why does DPO not need a reward model? Sketch the derivation.

The KL-regularised objective max E[r(x, y)] − β·KL(π || π_ref) has the closed-form optimum π*(y|x) = π_ref(y|x)·exp(r(x, y)/β)/Z(x). Rearranged, r(x, y) = β·log(π*(y|x)/π_ref(y|x)) + β·log Z(x). Substituting into the Bradley-Terry likelihood σ(r(x, y_w) − r(x, y_l)), the intractable Z(x) cancels because both responses share the prompt. What remains is a likelihood written entirely in terms of the policy, which DPO maximises directly.

Follow-up: What assumption does this hide? — That the policy class can represent the optimal policy and that the preference data come from a Bradley-Terry model; violations show up as overfitting to the pairs or drifting off the data distribution.
H
The DPO loss is falling but evaluation quality is getting worse. What is happening?

Typical causes: the policy is lowering the probability of both chosen and rejected responses (the margin grows anyway), moving mass to responses outside the dataset; the policy is overfitting a small preference set, driving margins very large; or β is too small and the policy has drifted far from the reference. Check chosen and rejected log-probabilities separately, held-out preference accuracy, KL to the reference and samples. Remedies include a larger β, fewer epochs, adding an SFT term on chosen responses, or methods designed for this failure.
H
Why is the gradient weight σ(−z) important?

It makes DPO focus on pairs it gets wrong: a pair with a large positive margin contributes almost nothing, while a misordered pair contributes nearly β times its log-probability difference gradient. The paper reports that a variant without this weighting (an unweighted 'increase chosen, decrease rejected' objective) can make the language model degenerate. It is also why margins saturate: once most pairs are ordered confidently, the gradient shrinks.
H
How does the gradient act on tokens that both responses share?

For a softmax policy, the gradient of log π(y) at position t is one-hot(y_t) − π_t. In the chosen-minus-rejected difference, if both responses have the same token at the same position and the same context, their terms cancel exactly — shared tokens get no gradient. The update concentrates on where the responses differ. With a real transformer, contexts differ after the first divergent token, so later positions do not cancel exactly, but shared prefixes do.

The DPO loss, the implicit reward β·log(π/π_ref), and the gradient −β·E[σ(r̂(y_l) − r̂(y_w))·(∇log π(y_w) − ∇log π(y_l))] with its interpretation.
The library's stable log-sigmoid, used here to cross-check.
log(1 + x) accurate for small x — the core of a stable softplus and log-sigmoid.

t: Int8 quantisation: absmax, zero-point, scales, int8 matmul and outliers
sum: Store weights in 8 bits and multiply them without losing the model: absmax and zero-point quantisation worked by hand, per-tensor versus per-channel versus per-group scales measured as SNR, a quantised matmul that accumulates in int32 (and why int16 overflows), the zero-point expansion, the outlier features that break vector-wise int8 in large models and LLM.int8()'s mixed-precision fix, and the memory each choice saves.
prereq: lm12
Quantisation stores weights in fewer bits to cut memory and bandwidth; a 7B model is 14 GB in 16-bit and about 7 GB in 8-bit.
gpu4
Number formats: float32, float16 and bfloat16 trade range for precision; integers have a fixed, evenly spaced grid.
mc21
LoRA adapters on a frozen base; QLoRA quantises that base to 4 bits.
mc11
A layer is a matrix product y = x·W; its cost and error depend on the inner dimension being summed over.
mc16
Attention and feed-forward projections are large matrix products, which is where quantised kernels apply.
why:
A 70-billion-parameter model in 16-bit floating point is 140 GB of weights. That does not fit on one 80 GB GPU, and even where it fits, every generated token requires reading all 140 GB from memory — the bottleneck of decoding. Storing the weights in 8 bits halves both problems; 4 bits quarters them. That is why quantisation is one of the first things done to a model before it is served, and why "implement int8 quantisation" is a standard ML coding question: it checks whether you understand that the hard part is not rounding but choosing scales, how quantised matrix products really execute, and why large language models broke the simple methods that worked for years on smaller networks.

The simple method is absmax: divide every value in a tensor by its largest magnitude, multiply by 127, round. It works when values are well behaved. It fails when one value is much larger than the rest, because that value sets the step size for everyone. In 2022, Dettmers and colleagues showed that transformers beyond about 6.7 billion parameters systematically develop exactly such values — a handful of hidden dimensions with activations of magnitude 6 and much higher, in most layers and positions — and that 8-bit methods which ignore them degrade sharply, while their LLM.int8() method, which multiplies those few dimensions in 16-bit and everything else in int8, matched 16-bit quality up to 175 billion parameters at about half the memory.

This lesson builds the pieces from scratch in NumPy: absmax and zero-point quantisation worked by hand on a four-value vector, and the same vector with one outlier; per-tensor, per-channel and per-group scales compared by signal-to-noise ratio; a quantised matrix product that multiplies int8 values and accumulates in int32, checked against a triple-loop version and against float, plus a demonstration that an int16 accumulator overflows; the zero-point product expansion; and an LLM.int8()-style decomposition that lifts a layer with outlier features from 25 dB to 48 dB SNR. It ends with the memory each scheme saves.
primer:
The analogy: a ruler with 255 marks

Imagine measuring things with a ruler that has exactly 255 evenly spaced marks, and you may only record which mark is closest. Before measuring a set of objects you choose how long the ruler is. If all your objects are between −3 and 3 cm, a 6 cm ruler gives marks every 0.024 cm — excellent. If one object in the set is 60 cm long, the ruler must be 120 cm and the marks are almost half a centimetre apart: the 60 cm object is measured fine, and every small object is now recorded to the nearest half centimetre — 0.5 becomes 0.47, 0.1 becomes 0. You could buy one ruler per drawer (per channel), or one per small box of objects (per group), so each set gets a ruler matched to its own range. And if your objects are all positive, a ruler centred on zero wastes half its marks; sliding the ruler so its first mark sits at your smallest object (a zero point) doubles the resolution.

The 255 marks are the int8 grid; the ruler's length is set by the scale; one ruler per tensor, channel or group is granularity; sliding the ruler is the zero point; the 60 cm object is an outlier. Measuring the giant object with a separate tape measure and the rest with the fine ruler is mixed-precision decomposition.

The analogy breaks in the matrix product: a quantised layer does not just store numbers, it multiplies them and sums thousands of products. The sum is done on the integer marks — exactly — and converted back to centimetres once at the end, which is why the conversion factors (scales) must be chosen so each dot product has a single, simple one.

What quantisation buys, and where it costs

Two different resources improve. Memory: weights take half (int8) or a quarter (int4) of the space of 16-bit, so bigger models fit on fewer GPUs and more memory is left for the KV cache of long contexts and many concurrent requests. Speed: at small batch sizes, decoding time is mostly the time to read the weights, so reading half as many bytes can nearly halve the time per token — but only if the kernels stream the low-bit weights directly. The cost is error, and how much depends on choices this lesson makes explicit: which values share a scale, whether the grid is centred, and what happens to the few values that do not fit. A good quantisation recipe is mostly a good answer to those three questions.

What the interviewer is checking

Whether you can write the formulas without notes and work an example; whether you know that scale granularity, not rounding, drives error, and can show it with a measurement; whether your matmul accumulates in int32 and applies scales once per output; whether you can expand a zero-point product; and whether you can explain, with numbers, why large language models broke naive int8 and how LLM.int8() fixed it.
body:
1. The problem as it is usually asked

"Implement int8 quantisation and dequantisation for a weight matrix, symmetric and asymmetric, with per-tensor and per-channel scales. Implement a quantised matrix multiply. Measure the error. What goes wrong for large language models and how is it fixed?" Clarify: int8 range (−127…127 for symmetric so ±127 are both representable; −128…127 for asymmetric); rounding (round half to even, as NumPy does); the layout (y = x·W with W of shape (in, out), so a "channel" is an output column); how error is measured (SNR in dB). Outline: hand examples, loop versions, vectorised quantiser with three granularities, int8 matmul with int32 accumulation, zero-point expansion, outlier decomposition, tests, memory arithmetic.

2. The maths in plain words

Absmax. Find the largest absolute value; the scale is 127 divided by it, so that value maps to ±127. Multiply everything by the scale and round to the nearest integer. To get approximate values back, divide by the scale. Each value moves by at most half a step, and the step is max|x|/127.

Zero-point. Find the minimum and maximum; the step is their difference divided by 255, so the range spans all 256 integer levels. Choose the integer zero point so that the minimum maps to −128. Each value becomes round(x / step) + zero point, clipped to −128…127; to dequantise, subtract the zero point and multiply by the step.

Granularity. Compute those statistics over the whole tensor, over each output column, or over each group of consecutive weights inside a column. Finer groups fit their own ranges better and cost more scales.

Quantised matmul. If each row of X has its own scale and each column of W has its own, then each output element is a dot product between one row and one column, which shares exactly one pair of scales. So multiply the integers, add the products up in a wide integer register, and divide the total by the two scales once.

3. The equations

absmax:      s = 127 / max|x|          q = clip(round(x·s), −127, 127)          x̂ = q / s
             |x − x̂| ≤ 0.5 / s
zero-point:  Δ = (max − min) / 255     z = round(−128 − min/Δ)
             q = clip(round(x/Δ) + z, −128, 127)                              x̂ = (q − z)·Δ
granularity: per tensor: one s;  per channel: s_j per column j;  per group: s_gj per (block of g rows, column)
SNR:         10·log10( Σ x² / Σ (x − x̂)² )  dB        (≈ 6 dB per bit)

vector-wise matmul (X: n×k, row scales s_x;  W: k×m, column scales s_w):
             C_i32[i, j] = Σ_t Xq[i, t]·Wq[t, j]        (int8 × int8 → int32 accumulate)
             C[i, j] ≈ C_i32[i, j] / (s_x[i]·s_w[j])
zero points: (A − z_a)(B − z_b) = A·B − z_a·colsum(B) − z_b·rowsum(A) + K·z_a·z_b
LLM.int8():  O = {h : any |X[:, h]| ≥ 6.0}
             C ≈ X[:, O]·W[O, :] (16-bit)  +  vector-wise int8( X[:, ¬O], W[¬O, :] )
memory:      bits/weight = b + scale_bits / g          (8.125 for int8 with 16-bit scales per 128)

4. A worked example by hand

Absmax. x = [0.5, −1.2, 3.0, −0.1]. max|x| = 3.0, scale = 127/3 = 42.333. x·scale = [21.17, −50.80, 127.00, −4.23] → round → [21, −51, 127, −4]. Dequantised: [21, −51, 127, −4]/42.333 = [0.4961, −1.2047, 3.0, −0.0945]. Errors: 0.0039, 0.0047, 0, 0.0055 — all below half a step, 0.5/42.333 = 0.0118.

Zero-point. min = −1.2, max = 3.0, step = 4.2/255 = 0.016471. Zero point = round(−128 − (−1.2/0.016471)) = round(−128 + 72.86) = round(−55.14) = −55. x/step = [30.36, −72.86, 182.14, −6.07] → round [30, −73, 182, −6] → + (−55) = [−25, −128, 127, −61]: the minimum lands on −128 and the maximum on 127. Dequantised: ([−25, −128, 127, −61] + 55) × 0.016471 = [0.4941, −1.2024, 2.9976, −0.0988]. The step is 0.0165 against absmax's 0.0236, because absmax spent half its grid on values below −1.2 that never occur.

The outlier. Replace 3.0 with 60. Absmax scale = 127/60 = 2.1167, step 0.47. x·scale = [1.06, −2.54, 127, −0.21] → [1, −3, 127, 0] → dequantised [0.472, −1.417, 60, 0]. The small values now have errors of 0.03, 0.22 and 0.1 — the −0.1 has vanished — because one value set the step for all. This is the whole outlier problem in four numbers. The first block asserts all of it.

import numpy as np

# The hand-worked example: one vector, absmax (symmetric) and zero-point (asymmetric) int8.
x = np.array([0.5, -1.2, 3.0, -0.1])
s = 127 / np.abs(x).max()                                      # 127 / 3.0 = 42.333
q = np.round(x * s).astype(np.int8)
assert q.tolist() == [21, -51, 127, -4]
deq = q / s
assert np.allclose(deq, [0.49606, -1.20472, 3.0, -0.09449], atol=1e-5)

scale = (x.max() - x.min()) / 255                              # 4.2 / 255 = 0.016471
zp = int(np.round(-128 - x.min() / scale))                     # -128 + 72.86 -> -55
qz = np.clip(np.round(x / scale) + zp, -128, 127).astype(np.int8)
assert zp == -55 and qz.tolist() == [-25, -128, 127, -61]      # the full range [-128, 127] is used
deqz = (qz.astype(np.int32) - zp) * scale
assert np.allclose(deqz, [0.49412, -1.20235, 2.99765, -0.09882], atol=1e-5)

# One outlier ruins absmax for everyone else in the vector.
xo = np.array([0.5, -1.2, 60.0, -0.1])
so = 127 / 60.0
qo = np.round(xo * so)
assert qo.tolist() == [1.0, -3.0, 127.0, -0.0]                 # 0.5 -> 1 level, -0.1 -> 0
assert np.allclose(qo / so, [0.47244, -1.41732, 60.0, 0.0], atol=1e-5)

def snr_db(ref, approx):
    return 10 * np.log10((ref ** 2).sum() / ((ref - approx) ** 2).sum())

5. The naive implementation

Two loops make the definitions concrete. quant_absmax_loop finds the maximum magnitude with a Python generator and quantises element by element with Python's round (which, like np.round, rounds halves to even). matmul_int8_loop is a triple loop that multiplies int8 pairs into a Python integer "accumulator", asserts it stays within the int32 range, and divides by the row and column scales once per output element — exactly what an integer matrix-multiply unit does, one multiply-add at a time.

def quant_absmax_loop(W):
    """Per-tensor symmetric int8, element by element."""
    m = max(abs(v) for v in W.ravel())
    sc = 127.0 / m
    Q = np.empty(W.shape, dtype=np.int8)
    for i in range(W.shape[0]):
        for j in range(W.shape[1]):
            Q[i, j] = int(round(W[i, j] * sc))                  # Python round: half to even, like np.round
    return Q, sc

def matmul_int8_loop(Xq, Wq, sx, sw):
    """int8 x int8 products accumulated in an int32 'register', then dequantised once.
    sx: one scale per row of X, sw: one scale per column of W (1-D)."""
    n, k = Xq.shape
    m = Wq.shape[1]
    C = np.empty((n, m))
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(m):
            acc = 0                                             # int32 accumulator (Python int, checked below)
            for t in range(k):
                acc += int(Xq[i, t]) * int(Wq[t, j])
            assert -2 ** 31 <= acc < 2 ** 31
            C[i, j] = acc / (sx[i] * sw[j])
    return C

6. The vectorised implementation

quantize handles all granularities with one reduction: for a per-tensor scale it reduces over everything, for per-channel over the rows (axis 0, giving one scale per column), and for per-group it first reshapes the (K, N) weight into (K/g, g, N) and reduces over the middle axis, giving one scale per group per column. keepdims keeps the scales broadcastable. The symmetric branch clips to ±127; the asymmetric branch computes a step and an integer zero point per slice. dequantize reverses either, reshaping groups back. matmul_int8 casts to int32 and multiplies — NumPy's integer matmul accumulates in the operands' dtype, so the cast is what provides the int32 accumulator — then divides by the outer product of scales via broadcasting. matmul_zeropoint implements the four-term expansion. llm_int8 finds the outlier columns of X (any |value| ≥ 6.0), multiplies them with the corresponding rows of W in floating point, quantises the rest vector-wise, and adds the two parts.

def quantize(W, axis=None, group=None, symmetric=True):
    """int8 quantisation with one scale per tensor (axis=None), per slice along `axis`
    (axis=0: one scale per column), or per group of `group` consecutive rows within each column.
    Returns (q, scale, zero_point) with W ≈ (q - zp) / scale broadcastable."""
    Wv = W
    if group is not None:                                       # (K, N) -> (K//g, g, N): a scale per (group, column)
        K, N = W.shape
        Wv = W.reshape(K // group, group, N)
        red = 1
    else:
        red = axis
    if symmetric:
        m = np.abs(Wv).max(axis=red, keepdims=True)
        sc = 127.0 / np.where(m == 0, 1.0, m)
        q = np.clip(np.round(Wv * sc), -127, 127).astype(np.int8)
        zp = np.zeros_like(sc, dtype=np.int32)
    else:
        lo, hi = Wv.min(axis=red, keepdims=True), Wv.max(axis=red, keepdims=True)
        step = np.where(hi > lo, (hi - lo) / 255.0, 1.0)
        zp = np.round(-128 - lo / step).astype(np.int32)
        q = np.clip(np.round(Wv / step) + zp, -128, 127).astype(np.int8)
        sc = 1.0 / step
    return q, sc, zp

def dequantize(q, sc, zp, shape=None):
    out = (q.astype(np.int32) - zp) / sc
    return out.reshape(shape) if shape is not None else out

def matmul_int8(Xq, Wq, sx, sw):
    """Vector-wise int8 matmul: X quantised per row (sx: (n,1)), W per column (sw: (1,m)).
    Products of int8 values are accumulated in int32, then scaled by the outer product of scales."""
    acc = Xq.astype(np.int32) @ Wq.astype(np.int32)             # exact integer accumulation
    return acc / (sx * sw)

def matmul_zeropoint(Aq, za, Bq, zb):
    """(A - za)(B - zb) for zero-point tensors, expanded so the int8 x int8 product stays the core:
    A·B - za·colsum(B) - zb·rowsum(A) + K·za·zb   (per-tensor zero points)."""
    A, B = Aq.astype(np.int32), Bq.astype(np.int32)
    K = A.shape[1]
    return A @ B - za * B.sum(axis=0, keepdims=True) - zb * A.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True) + K * za * zb

def llm_int8(X, W, threshold=6.0):
    """LLM.int8()-style mixed-precision decomposition: feature columns of X holding any |value| >= threshold
    (and the matching rows of W) are multiplied in floating point; the rest in vector-wise int8."""
    outl = np.any(np.abs(X) >= threshold, axis=0)               # outlier feature dimensions
    C = X[:, outl] @ W[outl]                                    # 16-bit path in the real thing
    Xr, Wr = X[:, ~outl], W[~outl]
    Xq, sx, _ = quantize(Xr, axis=1)                            # per row of X
    Wq, sw, _ = quantize(Wr, axis=0)                            # per column of W
    return C + matmul_int8(Xq, Wq, sx, sw), int(outl.sum())

7. Testing it

Nine checks. (1) Loop and vectorised absmax produce identical integers and scale, and the round-trip error is at most half a step. (2) On a 256 × 64 matrix whose column magnitudes vary by large random factors, per-channel scales give 43.2 dB against 33.0 dB per-tensor — the per-tensor scale is set by the biggest column and starves the small ones. (3) On a 1,024 × 64 matrix with 40 weights scattered and multiplied by 25, per-group scales (128 rows per group) give 36.4 dB against per-channel's 28.0 dB: a column's outlier only ruins its own block of 128. (4) On post-ReLU activations (all ≥ 0), zero-point quantisation gives 47.0 dB against symmetric's 40.8 dB, about one extra bit. (5) The vectorised int8 matmul equals the triple loop, equals the float product of the dequantised matrices, and approximates the true product at above 30 dB; and multiplying two int16 vectors of 4,096 copies of 127 without widening wraps around, while the int32 version gives exactly 66,064,384. (6) The zero-point expansion equals multiplying the shifted integers directly. (7) A 64 × 1,024 activation matrix with four feature columns scaled up 40× (to magnitudes of tens, like the outliers in large models) times a 1,024 × 256 weight: vector-wise int8 gives 25.1 dB; the decomposition finds exactly those 4 columns (0.4% of features), multiplies them in float, and reaches 48.0 dB. (8) Bits per weight with 16-bit scales per 128 are 8.125 (int8) and 4.125 (int4); a 7B model is 14.0 GB in 16-bit and 7.11 GB in grouped int8. (9) If PyTorch is installed, its rounding gives the same per-channel integers (except rare exact-half ties) and its int32 matmul gives the same accumulated result.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# 1. Loop and vectorised quantisers agree; round-trip error is at most half a step.
W = rng.normal(size=(64, 48))
Ql, scl = quant_absmax_loop(W)
Qv, scv, _ = quantize(W)
assert np.array_equal(Ql, Qv) and np.isclose(scl, scv.item())
assert np.abs(W - dequantize(Qv, scv, 0)).max() <= 0.5 / scl + 1e-12

# 2. Per-channel scales beat a per-tensor scale when columns have different ranges.
Wc = rng.normal(size=(256, 64)) * np.exp(rng.normal(scale=1.5, size=(1, 64)))   # column scales vary a lot
q_t, s_t, z_t = quantize(Wc)
q_c, s_c, z_c = quantize(Wc, axis=0)
snr_t, snr_c = snr_db(Wc, dequantize(q_t, s_t, z_t)), snr_db(Wc, dequantize(q_c, s_c, z_c))
assert snr_c > snr_t + 3                                       # per-channel is much better here

# 3. Per-group scales (128 rows per group) beat per-channel when weights have local outliers.
Wg = rng.normal(size=(1024, 64)); Wg[rng.integers(0, 1024, 40), rng.integers(0, 64, 40)] *= 25
q_g, s_g, z_g = quantize(Wg, group=128)
q_c2, s_c2, z_c2 = quantize(Wg, axis=0)
snr_g = snr_db(Wg, dequantize(q_g, s_g, z_g, Wg.shape))
snr_c2 = snr_db(Wg, dequantize(q_c2, s_c2, z_c2))
assert snr_g > snr_c2

# 4. Asymmetric (zero-point) quantisation wins on one-sided data such as post-ReLU activations.
A = np.maximum(rng.normal(size=(128, 64)), 0)
snr_sym = snr_db(A, dequantize(*quantize(A)))
snr_asym = snr_db(A, dequantize(*quantize(A, symmetric=False)))
assert snr_asym > snr_sym + 3                                  # roughly one extra bit of resolution

# 5. int8 matmul with int32 accumulation: the loop, the vectorised version and float on the
#    dequantised values all agree; an int16 accumulator overflows at realistic sizes.
X = rng.normal(size=(8, 512)); Wm = rng.normal(size=(512, 16))
Xq, sx, _ = quantize(X, axis=1); Wq, sw, _ = quantize(Wm, axis=0)
C_vec = matmul_int8(Xq, Wq, sx, sw)
C_loop = matmul_int8_loop(Xq[:2], Wq[:, :3], sx[:2, 0], sw[0, :3])
assert np.allclose(C_vec[:2, :3], C_loop)
assert np.allclose(C_vec, dequantize(Xq, sx, 0) @ dequantize(Wq, sw, 0))
assert snr_db(X @ Wm, C_vec) > 30                              # about 1% error in a 512-long dot product
big = np.full((1, 4096), 127, dtype=np.int16)
with np.errstate(over="ignore"):
    wrapped = (big @ big.T)[0, 0]                              # NumPy integer matmul accumulates in int16
assert int(wrapped) != 127 * 127 * 4096 and (big.astype(np.int32) @ big.T.astype(np.int32))[0, 0] == 66_064_384

# 6. The zero-point product expansion equals multiplying the shifted integers directly.
Aq = rng.integers(-128, 128, size=(5, 32)).astype(np.int8); Bq = rng.integers(-128, 128, size=(32, 7)).astype(np.int8)
za, zb = -17, 9
direct = (Aq.astype(np.int32) - za) @ (Bq.astype(np.int32) - zb)
assert np.array_equal(matmul_zeropoint(Aq, za, Bq, zb), direct)

# 7. Outlier features: vector-wise int8 collapses, the mixed-precision decomposition recovers.
Xo = rng.normal(size=(64, 1024)); Wo = rng.normal(size=(1024, 256)) * 0.02
cols = rng.choice(1024, size=4, replace=False)
Xo[:, cols] *= 40                                              # a few feature dimensions with huge values
ref = Xo @ Wo
Xq_o, sx_o, _ = quantize(Xo, axis=1); Wq_o, sw_o, _ = quantize(Wo, axis=0)
snr_vec = snr_db(ref, matmul_int8(Xq_o, Wq_o, sx_o, sw_o))
C_mixed, n_out = llm_int8(Xo, Wo)
snr_mix = snr_db(ref, C_mixed)
assert n_out == 4 and snr_mix > snr_vec + 10                   # 4 of 1,024 columns (0.4%) in float

# 8. Memory: bits per weight including scale overhead.
def bits_per_weight(bits, group=None, scale_bits=16):
    return bits + (scale_bits / group if group else 0)
assert bits_per_weight(8, 128) == 8.125 and bits_per_weight(4, 128) == 4.125
params = 7e9
assert round(params * 2 / 1e9, 1) == 14.0 and round(params * bits_per_weight(8, 128) / 8 / 1e9, 2) == 7.11

# 9. Cross-check the per-channel quantiser and the int8 matmul against PyTorch, if available.
try:
    import torch
    step = torch.tensor(1.0 / s_c)                             # (1, 64): torch-style step sizes
    tq = torch.clamp(torch.round(torch.tensor(Wc) / step), -127, 127).to(torch.int8)
    assert (tq.numpy() == q_c).mean() > 0.999                  # identical except rare exact-half ties
    acc_t = torch.tensor(Xq, dtype=torch.int32) @ torch.tensor(Wq, dtype=torch.int32)
    assert np.allclose(acc_t.numpy() / (sx * sw), C_vec)
except ImportError:
    pass
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"per-tensor {snr_t:.1f} dB, per-channel {snr_c:.1f} dB; per-channel {snr_c2:.1f} vs per-group {snr_g:.1f} dB")
    print(f"post-ReLU: symmetric {snr_sym:.1f} dB, zero-point {snr_asym:.1f} dB")
    print(f"outliers: vector-wise int8 {snr_vec:.1f} dB, LLM.int8() decomposition {snr_mix:.1f} dB")

8. Numerical and practical traps

Zero scales. An all-zero channel has max|x| = 0; guard the division (the code substitutes 1). Clipping range. Symmetric quantisation should clip to ±127, not −128, so that x and −x quantise symmetrically. Rounding mode. np.round and Python's round use round-half-to-even; other libraries may round half away from zero, which changes a few integers — compare with a tolerance on agreement, not equality. Accumulator width. Never accumulate int8 products in int8 or int16. Scale precision. Store scales in at least 16-bit float; an 8-bit scale multiplies every weight's error. Calibration for activations. Activation ranges change per input; computing scales on the fly (dynamic) is accurate but costs time, while fixed scales from calibration data (static) must cover rare large values without wasting range.

9. Edge cases worth naming

Constant tensors: zero-point step is zero — handle by using step 1 and storing the constant. A single large value per channel: per-group helps only if the group is smaller than the channel. Very small matrices: scale overhead dominates; keep them in 16-bit (biases, layer norms). Embedding and output layers: often more sensitive, commonly kept at higher precision. Outlier threshold: 6.0 is the paper's value for their models; data or model families with different activation scales may need tuning.

10. Complexity

Quantising an n-element tensor is O(n) — one pass for statistics, one to scale and round. The int8 matmul is O(n·k·m) multiply-adds like any matmul, but each is an 8-bit operation that hardware performs at 2-4× the throughput of 16-bit and with half the memory traffic; dequantisation is O(n·m). The LLM.int8() decomposition adds O(n·k) to scan for outliers and a small 16-bit matmul over |O| columns. Memory: b/8 bytes per weight plus scales.
