deep:
Why outliers appear in large transformers

Dettmers et al. tracked feature dimensions with magnitude at least 6.0 that appear in at least 25% of layers and 6% of sequence positions. In their analysis these emerge as models grow — a phase change around 6.7B parameters — after which they occur in almost all layers and positions, concentrated in very few dimensions (at most 7 for models up to 13B, up to 150,000 outlier values per 2,048-token sequence in a 13B model). They are not noise: removing them hurts attention and prediction badly. Later work links such dimensions to mechanisms like attention sinks and to layer normalisation interactions. Whatever their cause, their systematic placement is what makes the fix possible: if they lived in random dimensions, a column-wise split would not isolate them.

Weight-only quantisation and on-the-fly dequantisation

For single-stream decoding, the bottleneck is reading weights, not multiplying them. Weight-only schemes keep activations in 16-bit, store weights in int8 or int4 with group scales, and dequantise each block in fast on-chip memory just before multiplying in 16-bit. Bandwidth falls by 2-4×, activation outliers are irrelevant, and the error is confined to the weights. Methods such as GPTQ (a post-training method that quantises weights column by column) choose the rounding of each weight to compensate errors in others using second-order information, and AWQ (activation-aware weight quantisation) protects the weight channels that see the largest activations; both target 4-bit weights with group sizes around 128.

Moving outliers instead of isolating them

An alternative to mixed precision is to make activations easier to quantise by moving their scale into the weights. Because y = x·W = (x·diag(1/c))·(diag(c)·W), dividing each activation channel by a factor c and multiplying the corresponding weight row by the same factor leaves the output unchanged. Choosing c to shrink outlier channels flattens the activations at the cost of making some weights larger, which weights tolerate better because they are static and can use finer scales. SmoothQuant is the best-known example; it enables int8 for both weights and activations without a 16-bit side path.

Lower than 8 bits

At 4 bits there are only 16 levels, so the distribution of levels matters. QLoRA's 4-bit NormalFloat places levels at quantiles of a normal distribution, matching how pretrained weights are distributed, with block-wise scales over 64 weights and a second quantisation of the scales themselves to save memory. Formats with floating-point structure (FP8, 8-bit floating point, in its variants, and microscaling formats that share an exponent across a small block) are increasingly supported in hardware, combining a coarse shared scale with per-element exponent bits — the same "scale per group" idea built into the number format.

Quantisation-aware training versus post-training quantisation

Everything in this lesson is post-training quantisation (PTQ): take a trained model, choose scales, round. Quantisation-aware training (QAT) instead simulates rounding during training — the forward pass uses quantised values, the backward pass treats rounding as the identity (the straight-through estimator) — so the weights learn to sit where rounding hurts least. QAT recovers more accuracy at very low bit widths but needs training compute and data, which is why PTQ dominates for large language models and QAT for small models deployed on constrained hardware. The scale formulas, granularities and int8 matmul are the same in both.

Accumulation and the dequantise-once rule

The efficiency of integer matmuls relies on applying scales once per output, not per product. That works only if every product contributing to an output shares the same pair of scales — which is why activations are scaled per row and weights per column (vector-wise), and why per-group weight scales along the inner dimension force either partial sums per group (rescaled and added in floating point) or dequantising weights to 16-bit before the multiply. Knowing which granularities are "matmul-friendly" is what separates a quantiser that saves memory from one that also saves time.
prod:
Where quantisation runs

Quantised weights are the norm for serving large language models: int8 and int4 weight-only formats in inference servers and local runtimes, LLM.int8() in the bitsandbytes library that made 8-bit loading of very large models practical, 4-bit NormalFloat for QLoRA fine-tuning, and FP8 on recent accelerators for both training and inference. Each is a choice of the knobs in this lesson: bits, granularity, symmetric or zero-point, and what to do about outliers.

Failure modes and symptoms

Quality cliff at scale. Symptom: a quantisation recipe that worked on a 1B model breaks a 13B one. Cause: emergent outlier features. Fix: outlier handling (decomposition, smoothing) or weight-only quantisation.

Specific tasks degrade. Symptom: perplexity barely moves but long-context or arithmetic tasks drop. Cause: small per-layer errors compounding, or sensitive layers. Fix: evaluate on the tasks that matter; keep sensitive layers in higher precision.

No speedup. Symptom: memory falls but latency does not. Cause: no fused low-bit kernel, so weights are dequantised into a separate buffer; or compute-bound batch sizes where weight bandwidth was not the bottleneck; or per-group scales that the kernel handles slowly. Fix: use kernels designed for the format; measure at the batch sizes you serve.

NaNs or garbage. Cause: zero scales, overflowing accumulators, or scales stored in too low a precision. Fix: guards and tests like this lesson's.

Calibration mismatch. Symptom: a statically quantised model works on benchmark prompts and degrades on production traffic. Cause: activation scales calibrated on data with smaller ranges than real inputs (different languages, long documents, code). Fix: calibrate on representative traffic, or use dynamic activation scales.

What to monitor and tune

Per-layer output SNR on calibration data; perplexity and task scores versus 16-bit with intervals; memory per GPU and tokens per second at production batch sizes; fraction of outlier dimensions (if using decomposition) and its variation across inputs. Tune bits, group size (64-128 is common), symmetric versus asymmetric per tensor type, outlier threshold, and which layers stay in higher precision.

A cost estimate

A 13B model: 16-bit weights 26 GB; int8 with per-channel scales about 13 GB; int4 with groups of 128 and 16-bit scales 13e9 × 4.125 / 8 ≈ 6.7 GB. At batch size one, decoding reads the weights once per token, so on a GPU with 2 TB/s of bandwidth the floor is about 13 ms per token in 16-bit, 6.5 ms in int8 and 3.4 ms in int4 — assuming the kernels actually stream low-bit weights rather than dequantising them through memory.

The reference for this problem

Dettmers, Lewis, Belkada and Zettlemoyer, "LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale" (NeurIPS 2022), describe absmax and zero-point int8 and the int32 accumulation of int8 products; vector-wise quantisation with a scale per row of the hidden states and per column of the weights, dequantised by the outer product of scales; and mixed-precision decomposition, in which feature dimensions containing any value of magnitude at least α = 6.0 — about 0.1% of dimensions — are multiplied in 16-bit and the rest in int8, so that more than 99.9% of values are multiplied in 8-bit. Their perplexity table shows 8-bit absmax, zero-point, row-wise and vector-wise methods degrading at 13B while LLM.int8() matches 32-bit (12.45 perplexity), and they report memory reduced 1.96× for BLOOM-176B.
myths: Quantisation just rounds every number to 8 bits.

Rounding needs a scale: int8 has 255 evenly spaced levels, so a tensor is first divided by a scale that maps its range onto those levels. The choice of scale — one per tensor, per channel or per small group, symmetric or with a zero point — decides almost all the error. Rounding is the easy part.
One outlier in a tensor costs only that value's accuracy.

With a shared scale, the largest magnitude sets the step size for every value. In the lesson's example, a single 60 among values around 1 makes the step 0.47, so 0.5 rounds to 0.47, −1.2 to −1.42 and −0.1 to 0. Large transformers have such outliers systematically in a few feature dimensions, which is why plain int8 fails beyond a few billion parameters.
Multiplying int8 matrices produces int8 results.

A dot product of length 4,096 of int8 values can reach 4,096 × 127 × 127 ≈ 66 million, far beyond int8 or int16. Hardware multiplies int8 pairs and accumulates in int32, then rescales to floating point once at the end. Accumulating in int16 silently wraps around — the test shows it.
Symmetric quantisation is always good enough.

Symmetric (absmax) quantisation centres the grid on zero. For one-sided data such as post-ReLU activations, half the grid is wasted on negative values that never occur. Zero-point (asymmetric) quantisation shifts the grid to the data's actual range, gaining roughly one bit: 47.0 versus 40.8 dB SNR on the lesson's post-ReLU data.
8-bit weights mean 8 bits per weight.

Scales must be stored too. One 16-bit scale per group of 128 weights adds 0.125 bits, so per-group int8 is 8.125 bits per weight and int4 4.125 bits. Per-channel scales are negligible for large matrices; per-tensor scales cost nothing but give the most error.
lab:
Goal: run the solution, then vary it, break it and measure it. Python 3.12 with NumPy (the gpt_env venv); PyTorch only for the optional cross-check.

  1. Run the four blocks as one script. All assertions pass and it prints the SNR comparisons.
  2. Vary by hand. Quantise [2.0, −0.4, 0.9, −1.7] with absmax and with zero-point by hand, then check with quantize(x[None, :]).
  3. Measure bits. Repeat test 2 with 4-bit symmetric quantisation (levels −7…7) and confirm the SNR drops by about 6 dB per bit removed.
  4. Vary group size. On the scattered-outlier matrix, sweep group sizes 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 and 1,024 and plot SNR against bits per weight including 16-bit scales.
  5. Move the threshold. In llm_int8, try thresholds 3, 6 and 20 on test 7's data: count outlier columns and SNR each time.
  6. Smooth instead. Divide X's columns by c = sqrt(max|X[:, h]|) and multiply W's rows by c, then quantise both vector-wise with no decomposition. Compare SNR with test 7.

All of these run in well under a second, so sweep freely and keep a small table of SNR against bits per weight for each scheme — the shape of that table is what the interview answer should convey. What to look for: 6 dB per bit; diminishing returns from smaller groups as scale overhead grows; a threshold too low sends many columns to float, too high misses outliers; and smoothing recovers much of the decomposition's benefit without a 16-bit path.
recap: Quantisation maps floating-point values to a small integer grid through a scale (and possibly a zero point), and dequantisation maps them back.
Absmax (symmetric) int8 uses scale = 127 / max|x|, q = round(x·scale), x ≈ q / scale; the rounding error is at most half a step.
Zero-point (asymmetric) int8 uses step = (max − min)/255 and a zero point so that min maps to −128 and max to 127, using the whole grid for one-sided data.
Granularity trades accuracy for overhead: per tensor (one scale), per channel (one per output column), per group (one per block of, say, 128 weights).
Error is measured as signal-to-noise ratio in decibels, 10·log10(Σx² / Σ(x − x̂)²); every 6 dB is about one bit of precision.
A quantised matmul multiplies int8 values, accumulates in int32 and rescales once by the outer product of row scales of X and column scales of W.
With zero points, (A − za)(B − zb) expands into A·B plus cheap row and column sum corrections, so the int8 product stays the core.
Large transformers develop outlier feature dimensions with huge magnitudes; a few columns destroy the precision of every row they appear in.
LLM.int8() multiplies the outlier dimensions (any value at least 6.0) in 16-bit and the other 99.9% in vector-wise int8, keeping quality at about half the memory.
Memory: 16-bit to int8 halves weight storage, int4 quarters it, plus scale overhead.
glossary: Symmetric quantisation scaling by the largest absolute value so that it maps to ±127.
The register that sums products in a dot product; for int8 inputs it is int32 to avoid overflow.
Converting integers back to approximate real values by undoing the scale and zero point.
How many values share one scale: a whole tensor, a channel (row or column), or a small group.
Splitting a matrix product so a few outlier dimensions are computed in higher precision and the rest in int8.
A hidden dimension whose activations are consistently much larger in magnitude than the others.
One scale per output channel (a column of W here), adapting to each channel's range.
One scale per block of consecutive weights (for example 128), localising the effect of outliers.
The factor converting between real values and integer levels; its inverse is the step size.
Signal-to-noise ratio, here 10·log10 of signal energy over error energy, in decibels.
Quantising X with one scale per row and W with one scale per column, so each dot product has its own pair of scales.
The integer that represents real zero in asymmetric quantisation, shifting the grid to fit the data's range.
drill:
Work it out

(a) A layer computes y = x·W with an inner dimension of 16,384. What is the largest possible int32 accumulator magnitude for int8 inputs, and is int32 safe? (b) A 34B model is served with int4 weights in groups of 64 with 16-bit scales and zero points (both per group). What is the weight memory?

Answer 
worst = 16384 * 127 * 127
assert worst == 264_257_536 and worst < 2 ** 31 - 1          # about 12% of the int32 range
bits_d = 4 + (16 + 16) / 64                                   # scale and zero point per group of 64
mem_d = 34e9 * bits_d / 8 / 1e9
assert bits_d == 4.5 and round(mem_d, 2) == 19.12

(a) 16,384 × 127 × 127 = 264,257,536, about 12% of int32's maximum of 2,147,483,647, so int32 is safe with a wide margin; it would take an inner dimension of about 133,000 to risk overflow with worst-case values (and then the -128 corner case of asymmetric data deserves a check too). int16 would overflow after just 3 worst-case products. (b) Each group of 64 weights carries a 16-bit scale and a 16-bit zero point: 4 + 32/64 = 4.5 bits per weight, so 34e9 × 4.5 / 8 = 19.1 GB, versus 68 GB in 16-bit. The overhead of per-group metadata (0.5 bits here) is why some formats quantise the scales themselves.
qa: E
Quantise [0.5, −1.2, 3.0, −0.1] to int8 with absmax.
Scale = 127 / 3.0 = 42.33. Multiply and round: 21.2 → 21, −50.8 → −51, 127, −4.2 → −4. Dequantise by dividing: [0.496, −1.205, 3.0, −0.094]. Errors are below half a step, 0.5/42.33 = 0.0118.
E
What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric quantisation?

Symmetric (absmax) maps zero to zero and ±max|x| to ±127: simple, no zero point, but wasteful when data is one-sided. Asymmetric maps the actual min to −128 and max to 127 using a step (max − min)/255 and an integer zero point: the full grid covers the data, at the cost of handling the zero point in matmuls.
E
Why accumulate int8 products in int32?

Each product can be up to 127 × 127 = 16,129, and a dot product sums thousands of them: 4,096 terms can reach about 66 million. int16 tops out at 32,767 and would wrap around; int32 holds about ±2.1 billion, enough for inner dimensions in the tens of thousands. Hardware int8 instructions accumulate into int32 for exactly this reason.
M
Compare per-tensor, per-channel and per-group scales.

Per-tensor: one scale, no overhead, but the largest value anywhere sets every step. Per-channel: one scale per output column, adapting to columns with different ranges — 43.2 versus 33.0 dB SNR in the lesson when column scales vary. Per-group: one scale per block of, say, 128 weights within a column, so a local outlier only affects its block — 36.4 versus 28.0 dB for per-channel on weights with scattered outliers — at 0.125 extra bits per weight with 16-bit scales.
Follow-up: Why not per-element scales? — Then the scales are as big as the weights and nothing is saved.
M
How does a vector-wise int8 matmul work?

Quantise X with one scale per row and W with one scale per column. Multiply the int8 matrices with int32 accumulation to get C_i32. Each entry C[i, j] is a dot product of row i and column j, so it is dequantised by dividing by s_x[i]·s_w[j] — the outer product of the scale vectors. The result equals the float product of the dequantised matrices, exactly up to floating-point rounding.
M
How do zero points enter a matmul?

With A ≈ (A_q − z_a)/s_a and B ≈ (B_q − z_b)/s_b, the integer part is (A_q − z_a)(B_q − z_b) = A_q·B_q − z_a·colsum(B_q) − z_b·rowsum(A_q) + K·z_a·z_b. The int8 × int8 product stays the heavy core; the corrections are row and column sums computed once, so asymmetric quantisation costs little extra compute.
Follow-up: Why is symmetric quantisation preferred for weights? — Weights are roughly symmetric around zero, so a zero point gains little, and dropping it removes the correction terms entirely.
M
What is SNR and how do you read it?

10·log10(Σ x² / Σ (x − x̂)²): the ratio of signal energy to quantisation-error energy in decibels. Each additional bit of precision adds about 6 dB, so 8-bit uniform quantisation of well-behaved data lands around 40-50 dB. Comparing SNR across scale choices on the same tensor tells you which keeps more information; relative error is about 10^(−SNR/20).
M
Why are outliers the central problem for LLM quantisation?

Dettmers et al. found that beyond about 6.7B parameters, transformers develop a handful of hidden dimensions with very large activations — magnitudes of 6 and far above — in most sequence positions and layers. With row-wise scales for activations, each row's scale is set by its outlier, so the ordinary features in that row are quantised to a few levels and the layer's output degrades. Their perplexity table shows 8-bit absmax and row-wise methods falling apart at 13B while LLM.int8() matches 16-bit.
H
Describe LLM.int8().

Two parts. Vector-wise quantisation: separate scales per row of the hidden states and per column of the weights. Mixed-precision decomposition: find the feature dimensions where any activation reaches at least 6.0 in magnitude — about 0.1% of dimensions, at most 7 in models up to 13B — and compute those columns of X times the corresponding rows of W in 16-bit, the rest in int8, then add. Over 99.9% of values are multiplied in 8-bit; quality matches 16-bit up to 175B parameters; memory roughly halves (1.96× smaller for BLOOM-176B).

Follow-up: What does it cost? — Finding outliers and splitting the matmul adds overhead, so for small models it can be slower than 16-bit; the paper reports speedups only for very large matrix multiplications.
H
Weight-only versus weight-and-activation quantisation: which and when?

Weight-only (int8 or int4 weights, 16-bit activations, dequantised on the fly) attacks memory and bandwidth, which dominate single-stream decoding, and avoids the activation-outlier problem, so it is the common choice for LLM inference. Quantising activations too enables true int8 matmuls, which help when compute-bound (large batches), but requires handling outliers — mixed-precision decomposition, or methods that migrate activation outliers into the weights before quantising.
H
Estimate memory for a 70B model under different schemes.

16-bit: 70e9 × 2 bytes = 140 GB. Int8 with per-group (128) 16-bit scales: 70e9 × 8.125 / 8 ≈ 71 GB. Int4 with the same groups: 70e9 × 4.125 / 8 ≈ 36 GB. LLM.int8() is about half of 16-bit, near 70 GB, since only 0.1% of dimensions stay in 16-bit. Add the KV cache and activations, which weight quantisation does not shrink.
H
How would you validate a quantised model before shipping?

Layer-level: SNR or relative error of each quantised layer's output on real activations, to find sensitive layers. Model-level: perplexity on held-out text and task evaluations versus the 16-bit model, with confidence intervals (ld25), including long-context and code tasks where small errors compound. Look for outlier-sensitive failures: specific prompts or languages that degrade. Keep sensitive layers (often the first and last) in higher precision if needed.

Absmax and zero-point int8, vector-wise quantisation, the outlier threshold 6.0, mixed-precision decomposition keeping >99.9% of values in 8-bit, perplexity results to 13B and zero-shot results to 175B, and the 1.96× memory reduction for BLOOM-176B.

t: InfoNCE and the CLIP contrastive loss
sum: Learn embeddings by telling the right pair from the wrong ones: a batch of paired embeddings, the N × N similarity matrix, temperature, the symmetric cross-entropy CLIP uses with a stable log-softmax, gradients through the normalisation and the temperature checked by finite differences and autograd, how batch size and temperature move the loss, and two linear encoders trained to 98% retrieval.
prereq: mc10
Softmax cross-entropy computed stably with log-softmax; its gradient with respect to logits is softmax minus one-hot.
mc11
A gradient check compares analytic gradients with central finite differences.
mm2
CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder so matching image-caption pairs have high cosine similarity.
dl13
Contrastive self-supervised learning pulls positive pairs together and pushes negatives apart.
mc22
Dense retrieval ranks items by the dot product of normalised embeddings.
why:
Labelled datasets are expensive; paired data is everywhere. The internet is full of images with captions, questions with answers, code with its documentation, audio with transcripts. Contrastive learning turns pairs into a training signal without any labels: train two encoders so that the embeddings of things that belong together are close and those of things that do not are far apart. CLIP did this with 400 million image-text pairs and produced image and text encoders whose shared embedding space supports zero-shot classification — classify an image by finding which caption ("a photo of a dog", "a photo of a cat") it is closest to — and became a backbone of multimodal models and retrieval systems.

The loss behind it is InfoNCE, introduced by Oord, Li and Vinyals in 2018. It is cross-entropy in disguise: within a batch of N pairs, each image is a classification problem with N candidate captions, exactly one correct. The other N − 1 captions are free negatives. Compute all N × N similarities in one matrix product, divide by a temperature, apply a softmax along each row and each column, and penalise the probability on the diagonal. Everything that matters in practice — why batch size changes the loss, what temperature does to the gradient, why embeddings are normalised, why CLIP learns its temperature and clips it — follows from looking at that formula carefully.

The interview asks you to implement it from scratch. This lesson works a two-pair example by hand at two temperatures; derives the gradient through the similarity matrix, the unit-length normalisation and the temperature; implements a loop version and a vectorised one; checks them against each other, finite differences and PyTorch autograd; shows that random embeddings give log N, that a larger batch raises the loss at fixed quality, and that lower temperature focuses the gradient on the hardest negative; and trains two linear encoders on 200 synthetic pairs from a loss of 12.5 to 0.1 and 98% top-1 retrieval.
primer:
The analogy: matching name badges at a conference

A conference organiser has N people and N name badges in a pile, photographed separately. To check a badge-reading system, they show it each person's photo and ask: which of the N badges belongs to this person? Then the reverse: for each badge, which of the N people? The system gets credit for putting high confidence on the right answer, and since all the other badges are on the table, every wrong badge is a free test of whether the system can tell people apart. With 8 people this is easy; with 512 it is much harder, because there are many more look-alikes to rule out. And the organiser can make the system answer boldly (low temperature: "it's definitely this one") or cautiously (high temperature: "could be any of these").

The photos are image embeddings, the badges text embeddings, "which badge?" is a row of the similarity matrix with a softmax over it, the reverse question is the column direction, the other badges are in-batch negatives, the boldness is the temperature.

The analogy breaks usefully: the organiser's question has one right answer, but in real data two different captions can both describe an image well (two photos of the same landmark, two similar captions). InfoNCE still treats them as negatives — false negatives — which is one reason the loss never reaches zero on real data and why deduplication matters.

Where the loss sits in a model

A CLIP-style model has two encoders — a vision network for images and a transformer for text — each followed by a linear projection into a shared embedding space of a few hundred dimensions. The contrastive loss sits on top of those projections and is the only training signal; there is no classification head and no decoder. After training, the encoders are used separately: index images by their embeddings, embed a text query, and retrieve by cosine similarity, or classify zero-shot by embedding one caption per class. In this lesson the encoders are replaced by random embeddings and, in the training test, by two linear maps, which isolates the loss itself. CLIP (contrastive language–image pre-training) is the best-known example, but nothing in the loss is specific to images.

What the interviewer is checking

That you see the batch as an N-way classification with the diagonal as labels and implement it with one matrix product rather than loops; that you include both directions; that you normalise and divide by τ; that the softmax is stable; and that you can say what the loss value means — log N at random, rising with N at fixed quality, strongly dependent on τ. Deriving the gradient, especially through the normalisation and the temperature, is the depth signal; knowing why CLIP learns and clips τ is the practical one.
body:
1. The problem as it is usually asked

"Given a batch of paired image and text embeddings, implement the CLIP (symmetric InfoNCE) loss with a temperature, numerically stably, and its gradients. Show what happens as batch size and temperature change." Clarify: embeddings are normalised inside the loss (yes, as in CLIP); the temperature is a parameter to differentiate (yes, learned in log space); labels are the diagonal (pair i matches pair i); loss averaged over the batch and over both directions. Outline: hand example, loop version, vectorised version with gradients, tests including a batch and temperature sweep and a small training run.

2. The maths in plain words

Normalise every embedding to length one, so the dot product of an image and a text is their cosine similarity. Stack the images as rows of one matrix and the texts as rows of another; multiplying the first by the transpose of the second gives every image-text similarity at once. Divide by the temperature. Row i is a list of scores for "which text goes with image i?"; turn it into probabilities with a softmax and take minus the log of the probability on the correct text, i. Do the same down each column for "which image goes with text j?". Average the two directions and over the batch. That is the loss.

The gradient is the familiar softmax-cross-entropy rule applied twice: for each row, the probabilities minus the one-hot of the right answer; the same for each column; averaged. That gradient on the similarity matrix flows back to each embedding as a weighted sum of the other side's embeddings — pull towards the partner, push away from negatives in proportion to how much probability each currently takes — and through the normalisation, which keeps only the part that changes direction.

3. The equations

normalise:    Î = I / ‖I‖ (rows),  T̂ = T / ‖T‖           (N, d)
similarities: S = Î · T̂ᵀ / τ                              (N, N)
loss:         L_i2t = −(1/N) Σ_i log softmax_row(S)[i, i]
              L_t2i = −(1/N) Σ_j log softmax_col(S)[j, j]
              L = ½ (L_i2t + L_t2i)
gradients:    dS = ½ [ (softmax_row(S) − I_N) + (softmax_col(S) − I_N) ] / N
              dÎ = dS · T̂ / τ,      dT̂ = dSᵀ · Î / τ
              dI = (dÎ − Î ⊙ rowsum(Î ⊙ dÎ)) / ‖I‖        (same for T)
              dL/dτ = −Σ (dS ⊙ S) / τ
fixed gap:    if every positive beats every negative by g in cosine,
              L = log(1 + (N − 1)·e^(−g/τ))
InfoNCE bound: I(X; Y) ≥ log N − L

4. A worked example by hand

Two pairs. Images I1 = [1, 0], I2 = [0, 1]; texts T1 = [0.8, 0.6], T2 = [0.6, 0.8] — all already unit length. Similarities: I1·T1 = 0.8, I1·T2 = 0.6, I2·T1 = 0.6, I2·T2 = 0.8. Each positive beats its negative by a gap of 0.2.

  • τ = 1. Row 1 logits [0.8, 0.6]: −log(e0.8/(e0.8 + e0.6)) = log(1 + e−0.2) = 0.5981. Row 2 is the same by symmetry, and so are both columns, so L = 0.5981.
  • τ = 0.1. Logits [8, 6]: log(1 + e−2) = 0.1269. The embeddings have not changed; dividing by a smaller temperature made the same gap look ten times bigger.
  • More negatives. If a batch had N pairs and every positive beat every negative by the same 0.2, the loss would be log(1 + (N − 1)e−0.2/τ). At N = 1,024: 4.938 at τ = 0.1 and 4.090 at τ = 0.07. The same quality of embeddings gives a very different loss depending on N and τ.
  • Information bound. InfoNCE implies I(X; Y) ≥ log N − L: with N = 1,024 and τ = 0.07, log 1,024 − 4.090 = 2.841 nats. The bound can never exceed log N — about 6.93 nats here — however good the embeddings.
import math
import numpy as np

# The hand-worked example: two image and two text embeddings (already unit length).
I_h = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])
T_h = np.array([[0.8, 0.6], [0.6, 0.8]])
S_h = I_h @ T_h.T                                              # cosine similarities
assert np.allclose(S_h, [[0.8, 0.6], [0.6, 0.8]])
def row_ce_diag(logits):                                       # cross-entropy with the matching item as label
    return np.mean([math.log(sum(math.exp(v) for v in row)) - row[i] for i, row in enumerate(logits)])
for tau, expected in [(1.0, 0.5981), (0.1, 0.1269)]:
    L_i2t = row_ce_diag(S_h / tau); L_t2i = row_ce_diag((S_h / tau).T)
    assert round((L_i2t + L_t2i) / 2, 4) == expected            # log(1 + e^(-0.2/tau))
# With the same similarity gap, more negatives make the task harder: log(1 + (N-1) e^(-gap/tau)).
gap_loss = lambda N, tau, gap=0.2: math.log(1 + (N - 1) * math.exp(-gap / tau))
assert round(gap_loss(2, 0.1), 4) == 0.1269 and round(gap_loss(1024, 0.1), 3) == 4.938
assert round(gap_loss(1024, 0.07), 3) == 4.090
# The InfoNCE bound: mutual information >= log N - loss (in nats).
assert round(math.log(1024) - gap_loss(1024, 0.07), 3) == 2.841

5. The naive implementation

The loop version normalises, builds the similarity matrix as a list of lists, and for each i computes the row's log-sum-exp (subtracting the row maximum first) minus the diagonal entry, and the same for column i. It is slow and obviously right, and serves as the reference for the vectorised loss.

def l2_normalise(x, eps=1e-12):
    n = np.sqrt((x * x).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    return x / np.maximum(n, eps), n

def clip_loss_naive(img, txt, tau):
    """Symmetric InfoNCE with explicit loops: image i should pick text i, and text i image i."""
    N = len(img)
    I, _ = l2_normalise(img); T, _ = l2_normalise(txt)
    S = [[float(I[i] @ T[j]) / tau for j in range(N)] for i in range(N)]
    loss = 0.0
    for i in range(N):
        row = S[i]; col = [S[j][i] for j in range(N)]
        m_r, m_c = max(row), max(col)                           # subtract the max before exp
        loss += (m_r + math.log(sum(math.exp(v - m_r) for v in row))) - row[i]
        loss += (m_c + math.log(sum(math.exp(v - m_c) for v in col))) - col[i]
    return loss / (2 * N)

6. The vectorised implementation with gradients

One matrix product builds S; log_softmax along axis 1 gives the row distributions and along axis 0 the column distributions, both stable because each subtracts its maximum. The loss is minus half the sum of the two diagonals, divided by N. The gradient on S follows the softmax-minus-one-hot rule: exp(lp_r) − eye for rows and exp(lp_c) − eye for columns, averaged and divided by N. Through S = ÎT̂ᵀ/τ, the normalised embeddings receive dS·T̂/τ and dSᵀ·Î/τ, and the temperature −Σ(dS ⊙ S)/τ. Finally the normalisation: for x̂ = x/‖x‖, the Jacobian is (I − x̂x̂ᵀ)/‖x‖, so each row's gradient has its component along x̂ removed and is divided by the original norm. The function also returns top-1 retrieval accuracy averaged over both directions.

def log_softmax(z, axis=-1):
    z = z - z.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    return z - np.log(np.exp(z).sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True))

def clip_loss_and_grads(img, txt, tau):
    """Vectorised symmetric InfoNCE (CLIP loss) and gradients w.r.t. the raw embeddings and tau.
    L = 0.5 * (CE(S, diag) + CE(S^T, diag)),  S = (I_hat T_hat^T) / tau."""
    N = len(img)
    I, ni = l2_normalise(img); T, nt = l2_normalise(txt)
    S = (I @ T.T) / tau
    lp_r, lp_c = log_softmax(S, axis=1), log_softmax(S, axis=0)
    loss = -0.5 * (np.trace(lp_r) + np.trace(lp_c)) / N
    # dL/dS: rows give softmax - onehot, columns likewise; each averaged over N and halved.
    dS = 0.5 * ((np.exp(lp_r) - np.eye(N)) + (np.exp(lp_c) - np.eye(N))) / N
    dI_hat = dS @ T / tau
    dT_hat = dS.T @ I / tau
    dtau = -float((dS * S).sum()) / tau                         # S depends on tau as (I T^T) / tau
    # Back through x_hat = x / ||x||:  dx = (dx_hat - x_hat * (x_hat . dx_hat)) / ||x||
    d_img = (dI_hat - I * (I * dI_hat).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)) / ni
    d_txt = (dT_hat - T * (T * dT_hat).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)) / nt
    acc = float(((S.argmax(axis=1) == np.arange(N)).mean() + (S.argmax(axis=0) == np.arange(N)).mean()) / 2)
    return float(loss), d_img, d_txt, dtau, acc

7. Testing it

Seven checks. (1) Loop and vectorised losses agree at τ = 1, 0.1 and 0.03, and the hand example gives 0.1269. (2) 512 random, unrelated pairs give a loss of 6.258 against log 512 = 6.238; identical pairs at τ = 0.01 give almost zero. (3) Central finite differences at three coordinates of each embedding matrix match the analytic gradients to 10−7, and the temperature gradient matches too. (4) The share of row 0's negative gradient on its single hardest negative rises as τ goes from 3.0 to 0.3 to 0.03. (5) With the same noise level between pairs, the loss at τ = 0.1 is 0.006 for N = 8, 0.059 for N = 64 and 0.415 for N = 512 — more negatives, harder task. (6) Two linear encoders (20 → 8 for "images", 12 → 8 for "texts") trained with plain gradient descent on batches of 64 from 200 pairs that share a 6-dimensional latent: the batch loss falls from 12.5 to about 0.1 and top-1 retrieval among all 200 pairs reaches 98%; the learned temperature runs to its 0.01 floor, as CLIP's would without clipping. (7) PyTorch with F.normalize and F.cross_entropy in both directions gives the same loss and the same gradients for both embeddings and the temperature.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, d = 16, 8
img = rng.normal(size=(N, d)); txt = img + 0.8 * rng.normal(size=(N, d))   # matching pairs are correlated

# 1. Loop and vectorised losses agree; the hand example reproduces.
for tau in (1.0, 0.1, 0.03):
    assert np.isclose(clip_loss_naive(img, txt, tau), clip_loss_and_grads(img, txt, tau)[0])
assert round(clip_loss_and_grads(I_h, T_h, 0.1)[0], 4) == 0.1269

# 2. Random, unrelated embeddings give a loss near log N; a perfect match at low tau goes to 0.
far = rng.normal(size=(512, 32))
L_rand = clip_loss_and_grads(far, rng.normal(size=(512, 32)), 1.0)[0]
assert abs(L_rand - math.log(512)) < 0.05
assert clip_loss_and_grads(far, far, 0.01)[0] < 1e-3

# 3. Finite-difference checks of the gradients w.r.t. image, text and tau.
L0, gI, gT, gtau, _ = clip_loss_and_grads(img, txt, 0.1)
for arr, g in ((img, gI), (txt, gT)):
    for idx in [(0, 0), (5, 3), (15, 7)]:
        old = arr[idx]
        arr[idx] = old + 1e-6; lp = clip_loss_and_grads(img, txt, 0.1)[0]
        arr[idx] = old - 1e-6; lm = clip_loss_and_grads(img, txt, 0.1)[0]
        arr[idx] = old
        assert abs((lp - lm) / 2e-6 - g[idx]) < 1e-7
num_tau = (clip_loss_and_grads(img, txt, 0.1 + 1e-7)[0] - clip_loss_and_grads(img, txt, 0.1 - 1e-7)[0]) / 2e-7
assert abs(num_tau - gtau) < 1e-5

# 4. Lower temperature concentrates the gradient on the hardest negative.
def weight_on_hardest(tau):
    I, _ = l2_normalise(img); T, _ = l2_normalise(txt)
    p = np.exp(log_softmax((I @ T.T)[0] / tau)); p[0] = 0      # negatives of row 0 only
    return p.max() / p.sum()
assert weight_on_hardest(0.03) > weight_on_hardest(0.3) > weight_on_hardest(3.0)

# 5. With fixed embedding quality, bigger batches mean a bigger loss (more negatives to beat).
losses = [clip_loss_and_grads(*(lambda a: (a, a + 0.8 * rng.normal(size=a.shape)))(rng.normal(size=(n, 64))), 0.1)[0]
          for n in (8, 64, 512)]
assert losses[0] < losses[1] < losses[2]

# 6. Training two linear encoders on paired data: loss falls, retrieval accuracy rises.
P = 200
z = rng.normal(size=(P, 6))                                   # shared latent content
Ximg = z @ rng.normal(size=(6, 20)) + 0.3 * rng.normal(size=(P, 20))
Xtxt = z @ rng.normal(size=(6, 12)) + 0.3 * rng.normal(size=(P, 12))
Wi, Wt = 0.1 * rng.normal(size=(20, 8)), 0.1 * rng.normal(size=(12, 8))
log_tau = math.log(0.07)                                      # learn tau in log space, as CLIP does
hist = []
for step in range(300):
    b = rng.choice(P, 64, replace=False)
    L, gI_, gT_, gtau_, acc = clip_loss_and_grads(Ximg[b] @ Wi, Xtxt[b] @ Wt, math.exp(log_tau))
    Wi -= 0.5 * Ximg[b].T @ gI_; Wt -= 0.5 * Xtxt[b].T @ gT_
    log_tau = min(max(log_tau - 0.05 * gtau_ * math.exp(log_tau), math.log(0.01)), math.log(1.0))
    hist.append((L, acc))
L_full, *_, acc_full = clip_loss_and_grads(Ximg @ Wi, Xtxt @ Wt, math.exp(log_tau))
assert hist[-1][0] < 0.5 * hist[0][0] and acc_full > 0.5        # top-1 retrieval among all 200 pairs

# 7. Cross-check the loss and gradients with PyTorch autograd, if available.
try:
    import torch
    ti = torch.tensor(img, requires_grad=True); tt = torch.tensor(txt, requires_grad=True)
    tau_t = torch.tensor(0.1, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
    Sn = torch.nn.functional.normalize(ti, dim=1) @ torch.nn.functional.normalize(tt, dim=1).T / tau_t
    lab = torch.arange(N)
    Lt = 0.5 * (torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(Sn, lab) + torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(Sn.T, lab))
    Lt.backward()
    assert np.isclose(Lt.item(), L0) and np.allclose(ti.grad.numpy(), gI) and np.allclose(tt.grad.numpy(), gT)
    assert np.isclose(tau_t.grad.item(), gtau)
except ImportError:
    pass
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"random loss {L_rand:.3f} vs log 512 = {math.log(512):.3f}; batch losses {np.round(losses, 3)}")
    print(f"training: loss {hist[0][0]:.3f} -> {hist[-1][0]:.3f}, full-set top-1 {acc_full:.2f}, tau {math.exp(log_tau):.3f}")

8. Numerical and practical traps

Small τ overflow. At τ = 0.01 logits reach 100 and e100 overflows float16; always subtract the maximum (log-softmax) and compute the loss in float32. Zero-norm embeddings. Guard the normalisation with a small epsilon. One direction only. Easy to forget the column term; the gradient then pushes only images. Temperature collapse. Without a floor, τ heads to zero; clip the logit scale (CLIP: at most 100). False negatives. Duplicates in a batch are treated as negatives; deduplicate or mask them. Comparing losses across batch sizes. Not meaningful; report retrieval accuracy.

9. Edge cases worth naming

N = 1: there are no negatives and the loss is always zero — contrastive learning needs at least two pairs. Unequal numbers of images and texts (several captions per image): use a rectangular matrix and multi-positive targets. Identical items in a batch: both diagonal and off-diagonal entries equal, so the best possible row probability is ½, and the loss cannot fall below log 2 for that row. Very large N: the N × N matrix dominates memory (32,768² entries is about 4 GB in float32), so it is computed in blocks across devices.

10. Complexity

The similarity matrix costs O(N²·d) multiply-adds and O(N²) memory; the softmaxes and gradients are O(N²); back-propagation to embeddings is another O(N²·d). Normalisation is O(N·d). Encoder forward and backward passes dominate for moderate N; the N² terms dominate for very large batches, which is why large-batch contrastive training is sharded.

11. Talking through the design

Lead with the matrix picture (diagonal positives, in-batch negatives), write the loss in both directions with τ, mention stability, derive dS and its path back through normalisation, then discuss the behaviour: log N at random, dependence on N and τ, hard-negative focus at low τ, CLIP's learned and clipped temperature, and what you would monitor (retrieval accuracy both ways).
deep:
Why InfoNCE bounds mutual information

Oord et al. frame each row as identifying the true partner among N candidates, N − 1 of them drawn independently. The optimal scoring function for that task is proportional to the density ratio p(y|x)/p(y), and plugging it in shows that the expected loss is at least log N − I(X; Y). Rearranged, I(X; Y) ≥ log N − L. Two consequences matter in practice: the bound saturates at log N, so estimating or learning large amounts of shared information needs many negatives; and lowering the loss at fixed N tightens the bound, which is the formal sense in which contrastive training extracts information shared between the two views.

Temperature as a hardness dial

The gradient on a negative j in row i is proportional to softmax(Si)j, which for small τ is dominated by the largest similarities. So τ decides whether learning focuses on separating the anchor from the few negatives that look most like it (low τ) or from all negatives roughly equally (high τ). Very low τ makes training sensitive to false negatives — a near-duplicate caption takes most of the gradient — and to noise; high τ wastes effort on easy negatives. Learning τ lets the model pick a hardness level as training proceeds, which in practice drifts towards low values as embeddings improve.

Uniformity and alignment

Another way to read the contrastive loss: the positive term pulls matched pairs together (alignment), and the log-sum-exp over negatives pushes all embeddings apart on the unit sphere (uniformity). A model that maps everything to one point is perfectly aligned but has a loss of log N; one that spreads points uniformly but ignores pairing also gets log N. Good representations do both, which is why normalisation to the sphere is part of the method, not a detail.

SigLIP: dropping the softmax

The softmax couples every item in a row: each probability depends on all N similarities, so the loss needs the full matrix and its normalisation. SigLIP replaces it with an independent binary classification per cell — sigmoid of (similarity × scale + bias), target 1 on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere — so cells can be computed in blocks without a global normaliser, which simplifies very large batches and distributed training. It shows the core idea of this lesson — paired data with in-batch negatives — is separable from the particular softmax form.

Getting many negatives without a huge batch

Memory limits the batch, and the batch limits the negatives. Three techniques decouple them. A memory bank or queue (as in MoCo) keeps embeddings from recent batches and uses them as extra negatives, often produced by a slowly updated momentum encoder so they stay consistent. Gradient caching computes all embeddings of a large batch without storing activations, computes the contrastive loss and the gradient with respect to each embedding, then re-runs each sub-batch's encoder with those embedding gradients — exact large-batch training in small-batch memory. Distributed all-gather pools embeddings across devices so the global batch provides the negatives. All three exist because the loss in this lesson gets better with more negatives.

More than one positive

Real datasets often have several valid partners per item — five captions per image, several relevant passages per query. The cross-entropy target then becomes a distribution spread over all positives in the row, or each positive is treated in turn with the others masked out of the negatives. Treating extra positives as negatives (what the plain loss does) pushes apart things that should be close and caps achievable accuracy.

Beyond images and text

The same loss trains text embedding models for retrieval (query and relevant passage as the pair, other passages in the batch as negatives), code search, audio-text models and recommendation two-tower models (user and item embeddings). The practical differences are in how pairs and hard negatives are mined, how false negatives are filtered, and whether the two encoders share weights. The implementation in this lesson carries over unchanged.

Why the loss transfers zero-shot

A classifier trained with cross-entropy learns a fixed set of class vectors; a contrastive model learns an encoder for the class descriptions themselves. At test time any set of labels can be written as captions, embedded, and used as the rows of the classifier — which is why a CLIP model can classify into categories it never saw as labels. The same view explains its weaknesses: the zero-shot classifier is only as good as the caption wording (prompt templates such as "a photo of a {label}" measurably help), and fine-grained or abstract categories that rarely appear in captions are hard.
prod:
Where this loss runs

Contrastive losses train CLIP-style vision-language encoders, sentence and passage embedding models used for semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation, and two-tower retrieval models in recommendation. In all of them the batch is the main source of negatives, often augmented with mined hard negatives, and training is distributed so that the global batch — and therefore the number of negatives — is large.

Failure modes and symptoms

Loss stuck near log N. Encoders are not learning: check normalisation, the learning rate, and that pairs are actually aligned (shuffled captions produce exactly this).

Temperature collapse and instability. Logit scale climbs until training diverges; clip it.

False negatives. Duplicate or near-duplicate pairs in a batch are pushed apart, hurting retrieval for popular items; deduplicate data and mask known duplicates.

Batch-size mismatch. A model fine-tuned with a much smaller batch than it was pre-trained with sees easier tasks and can lose quality; use gradient caching or memory banks to keep negatives numerous.

Asymmetric quality. Text-to-image retrieval much worse than image-to-text: often a missing or down-weighted direction in the loss.

Shortcut learning. Symptom: excellent training retrieval, poor transfer. Cause: pairs can be matched by a trivial cue — a watermark, a timestamp in the caption, image size, or a source-specific template — so the encoders learn the cue instead of the content. Fix: audit what distinguishes pairs, strip boilerplate, and evaluate on data from a different source.

Distributed gather bugs. Symptom: multi-device training is worse than single-device at the same global batch. Cause: each device computes the loss only against its local negatives, or the gathered embeddings do not carry gradient back. Fix: gather embeddings from all devices for the similarity matrix and make sure the local slice still gets gradient.

Embedding drift between index and query. Symptom: retrieval quality drops after a model update. Cause: stored item embeddings came from the old encoder while queries use the new one; contrastive spaces are not compatible across training runs. Fix: re-embed the whole index when either encoder changes, or train with a compatibility constraint.

What to monitor and tune

Top-1 and top-5 retrieval in both directions on held-out pairs at a fixed batch size; the learned temperature; the loss relative to log N; gradient norms; and for production retrieval, recall@k on real queries. Tune batch size (as large as memory allows), the temperature initialisation and floor, the learning rate, and the mix of hard negatives.

A cost estimate

At CLIP's batch of 32,768 with 512-dimensional embeddings, the similarity matrix needs 32,768² × 512 ≈ 5.5 × 1011 multiply-adds and holds about 1.07 billion entries (4.3 GB in float32) if materialised whole — small next to the encoders' compute but large enough in memory that it is computed in per-device blocks.

The reference for this problem

Radford et al.'s CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) paper gives the loss as numpy-like pseudocode — normalise both embeddings, compute logits = I_e · T_eᵀ · exp(t), take cross-entropy along both axes with labels arange(n), and average — and reports that the temperature τ "was initialized to the equivalent of 0.07 … and clipped to prevent scaling the logits by more than 100", that it is "directly optimized during training as a log-parameterized multiplicative scalar", and that training used "a very large minibatch size of 32,768". Oord, Li and Vinyals introduced InfoNCE and the mutual-information bound.
myths: Contrastive learning needs explicit negative examples.

In InfoNCE with in-batch negatives, every other item in the batch is a negative for free: N pairs give each anchor one positive and N − 1 negatives. The similarity matrix contains all of them, and one cross-entropy per row uses them all. That is why batch size matters so much — it is the number of negatives.
The loss should go to zero.

With the same embedding quality, the loss grows with batch size because there are more negatives to beat: log(1 + (N − 1)·e^(−gap/τ)). A loss of 0.4 at N = 512 can mean better embeddings than 0.006 at N = 8, as the lesson's batch sweep shows. Compare losses only at equal batch size and temperature, and track retrieval accuracy instead.
Temperature is a cosmetic scale factor.

It changes what the gradient attends to. Low τ makes the softmax over negatives sharp, concentrating gradient on the hardest negatives; high τ spreads it over all of them and flattens the loss towards log N. CLIP learns τ (initialised at 0.07, logits clipped at a scale of 100) because the right value matters and is hard to tune by hand.
Only one direction of the loss is needed.

Image-to-text and text-to-image are different classification problems: each row of the similarity matrix asks which caption matches this image, each column which image matches this caption. CLIP averages both. With one direction, the other's retrieval can be noticeably worse.
Normalising embeddings is optional.

Without normalisation, the model can lower the loss by growing embedding norms instead of improving directions, and similarities become unbounded. Normalising to unit length makes the dot product a cosine similarity in [−1, 1] and puts all scale control in τ. Its gradient then removes the component along the embedding: only direction is learned.
lab:
Goal: run the solution, then vary it, break it and measure it. Python 3.12 with NumPy (the gpt_env venv); PyTorch only for the optional cross-check.

  1. Run the four blocks as one script. All assertions pass and it prints the random-embedding loss, the batch sweep and the training summary.
  2. Vary by hand. Redo section 4 with T1 = [0.6, 0.8] and T2 = [0.8, 0.6] (the captions swapped). What is the loss at τ = 0.1, and what does the model "believe"?
  3. Break it. Drop the column term from the loss and gradient. Train again and measure text-to-image retrieval separately from image-to-text.
  4. Break the normalisation. Remove l2_normalise from training and watch the embedding norms and the loss.
  5. Sweep temperature. Train with τ fixed at 1.0, 0.1 and 0.01 (no learning) and compare final retrieval accuracy.
  6. Add false negatives. Duplicate 20 of the 200 pairs so duplicates often share a batch, and measure the effect on retrieval for those items.

Each run takes a second or two, so record a small table — setting, loss, retrieval in each direction, final τ — for every experiment; the comparisons are the point. What to look for: swapped captions give a loss above log 2 — the model is confidently wrong; one direction only hurts the other direction's retrieval; unnormalised embeddings grow without bound; τ that is too high learns slowly, too low is unstable; duplicates in a batch cap how well those items can be retrieved. Write down your expected result before each run; surprises are where you learn the most.
recap: InfoNCE scores a positive pair against negatives with a softmax and minimises the cross-entropy of picking the positive.

The CLIP loss is the average of cross-entropy over rows (image → text) and over columns (text → image) with the diagonal as the labels.
Log-softmax with the maximum subtracted keeps the loss stable for small τ, where logits reach 1/τ = 100.

drill:
Work it out

(a) Your embeddings separate every positive from every negative by a cosine gap of 0.3. What is the loss at N = 256 for τ = 0.05 and τ = 0.2? (b) A team reports that their new model's contrastive loss dropped from 2.1 to 1.4 after doubling the batch from 4,096 to 8,192. Is that evidence the embeddings improved?

Answer 
L_low = gap_loss(256, 0.05, gap=0.3)
L_high = gap_loss(256, 0.2, gap=0.3)
assert round(L_low, 3) == 0.490 and round(L_high, 3) == 4.059

(a) log(1 + 255·e−0.3/0.05) = log(1 + 255·e−6) = 0.490; at τ = 0.2, log(1 + 255·e−1.5) = 4.059. Identical embeddings, losses more than eight times apart: temperature dominates the number. (b) It is strong evidence, but for a reason the team may not have intended: doubling the number of negatives should raise the loss at fixed quality (adding about log 2 ≈ 0.69 when many negatives are close), so a 0.7 drop alongside it means the embeddings improved substantially — unless the temperature also changed, which can move the loss by more than that. Check the learned τ at both points and compare retrieval accuracy at a fixed evaluation batch size before concluding.
qa: E
Write the CLIP loss.

Normalise image and text embeddings to unit length; S = I·Tᵀ/τ, an N × N matrix; labels are 0…N−1 (the diagonal). Loss = ½·[CE(S, labels) over rows + CE(Sᵀ, labels)], where CE is softmax cross-entropy averaged over the batch. CLIP's own pseudocode computes cross-entropy along both axes and averages.
E
What does the loss equal for random embeddings, and why?

About log N. If embeddings carry no information, every row's softmax is roughly uniform over N candidates, and the cross-entropy of a uniform distribution at the correct label is log N. The lesson measures 6.258 for N = 512 against log 512 = 6.238. A loss near log N after training means nothing was learned.
E
Why normalise the embeddings?

So the similarity is a cosine in [−1, 1] and the only way to sharpen the softmax is through τ. Unnormalised dot products let the model lower the loss by inflating norms. With normalisation, the gradient with respect to the raw embedding has its component along the embedding removed: training changes directions, not lengths.
M
Work the two-pair example with τ = 1 and τ = 0.1.

Images [1, 0] and [0, 1]; texts [0.8, 0.6] and [0.6, 0.8]. Similarities: diagonal 0.8, off-diagonal 0.6. Each row's cross-entropy is −log(e^0.8/(e^0.8 + e^0.6)) = log(1 + e^−0.2) = 0.598 at τ = 1, and log(1 + e^−2) = 0.127 at τ = 0.1. The matrix is symmetric, so both directions agree and the loss is 0.598 and 0.127. The same embeddings look ten times more confident at lower temperature.
M
Derive the gradient with respect to the similarity matrix.

Row-wise CE averaged over N contributes (softmax_rows(S) − I)/N; column-wise contributes (softmax_cols(S) − I)/N; the loss averages the two, so dL/dS = ½·[(P_r − I) + (P_c − I)]/N. Then S = Î·T̂ᵀ/τ gives dÎ = dS·T̂/τ and dT̂ = dSᵀ·Î/τ, and the normalisation adds the projection (dx̂ − x̂(x̂·dx̂))/‖x‖.
Follow-up: And with respect to τ? — S = (Î·T̂ᵀ)/τ, so dS/dτ = −S/τ and dL/dτ = −Σ(dS ⊙ S)/τ.
M
How does batch size affect the loss and the learning?

More pairs means more negatives per anchor. With a fixed similarity gap, the loss is log(1 + (N − 1)e^(−gap/τ)), which grows with N, so absolute loss values are not comparable across batch sizes. More negatives also make the task harder and the representation better, which is why CLIP used a batch of 32,768. The lesson's sweep: 0.006, 0.059 and 0.415 at N = 8, 64 and 512 with the same embedding quality.
M
What does temperature do to the gradient?

The gradient on each negative is proportional to its softmax probability. At low τ the softmax is sharp, so most of the push goes to the most similar (hardest) negatives; at high τ the push is spread evenly and is weak because the loss flattens towards log N. The lesson measures the share of gradient on row 0's hardest negative rising as τ goes from 3.0 to 0.3 to 0.03.
M
What is the InfoNCE bound?

Oord et al. show that minimising InfoNCE maximises a lower bound on the mutual information between the paired variables: I(X; Y) ≥ log N − L_N. The bound can never exceed log N, so estimating large mutual information needs large batches, another reason for big batch sizes. With N = 1,024, τ = 0.07 and a 0.2 gap, L = 4.09 and the bound is 2.84 nats.
H
Why does CLIP learn the temperature in log space and clip it?

τ must stay positive and spans orders of magnitude, so learning log τ (CLIP multiplies by exp of a learned scalar) gives well-behaved gradient steps. Left alone, the loss keeps rewarding sharper softmaxes, driving τ towards zero and the logits towards infinity, which destabilised training; CLIP clips the logit scale at 100 (τ ≥ 0.01). In the lesson's toy training τ also runs straight to its 0.01 floor.

Follow-up: What does SigLIP change? — It replaces the softmax over the batch with an independent sigmoid per pair, removing the need for the full-row normalisation and making very large batches cheaper.
H
How is the loss computed when the batch is spread over many GPUs?

Each device holds its local embeddings; the similarity matrix needs every image against every text. Devices all-gather the embeddings, compute the rows (or blocks) for their local items, and compute local losses; gradients flow back to the local embeddings and are combined. CLIP sharded the similarity computation so each GPU computes only the pairwise similarities it needs for its local batch. Memory for the N × N matrix grows quadratically, which bounds the global batch.
H
Training loss falls but zero-shot retrieval is poor. What do you check?

Whether the loss is falling only because τ is shrinking (compare accuracy at fixed τ); whether in-batch negatives contain false negatives (duplicate captions or near-identical images counted as negatives); whether batch composition is too easy (all negatives from different domains); whether evaluation embeddings are normalised the same way; and whether one direction dominates. Track top-1 retrieval in both directions on a held-out set at a fixed batch size.
H
How would you add hard-negative mining?

Beyond in-batch negatives, add negatives chosen to be similar: retrieve near neighbours from a memory bank or from the previous step's embeddings, filter out false negatives (true matches), and append their similarities as extra columns in each row's softmax. Weight them carefully: too many hard negatives (or wrong ones) destabilise training; in-batch negatives at a well-learned temperature already emphasise hard cases.
