sum: Learn word vectors from co-occurrence: (centre, context) pairs from a sliding window, the unigram^0.75 noise distribution, the skip-gram negative-sampling loss and its gradients worked by hand, a per-pair SGD loop and a mini-batch version that accumulates repeated words correctly, finite-difference and autograd checks, and a tiny corpus on which king's nearest neighbours become prince, queen and princess.
prereq: ml21
Word embeddings: dense vectors where words used in similar contexts end up close; word2vec, GloVe and fastText.
mc10
Softmax over a vocabulary and its cost; log-sigmoid computed stably.
mc28
Contrastive learning: pull a positive pair together, push sampled negatives apart.
mc11
Gradient checks against central finite differences.
mc2
Logistic regression: σ(w·x) with log-loss, whose gradient is (σ − y)·x.
why:
Before 2013, most language models represented words as indices into a vocabulary — one-hot vectors with no notion that "king" and "queen" are related. word2vec changed that with an almost embarrassingly simple idea: train a vector for every word so that it can predict the words around it. Words that appear in similar contexts end up with similar vectors, and the resulting embeddings captured relations well enough that "king − man + woman" landed near "queen". The method trained on billions of words on a single machine, and dense word vectors became the default input to NLP systems for years, until contextual models like BERT and GPT replaced them. The ideas — a context window as supervision, learning by telling real pairs from noise, and embedding tables updated sparsely — run through modern recommendation, retrieval and contrastive learning.

The obstacle Mikolov and colleagues had to remove was the softmax. Predicting a context word means a probability distribution over the whole vocabulary — a million words — for every training pair. Their fix, negative sampling, turns each pair into a small binary classification: is this word a real context of the centre word, or a random word drawn from a noise distribution? Each update then touches only k + 1 output vectors. Two further details made it work well: draw the noise words from the word frequencies raised to the 3/4 power, and randomly drop occurrences of very frequent words.

Implementing skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS) from scratch is a standard ML coding question because it tests pair generation, a sampled loss, deriving gradients through a sigmoid for two embedding tables, and the sparse-update trap that catches most first implementations. This lesson computes the noise distribution and one full update by hand; writes a per-pair SGD loop and a vectorised mini-batch version that accumulates repeated words with np.add.at; checks the gradients with finite differences and PyTorch autograd; and trains 16-dimensional vectors on a synthetic corpus of 3,000 sentences, after which each royal's, animal's, food's and place's nearest neighbours are the other members of its group. It also records the failure on the way: with a learning rate of 0.5 per pair, the frequent word "the" received dozens of summed updates per batch and the whole model diverged to infinity.
primer:
The analogy: guessing who sits near whom at a wedding

At a large wedding, you never see the guest list, but you see who sits near whom at every table. After enough tables, you can tell that the bride's college friends cluster together and so do the groom's colleagues, and that the two cousins who always sit by the same aunt are similar in some sense — not because you know anything about them, but because their neighbours overlap. If someone asks "is Sam likely to sit next to Priya?", you can answer by comparing what you have learned about each. And to learn faster, you do not consider every possible guest each time: for each real neighbour pair you saw, you also pick a few random guests and remind yourself they were not sitting there.

The guests are words, the tables are context windows, "who sits near whom" is the set of (centre, context) pairs, what you learn about each guest is its vector, comparing two guests is a dot product, and the random guests you remind yourself about are negative samples. Picking random guests mostly from the frequently seen ones — but not exclusively — is the 3/4-power noise distribution.

The analogy breaks in one technical way: each word has two descriptions, one for when it is the guest in focus (the input vector) and one for when it is a neighbour (the output vector). That separation is what lets "dog" be a likely neighbour of "cat" without asking any word to be its own neighbour.

Why "context predicts meaning" works at all

The idea behind word2vec is older than the method: linguists observed that you can learn a lot about a word from the company it keeps. If "sceptre" appears near "king", "queen", "throne" and "crown", and "wand" appears near "wizard", "spell" and "magic", a learner that only sees which words appear together can still place "sceptre" near "crown" and far from "spell". word2vec makes the learner a pair of vector tables and the lesson a prediction task, and lets gradient descent find vectors in which these co-occurrence patterns become geometry: words with overlapping neighbourhoods point in similar directions. Nothing in the training says what any word means; the structure comes entirely from the statistics of the corpus — which is both why it works with no labels and why it reproduces the corpus's quirks.

What the interviewer is checking

That you can generate pairs correctly (window bounds, no self-pairs, sentence boundaries); that you know why negative sampling exists and write its loss with σ and the minus sign on negatives; that you derive the three gradients; that your vectorised version accumulates repeated indices; that you sample negatives from the right distribution; and that you know the practical details — learning rate per pair, subsampling, two embedding tables — and what the result does and does not capture.
body:
1. The problem as it is usually asked

"Implement word2vec skip-gram with negative sampling in NumPy: build training pairs from a corpus, implement the loss and gradients, train with SGD, and show nearest neighbours." Clarify: window size (2 here), number of negatives k (5), embedding dimension (16), noise distribution (unigram0.75), which vectors are reported (input vectors), and whether subsampling is required (discussed, not needed on a tiny corpus). Outline: hand examples, pair builder and per-pair SGD, vectorised mini-batch loss and gradients, tests and training.

2. The maths in plain words

Give every word two vectors: one for when it is the centre (v) and one for when it appears as a context (u). For a real pair, the dot product ucontext·vcentre should be large, so that σ of it — the predicted probability the pair is real — is near 1. For each of k noise words drawn at random, the dot product should be small, so σ is near 0. The loss is the sum of the log-losses of these k + 1 tiny logistic regressions.

The gradients are the logistic-regression rule (prediction minus label, times the input) applied to each dot product. For the real pair, the label is 1, so the factor is σ(s) − 1, negative: the centre vector moves towards the context vector and the context vector towards the centre. For a noise word, the label is 0, so the factor is σ(sk), positive: they move apart. The centre vector collects all k + 1 contributions.

3. The equations

pairs:       (c, o) for each centre c and each o within ±w positions, same sentence
noise:       P_n(w) = count(w)^(3/4) / Σ_w' count(w')^(3/4)
loss:        ℓ(c, o) = −log σ(u_o·v_c) − Σ_{i=1..k} log σ(−u_{n_i}·v_c),     n_i ~ P_n
gradients:   g = σ(u_o·v_c) − 1,     g_i = σ(u_{n_i}·v_c)
             ∂ℓ/∂v_c = g·u_o + Σ_i g_i·u_{n_i}
             ∂ℓ/∂u_o = g·v_c,        ∂ℓ/∂u_{n_i} = g_i·v_c
mini-batch:  average ℓ over B pairs; scatter-add each row's gradient into V and U (np.add.at)
subsampling: discard an occurrence of w with probability 1 − √(t / f(w))
stability:   log σ(z) = min(z, 0) − log1p(exp(−|z|))

4. A worked example by hand

Noise distribution. Three words with counts 100, 10 and 1 ("the", "king", "sceptre"). Unigram shares: 100/111 = 0.901, 0.090, 0.009. Raise counts to 3/4: 1000.75 = 31.62, 100.75 = 5.62, 10.75 = 1; total 38.25. Noise shares: 0.827, 0.147, 0.026. "sceptre" is now drawn almost three times as often as its frequency alone would suggest, "the" a little less.

One update. Centre vc = [0.5, 0], true context uo = [0.4, 0.2], one negative uk = [0.2, −0.4].

  • Scores: s = uo·vc = 0.2; sk = uk·vc = 0.1.
  • Loss: −log σ(0.2) − log σ(−0.1) = log(1 + e−0.2) + log(1 + e0.1) = 0.5981 + 0.7444 = 1.3425.
  • Factors: g = σ(0.2) − 1 = 0.5498 − 1 = −0.4502; gk = σ(0.1) = 0.5250.
  • Gradients: ∂ℓ/∂vc = −0.4502·[0.4, 0.2] + 0.5250·[0.2, −0.4] = [−0.1801 + 0.1050, −0.0900 − 0.2100] = [−0.0751, −0.3000]; ∂ℓ/∂uo = −0.4502·[0.5, 0] = [−0.2251, 0]; ∂ℓ/∂uk = 0.5250·[0.5, 0] = [0.2625, 0].
  • Step with learning rate 0.5: vc = [0.5375, 0.1500], uo = [0.5125, 0.2], uk = [0.0688, −0.4]. New scores 0.306 and −0.023; loss 1.2337.

The centre moved towards the real context (its second coordinate grew towards uo's positive 0.2) and away from the negative (whose second coordinate is negative). The block asserts all of it.

import math
import numpy as np

# The hand-worked example. Noise distribution: unigram counts raised to 3/4, renormalised.
counts = np.array([100.0, 10.0, 1.0])                          # "the", "king", "sceptre"
unigram = counts / counts.sum()
noise = counts ** 0.75 / (counts ** 0.75).sum()
assert np.allclose(unigram, [0.9009, 0.0901, 0.0090], atol=1e-4)
assert np.allclose(noise, [0.8268, 0.1470, 0.0261], atol=1e-4)   # rare words sampled ~3x more often

# One SGNS update by hand: centre v_c, true context u_o, one negative u_k (2-d embeddings).
sig = lambda t: 1 / (1 + math.exp(-t))
v_c, u_o, u_k = np.array([0.5, 0.0]), np.array([0.4, 0.2]), np.array([0.2, -0.4])
s_pos, s_neg = u_o @ v_c, u_k @ v_c                            # 0.2 and 0.1
loss = -math.log(sig(s_pos)) - math.log(sig(-s_neg))
assert round(loss, 4) == 1.3425                                # 0.5981 + 0.7444
g_pos, g_neg = sig(s_pos) - 1, sig(s_neg)                      # -0.4502, 0.5250
d_vc = g_pos * u_o + g_neg * u_k
d_uo, d_uk = g_pos * v_c, g_neg * v_c
assert np.allclose(d_vc, [-0.0751, -0.3000], atol=1e-4)
assert np.allclose(d_uo, [-0.2251, 0.0], atol=1e-4) and np.allclose(d_uk, [0.2625, 0.0], atol=1e-4)
lr = 0.5
v2, uo2, uk2 = v_c - lr * d_vc, u_o - lr * d_uo, u_k - lr * d_uk
loss2 = -math.log(sig(uo2 @ v2)) - math.log(sig(-(uk2 @ v2)))
assert loss2 < loss and round(loss2, 4) == 1.2337

5. The naive implementation

build_corpus generates 3,000 sentences from six templates — royals rule or live in places, animals chase animals or run, people eat or like foods — so the "right answer" for nearest neighbours is known: words that fill the same slot. skipgram_pairs slides a ±2 window inside each sentence. sgns_step_naive is the textbook per-pair stochastic gradient descent: for each pair, compute the positive score and factor, update the context's output vector, loop over its k negatives updating each output vector and accumulating the centre's gradient, then update the centre's input vector — reading the centre vector before any update so all gradients are computed at the same point.

def build_corpus(seed=0, n_sentences=3000):
    """A tiny synthetic corpus with structure: royals rule places, animals chase animals, people eat food."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    royals, places = ["king", "queen", "prince", "princess"], ["kingdom", "castle", "realm"]
    animals, foods = ["dog", "cat", "fox", "wolf"], ["bread", "cheese", "apple", "soup"]
    people = ["man", "woman", "child"]
    templates = [
        lambda: ["the", r.choice(royals), "rules", "the", r.choice(places)],
        lambda: ["the", r.choice(royals), "lives", "in", "the", r.choice(places)],
        lambda: ["a", r.choice(animals), "chases", "a", r.choice(animals)],
        lambda: ["the", r.choice(animals), "runs", "fast"],
        lambda: ["the", r.choice(people), "eats", r.choice(foods)],
        lambda: ["a", r.choice(people), "likes", r.choice(foods)],
    ]
    sents = [templates[r.integers(len(templates))]() for _ in range(n_sentences)]
    vocab = sorted({w for s in sents for w in s})
    idx = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(vocab)}
    return [[idx[w] for w in s] for s in sents], vocab

def skipgram_pairs(sents, window=2):
    """(centre, context) for every word and every neighbour within the window, same sentence."""
    pairs = []
    for s in sents:
        for i, c in enumerate(s):
            for j in range(max(0, i - window), min(len(s), i + window + 1)):
                if j != i:
                    pairs.append((c, s[j]))
    return np.array(pairs)

def sgns_step_naive(V, U, pairs, negs, lr):
    """Plain SGD, one (centre, context) pair at a time, K negatives each. V: centre vectors, U: context vectors."""
    total = 0.0
    for (c, o), ks in zip(pairs, negs):
        v = V[c].copy()
        s = U[o] @ v
        g = 1 / (1 + math.exp(-s)) - 1                           # d loss / d s_pos
        dv = g * U[o]
        total += -math.log(1 / (1 + math.exp(-s)))
        U[o] -= lr * g * v
        for k in ks:
            sk = U[k] @ v
            gk = 1 / (1 + math.exp(-sk))                         # d loss / d s_neg
            dv += gk * U[k]
            total += -math.log(1 / (1 + math.exp(sk)))
            U[k] -= lr * gk * v
        V[c] -= lr * dv
    return total / len(pairs)

6. The vectorised implementation

sgns_loss_grads processes a batch of B pairs with k negatives each. It gathers the centre vectors (B, d), computes positive scores with a row-wise dot product and negative scores with one einsum against the gathered negatives (B, k, d), and computes the mean loss with the stable log-sigmoid. The factors σ(s) − 1 and σ(sk) come from exp(log σ) so they inherit stability. The centre gradients are one expression, and then the essential step: np.add.at scatters each row's gradient into the full V and U matrices, accumulating when the same word appears several times in the batch as a centre, context or negative. Plain fancy-indexed assignment would keep only one of those contributions. noise_distribution computes unigram0.75 from the corpus, and nearest ranks words by cosine similarity of their input vectors.

def log_sigmoid(z):
    return np.minimum(z, 0) - np.log1p(np.exp(-np.abs(z)))

def sgns_loss_grads(V, U, C, O, K):
    """Mini-batch SGNS. C, O: (B,) centre and context ids; K: (B, k) negative ids.
    loss = mean_b [ -log s(u_o.v_c) - sum_k log s(-u_k.v_c) ]."""
    v = V[C]                                                     # (B, d)
    s_pos = (U[O] * v).sum(axis=1)                               # (B,)
    s_neg = np.einsum("bkd,bd->bk", U[K], v)                     # (B, k)
    loss = -(log_sigmoid(s_pos).sum() + log_sigmoid(-s_neg).sum()) / len(C)
    g_pos = (np.exp(log_sigmoid(s_pos)) - 1) / len(C)            # sigma(s) - 1
    g_neg = np.exp(log_sigmoid(s_neg)) / len(C)                  # sigma(s_k)
    dv = g_pos[:, None] * U[O] + np.einsum("bk,bkd->bd", g_neg, U[K])
    dV, dU = np.zeros_like(V), np.zeros_like(U)
    np.add.at(dV, C, dv)                                         # words repeat in a batch: accumulate
    np.add.at(dU, O, g_pos[:, None] * v)
    np.add.at(dU, K, g_neg[:, :, None] * v[:, None, :])
    return float(loss), dV, dU

def noise_distribution(ids, n_vocab, power=0.75):
    c = np.bincount(ids, minlength=n_vocab).astype(float)
    p = c ** power
    return p / p.sum()

def nearest(V, vocab, word, k=3):
    E = V / np.linalg.norm(V, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    sims = E @ E[vocab.index(word)]
    order = [i for i in np.argsort(-sims) if vocab[i] != word]
    return [str(vocab[i]) for i in order[:k]]

7. Testing it

Six checks. (1) Pair construction: a five-word sentence with window 2 gives 14 pairs, and a three-word sentence with window 1 gives exactly the four adjacent pairs. (2) On the corpus, the 3/4 power lowers "the"'s share and raises the rarest word's. (3) Central finite differences at three entries of each matrix — chosen to be a centre, a context and a negative in the batch — match the analytic gradients to 10−8. (4) Twenty passes of the naive per-pair SGD over a fixed batch lower its loss. (5) Six epochs of mini-batch SGD over 37,940 pairs (batches of 128, learning rate 0.025 per pair, input vectors initialised small and output vectors at zero as in word2vec) lower the loss from about 3.47 to 1.77; and every group's nearest neighbours are exactly its other members: king → prince, queen, princess; dog → wolf, fox, cat; bread → soup, apple, cheese; castle → realm, kingdom. (6) PyTorch autograd on the same loss built from logsigmoid gives identical loss and gradients for both matrices.

sents, vocab = build_corpus()
pairs = skipgram_pairs(sents)
n_vocab, dim, k = len(vocab), 16, 5
flat = np.array([w for s in sents for w in s])
P_noise = noise_distribution(flat, n_vocab)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

# 1. Pair construction: a 5-word sentence with window 2 gives 2+3+4+3+2 = 14 pairs.
assert len(skipgram_pairs([[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]])) == 14
assert set(map(tuple, skipgram_pairs([[7, 8, 9]], window=1))) == {(7, 8), (8, 7), (8, 9), (9, 8)}

# 2. The 3/4 power flattens the distribution: frequent words lose share, rare ones gain.
uni = np.bincount(flat, minlength=n_vocab) / len(flat)
the, rare = vocab.index("the"), int(np.argmin(uni))
assert P_noise[the] < uni[the] and P_noise[rare] > uni[rare]

# 3. Gradient check of the mini-batch loss.
V = rng.normal(scale=0.3, size=(n_vocab, dim)); U = rng.normal(scale=0.3, size=(n_vocab, dim))
b = rng.choice(len(pairs), 32, replace=False)
C, O = pairs[b, 0], pairs[b, 1]
K = rng.choice(n_vocab, size=(32, k), p=P_noise)
L0, dV, dU = sgns_loss_grads(V, U, C, O, K)
for M, G in ((V, dV), (U, dU)):
    for i in [(int(C[0]), 0), (int(O[3]), 5), (int(K[2, 1]), 15)]:
        old = M[i]; M[i] = old + 1e-6; lp = sgns_loss_grads(V, U, C, O, K)[0]
        M[i] = old - 1e-6; lm = sgns_loss_grads(V, U, C, O, K)[0]; M[i] = old
        assert abs((lp - lm) / 2e-6 - G[i]) < 1e-8

# 4. The naive per-pair SGD and the batched version both reduce the loss on the same data.
Vn, Un = V.copy(), U.copy()
before = sgns_loss_grads(Vn, Un, C, O, K)[0]
for _ in range(20):
    sgns_step_naive(Vn, Un, list(zip(C.tolist(), O.tolist())), K.tolist(), lr=0.05)
assert sgns_loss_grads(Vn, Un, C, O, K)[0] < before

# 5. Train with mini-batch SGD; words used in the same contexts end up as nearest neighbours.
V = rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=(n_vocab, dim)); U = np.zeros((n_vocab, dim))   # word2vec-style init
hist = []
for epoch in range(6):
    order = rng.permutation(len(pairs))
    for start in range(0, len(order), 128):
        bb = order[start:start + 128]
        Kb = rng.choice(n_vocab, size=(len(bb), k), p=P_noise)
        L, dV, dU = sgns_loss_grads(V, U, pairs[bb, 0], pairs[bb, 1], Kb)
        V -= 0.025 * len(bb) * dV; U -= 0.025 * len(bb) * dU                # lr 0.025 per pair, word2vec's default
        hist.append(L)
assert np.mean(hist[-20:]) < 0.6 * np.mean(hist[:20])
groups = {"king": {"queen", "prince", "princess"}, "dog": {"cat", "fox", "wolf"},
          "bread": {"cheese", "apple", "soup"}, "castle": {"kingdom", "realm"}}
for w, same in groups.items():
    assert set(nearest(V, vocab, w, k=len(same))) == same, (w, nearest(V, vocab, w))

# 6. Cross-check loss and gradients with PyTorch autograd, if available.
try:
    import torch
    Vt = torch.tensor(V, requires_grad=True); Ut = torch.tensor(U, requires_grad=True)
    Ct, Ot, Kt = torch.tensor(C), torch.tensor(O), torch.tensor(K)
    vv = Vt[Ct]
    Lt = -(torch.nn.functional.logsigmoid((Ut[Ot] * vv).sum(1)).sum()
           + torch.nn.functional.logsigmoid(-(Ut[Kt] @ vv[:, :, None])[..., 0]).sum()) / len(C)
    Lt.backward()
    Ln, dVn, dUn = sgns_loss_grads(V, U, C, O, K)
    assert np.isclose(Lt.item(), Ln) and np.allclose(Vt.grad.numpy(), dVn) and np.allclose(Ut.grad.numpy(), dUn)
except ImportError:
    pass
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"{len(sents)} sentences, {len(pairs)} pairs, vocab {n_vocab}; loss {np.mean(hist[:20]):.3f} -> {np.mean(hist[-20:]):.3f}")
    for w in groups:
        print(w, "->", nearest(V, vocab, w))

The first version of test 5 used a learning rate of 0.5 per pair with batches of 256 and diverged within an epoch: losses overflowed to 10290. The cause was not a bug in the gradient — the gradient check passed — but the interaction of a correct scatter-add with frequent words: "the" appears in a large share of pairs, so its summed gradient in one batch was dozens of single-pair updates applied at once. Dropping to word2vec's default 0.025 per pair fixed it.

8. Numerical and practical traps

Accumulation. Use np.add.at (or a scatter-add); fancy-index assignment silently drops repeats. Learning rate with repeats. Set the rate per pair and keep it small; frequent words multiply it. Log-sigmoid stability. Scores grow as training proceeds; use the stable form. Initialisation. Output vectors at zero and small random input vectors (word2vec's choice) start every score at zero; initialising both large makes early gradients noisy. Negatives that equal the context. Occasionally the sampled negative is the true context; word2vec does not exclude it, and the effect averages out. Sentence boundaries. Windows should not cross sentences or documents.

9. Edge cases worth naming

Words seen once get few updates and poor vectors; word2vec drops words below a minimum count (5 by default in the original tool). Out-of-vocabulary words have no vector at all; fastText fixes this with character n-gram vectors. Very short sentences produce few pairs. Polysemy: "bank" gets one vector mixing its senses. A vocabulary of millions makes the noise sampling itself a cost; word2vec precomputes a large table of word ids in proportion to Pn and samples indices from it.

10. Complexity

Per pair: O((k + 1)·d) for scores and gradients, independent of vocabulary size — the point of negative sampling — versus O(V·d) for a full softmax. An epoch over a corpus of T tokens with window w costs O(T·2w·(k + 1)·d). Memory: two V × d matrices. In the toy: 37,940 pairs × 6 negatives × 16 dimensions per epoch, a fraction of a second in NumPy.

11. Talking through the design

Start with the softmax objective and why it is too expensive, introduce negative sampling as k + 1 logistic regressions, give the noise distribution and the reason for 3/4, derive the gradients, then implement with attention to accumulation and learning rate. Finish with subsampling, what the vectors capture (context similarity, including bias), and the link to PMI matrix factorisation.
deep:
SGNS as matrix factorisation

Levy and Goldberg showed that if the embedding dimension is large enough, the SGNS objective is optimised when uo·vc = PMI(c, o) − log k, where PMI is the pointwise mutual information log(P(c, o)/(P(c)·P(o))). So word2vec implicitly factorises a shifted PMI matrix of word-context co-occurrences into V·Uᵀ. That explains several empirical facts: why two vectors per word are needed (the matrix is not symmetric in general), why k acts as a shift that discourages low-PMI pairs, and why count-based methods — build the PMI matrix, take a truncated SVD — perform comparably when their hyperparameters are tuned the same way. GloVe takes the explicit route, fitting log co-occurrence counts with a weighted least-squares loss.

CBOW, the sibling model

Continuous bag-of-words reverses skip-gram: average the context words' input vectors and predict the centre. It is faster (one prediction per position rather than 2w) and smooths over contexts, which tends to help frequent words; skip-gram treats each context pair separately and tends to give better vectors for rare words. Both can use negative sampling or hierarchical softmax, and the loss and gradient structure is the same as in this lesson with the averaged context in place of the centre vector.

Hierarchical softmax

The alternative to negative sampling in the paper replaces the flat softmax with a binary tree over the vocabulary — a Huffman tree, so frequent words have short paths — and models p(w | c) as the product of left/right sigmoid decisions along w's path, about log2(V) of them. It computes a proper normalised probability at O(log V) cost, whereas negative sampling computes none at O(k). For learning vectors, negative sampling usually works better and is simpler, which is why it became the default.

From word2vec to modern embeddings

Static word vectors give each word one vector regardless of context, so "bank" in "river bank" and "bank account" are the same. Contextual models compute a vector per occurrence from the whole sentence and have replaced static vectors for most tasks. But the training ideas persist: predicting neighbours as self-supervision (masked language modelling generalises it), contrasting real pairs with noise (mc28's InfoNCE), and sparse embedding tables trained with negative sampling, which remain central to large-scale recommendation, where item-to-item "word2vec" over user sessions is still a strong baseline.

Why the learning rate is per pair

The original word2vec tool processes one pair at a time with a learning rate that starts at 0.025 and decays linearly to near zero over training, with several threads updating the shared matrices without locks. Each update is small and immediately visible to the next pair. A mini-batch implementation that averages gradients over B pairs and steps with rate η is equivalent to applying B single-pair updates simultaneously, each at rate η/B — except that the gradients are all computed at the same old point. For rare words that difference is negligible; for a word that appears in a quarter of the batch, its single summed update equals dozens of sequential ones computed at a stale position, which overshoots. Scaling the step as rate × B × mean gradient (as the lesson does) keeps the per-pair rate fixed, so 0.025 per pair matches the original tool's behaviour and stays stable.

Bias in, bias out

Because vectors encode co-occurrence statistics, they encode whatever associations the corpus contains, including social stereotypes; well-known analyses found occupation words aligned with gender directions in news-trained embeddings. Debiasing methods project out identified directions, but the safer engineering stance is to measure associations relevant to the application and to remember that nearest neighbours reflect the training text, not ground truth.
prod:
Where this still runs

Pre-trained word2vec, GloVe and fastText vectors remain common in lightweight classifiers, feature pipelines and resource-constrained settings. The SGNS training recipe itself is widely used beyond words: "item2vec"-style embeddings trained on sequences of products viewed or bought, graph embeddings trained on random walks (DeepWalk, node2vec), and candidate-generation embeddings in recommender systems, all with negative sampling and sparse updates.

Failure modes and symptoms

Divergence or NaNs. Frequent ids receiving summed updates with too large a learning rate; fix with a smaller per-pair rate, subsampling, or adaptive optimisers.

Rare items with junk vectors. Too few updates; raise the minimum count, use character or attribute features (fastText), or share parameters.

Popularity dominating neighbours. Everything is near the most frequent items; negative sampling distribution too flat, or no subsampling. Tune the noise exponent and subsampling threshold.

Stale vocabulary. New words or items have no vectors; plan for periodic retraining or a fallback.

Leaking sentence boundaries. Symptom: unrelated words become neighbours because they often end and start consecutive documents. Cause: windows crossing document or sentence boundaries. Fix: build pairs within sentences or documents only.

What to monitor and tune

Training loss per epoch; nearest-neighbour spot checks on known groups; downstream task metrics; vector norms (exploding norms precede divergence). Tune dimension (100-300 for words), window (larger for topical similarity, smaller for syntactic), negatives k, the noise exponent (0.75 default), subsampling threshold t, minimum count and the learning rate schedule (word2vec decays linearly from 0.025).

A cost estimate

A corpus of 1 billion tokens, window 5, k = 5, d = 300: about 10 pairs per token and 6 dot products of 300 dimensions per pair, plus the same again for gradients — roughly 109 × 10 × 6 × 300 × 2 ≈ 3.6 × 1013 multiply-adds per epoch, minutes to hours on a multi-core CPU, which is why word2vec could be trained without accelerators. Subsampling frequent words typically removes a large share of tokens and speeds this further.

The reference for this problem

Mikolov, Sutskever, Chen, Corrado and Dean (2013) define the negative-sampling objective log σ(v′wOᵀvwI) + Σi=1..k Ewi∼Pn(w)[log σ(−v′wiᵀvwI)], report that k in the range 5-20 is useful for small training datasets and 2-5 for large ones, find that the unigram distribution raised to the 3/4 power outperformed the unigram and uniform distributions, and introduce subsampling of frequent words with discard probability 1 − √(t/f(w)). They note explicitly that, unlike NCE, negative sampling does not approximately maximise the softmax log-probability, which does not matter for their purpose.
myths: word2vec learns meaning.

It learns which words appear near which other words. Words used in the same contexts get similar vectors, which often lines up with meaning (king and queen, dog and cat) but also groups antonyms (hot and cold share contexts) and reflects every bias in the corpus. The distributional hypothesis is a useful approximation, not a definition of meaning.
Negative sampling approximates the softmax.

Noise-contrastive estimation can be shown to approximate the softmax's log-likelihood; negative sampling, the simplification word2vec uses, does not — it optimises a different objective (logistic regression of real pairs against noise pairs). Mikolov et al. say so directly: they only care about the vector quality, not the probabilities.
Each word has one vector.

Skip-gram trains two: an input (centre) vector and an output (context) vector per word. The input vectors are usually kept as the embeddings; some practitioners average the two. Using one shared matrix changes the objective — a word would then be pushed to be similar to itself.
Negatives should be drawn uniformly or by frequency.

Uniform sampling picks mostly rare words, which are easy negatives; frequency sampling picks mostly 'the' and 'a'. The paper found the unigram distribution raised to the 3/4 power beats both: it keeps frequent words common as negatives but gives rare ones roughly proportionally more chances — in the lesson's example, a word with 1% of the counts goes from 0.9% to 2.6% of the samples.
Mini-batch updates can just assign gradients by index.

Frequent words appear many times in a batch. Writing grad[ids] = values keeps only one of the contributions; you must accumulate with np.add.at (or a scatter-add). And because those contributions add up, a learning rate that is fine per pair can blow up 'the' — the lesson's first attempt diverged exactly this way.
lab:
Goal: run the solution, then vary it, break it and measure it. Python 3.12 with NumPy (the gpt_env venv); PyTorch only for the optional cross-check.

  1. Run the four blocks as one script. All assertions pass and it prints the loss before and after training and each group's nearest neighbours.
  2. Vary by hand. Redo the update in section 4 with two negatives, adding uk2 = [−0.3, 0.1], and check the new centre gradient with the batched function.
  3. Break the accumulation. Replace np.add.at(dV, C, dv) with dV[C] = dv. Does the gradient check catch it? Does training still find the groups?
  4. Reproduce the divergence. Set the learning rate back to 0.5 per pair with batches of 256 and watch the vector norm of "the" each epoch.
  5. Change the noise. Train with exponents 0 (uniform), 0.75 and 1.0 (unigram) and compare the nearest neighbours and final loss.
  6. Add subsampling. Drop each occurrence of a word with probability max(0, 1 − √(t/f)) for t = 0.01 before building pairs; how many pairs remain, and how do the neighbours change?

Each run takes a few seconds; keep the seed fixed when comparing settings so differences come from the change, not from sampling. What to look for: the overwrite bug passes the single-coordinate gradient check only when the checked index is not repeated; divergence starts with the most frequent word; uniform noise makes negatives too easy; subsampling removes most "the" pairs without hurting the groups.
recap: Skip-gram predicts context words from a centre word; training pairs are (centre, context) within a window of ±w words.
Each word has an input vector v and an output vector u; the score of a pair is u_o·v_c.
A full softmax over the vocabulary is too expensive, so negative sampling turns each pair into a logistic-regression problem: real context versus k noise words.
The per-pair loss is −log σ(u_o·v_c) − Σ_k log σ(−u_k·v_c), with negatives drawn from unigram counts raised to the 3/4 power.
Gradients: with g = σ(u_o·v_c) − 1 and g_k = σ(u_k·v_c), dv_c = g·u_o + Σ g_k·u_k, du_o = g·v_c, du_k = g_k·v_c.
In a mini-batch, repeated words must accumulate their gradients (np.add.at).
Frequent words receive many updates per batch, so learning rates are set per pair and kept small (word2vec's default 0.025).
Subsampling discards frequent words with probability 1 − √(t/f) to spend training on informative pairs.
After training, cosine similarity between input vectors finds words used in similar contexts.
Correctness is checked against finite differences and autograd; quality by nearest neighbours on a corpus with known structure.

drill:
Work it out

(a) A corpus has 1,000,000 tokens; "the" occurs 60,000 times and "sceptre" 20. With subsampling threshold t = 10−4, what fraction of each word's occurrences are discarded? (b) After subsampling, what are their shares in a unigram0.75 noise distribution relative to each other?

Answer 
f_the, f_sc = 60_000 / 1e6, 20 / 1e6
drop = lambda f, t=1e-4: max(0.0, 1 - math.sqrt(t / f))
assert round(drop(f_the), 3) == 0.959 and drop(f_sc) == 0.0
kept_the = 60_000 * (1 - drop(f_the))
ratio = (kept_the / 20) ** 0.75
assert round(kept_the) == 2449 and round(ratio, 1) == 36.8

(a) "the" has frequency 0.06, so it is discarded with probability 1 − √(10−4/0.06) = 1 − 0.0408 = 95.9%; "sceptre" has frequency 2 × 10−5, below t, so √(t/f) > 1 and nothing is discarded. (b) About 2,449 occurrences of "the" remain against 20 of "sceptre", a ratio of 122; raised to 3/4 it becomes 36.8: "the" is still drawn as a negative about 37 times as often as "sceptre", against 3,000 times in the raw unigram distribution. Subsampling and the 3/4 power together move a lot of training effort from frequent to rare words.
qa: E
How are skip-gram training pairs built?

Slide a window over each sentence; for each centre word, every word within w positions on either side (in the same sentence) gives a (centre, context) pair. A 5-word sentence with w = 2 gives 2 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 14 pairs. word2vec also samples the window size per position from 1 to w, which weights nearer words more.
E
Why not use a softmax over the vocabulary?

p(o | c) = exp(u_o·v_c)/Σ_w exp(u_w·v_c) needs a dot product with every word's output vector for every pair — 10⁵-10⁷ terms in real vocabularies — and its gradient touches every output vector. Negative sampling replaces the sum with k + 1 dot products: the true context and k sampled noise words.
E
Write the SGNS loss for one pair.

−log σ(u_o·v_c) − Σ_{i=1..k} log σ(−u_{n_i}·v_c), where n_i are drawn from the noise distribution. The first term rewards a high score for the real context; the second rewards low scores for the noise words. It is logistic regression with label 1 for the real pair and 0 for each noise pair.
M
Derive the gradients.

Let s = u_o·v_c and s_k = u_k·v_c. d/ds of −log σ(s) is σ(s) − 1; d/ds_k of −log σ(−s_k) is σ(s_k). So dv_c = (σ(s) − 1)·u_o + Σ σ(s_k)·u_k, du_o = (σ(s) − 1)·v_c, du_k = σ(s_k)·v_c. The centre moves towards its real context and away from the noise words, each output vector moves towards (real) or away from (noise) the centre.
Follow-up: What if the same word is drawn as a negative twice? — Its gradients add; it gets pushed twice as hard, which is the correct gradient of the sampled objective.
M
Work one update by hand.
M
Why raise the unigram distribution to the 3/4 power?

It flattens the distribution: frequent words still dominate but less, and rare words are sampled more than their raw frequency. Counts 100, 10, 1 have unigram shares 0.901, 0.090, 0.009 but noise shares 0.827, 0.147, 0.026. Mikolov et al. found U(w)^(3/4)/Z significantly outperformed both the unigram and the uniform distributions.
M
How many negatives?

The paper reports k in the range 5-20 is useful for small training datasets, while for large datasets k can be as small as 2-5. More negatives cost more compute per pair; with lots of data, each word sees enough negatives across many pairs anyway.
M
What does subsampling do?

Each occurrence of word w is discarded with probability 1 − √(t/f(w)), where f is its frequency and t a small threshold. Very frequent words like 'the' are dropped most of the time; rare words are never dropped. It speeds training and improves rare-word vectors, because 'France'–'Paris' co-occurrences teach more than 'France'–'the'.
H
Your mini-batch implementation diverges though the per-pair version trains. Why?

Repeated words: in a batch of 256 pairs, 'the' may appear dozens of times as centre, context or negative. Accumulating its gradients (correctly, with add.at) and stepping with a learning rate tuned for a single pair multiplies its update by its count, so its vector explodes and spreads NaNs. Fixes: a smaller per-pair rate (word2vec uses 0.025 with linear decay), smaller batches, subsampling frequent words, or optimisers with per-parameter scaling such as Adagrad or sparse Adam.

Follow-up: Why did the original C code not have this problem? — It updates one pair at a time with Hogwild-style asynchronous threads, so a frequent word's updates are applied sequentially rather than summed.
H
What does SGNS optimise, in matrix terms?

Levy and Goldberg showed that, at its optimum and with enough dimensions, SGNS implicitly factorises a word-context matrix whose entries are the pointwise mutual information of the pair shifted by log k: u_o·v_c ≈ PMI(c, o) − log k. That connects word2vec to classic count-based methods (PMI matrices and SVD) and explains why both work similarly when tuned comparably.
H
Why keep two vectors per word?

With a single vector, a word's score with itself, v_w·v_w = ‖v_w‖², is always large, but words rarely appear in their own context; a single matrix would be pulled to make words dissimilar to themselves. Separate input and output matrices let 'dog' be a likely context of 'cat' without forcing any word to predict itself. After training, the input vectors are usually used; summing both is a common variant.
H
How would you evaluate the embeddings?

Intrinsically with word similarity benchmarks (correlation of cosine similarity with human ratings) and analogy tasks (king − man + woman ≈ queen); extrinsically by plugging them into a downstream model. On a synthetic corpus, as here, check that words generated from the same slot become nearest neighbours. Beware analogy tests: they exclude the input words from the answers, and results are sensitive to that choice.

t: Matrix factorisation for recommendations: SGD, ALS, biases and implicit feedback
sum: Predict a rating as global mean + user bias + item bias + a dot product of latent factors: one SGD step and one ALS solve worked by hand, Funk-style SGD and closed-form alternating least squares on synthetic ratings, test RMSE falling from 1.10 (mean) to 0.94 (biases) to 0.51 (factors), overfitting without regularisation, and the implicit-feedback weighted ALS with its YᵀY speed-up checked against a direct solve.
prereq: rec3
Collaborative filtering: neighbourhood methods and matrix factorisation (ALS and SGD) learn from the user-item interaction matrix; implicit feedback is weighted differently.
mc1
Ridge regression has the closed form w = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy; regularisation shrinks weights to reduce overfitting.
mc12
Stochastic gradient descent updates parameters a little after each example.
mc8
The SVD factorises a complete matrix into low-rank factors; it is undefined for a matrix with missing entries.
mc11
Checking a gradient or update rule against autograd or finite differences.
why:
A streaming service knows which of its million users watched or rated which of its fifty thousand titles. Almost all of that table is empty: a typical user has rated a few dozen titles. The business question is how to fill in the blanks — which unseen titles would this user rate highly? — and in 2006 Netflix offered a million dollars for a 10% improvement on its own system's error. The techniques that won, and that still sit inside many recommender systems, came from treating the user-item matrix as approximately low-rank: each user and each item is a short vector of hidden "taste" coordinates, and a rating is roughly the dot product of the two.

Koren, Bell and Volinsky — members of the winning team — summarised the approach in a 2009 article: fit user and item factor vectors to the observed ratings only, regularise them so they do not memorise, add biases for generous users and popular items, and optimise either by stochastic gradient descent, as popularised by Simon Funk's blog post during the competition, or by alternating least squares, which turns the non-convex problem into a sequence of small exact ridge regressions. A year earlier, Hu, Koren and Volinsky had adapted the method to implicit feedback — clicks, plays, purchases — where there are no ratings, only behaviour with varying confidence, and showed how to fit over every user-item pair without paying for every pair.

The interview problem asks you to build this from scratch: the model with biases, an SGD trainer, an ALS trainer, held-out evaluation, and an explanation of regularisation and implicit feedback. This lesson works one SGD step and one ALS solve by hand; implements both optimisers on synthetic ratings generated from a known rank-3 model with biases and noise; shows test RMSE falling from 1.104 for the global mean to 0.937 with biases and 0.509-0.511 with factors, while the ALS objective decreases every sweep; shows that 20 factors with no regularisation reach a training RMSE of 0.001 and a test RMSE worse than the mean; and checks the implicit-feedback ALS shortcut against a direct weighted solve.
primer:
The analogy: a taste profile and a flavour profile

A wine shop wants to predict how much each customer will like each bottle. The owner describes every bottle by a few flavour scores — how fruity, how oaky, how tannic — and every customer by how much they like each of those flavours. A customer's predicted enjoyment is the sum over flavours of (how much the bottle has it) × (how much the customer likes it): a dot product. Some customers are simply enthusiastic and score everything high; some bottles are just good and everyone likes them more; so the owner also notes a personal offset for each customer and each bottle. Nobody hands the owner the flavour scores. Instead the owner guesses them, compares predictions with the ratings customers actually gave, and adjusts: when a customer liked a bottle more than predicted, nudge the customer's profile towards that bottle's flavours and the bottle's flavours towards that customer's tastes.

The flavour scores are item factors qi, the tastes are user factors pu, the offsets are biases bu and bi, the shop's average rating is μ, and nudging after each rating is SGD. An alternative routine — fix every bottle's flavours, then work out each customer's best tastes exactly; then fix the tastes and work out each bottle's flavours exactly — is alternating least squares.

The analogy breaks where it matters most: the owner chose the flavour dimensions, but the model does not. Its factors are whatever directions best explain the ratings, and they rarely correspond neatly to named attributes. They are useful because they predict, not because they explain.

Where this sits in a recommender

A production recommender usually has stages: candidate generation narrows millions of items to a few hundred per user, ranking scores those candidates with a richer model, and re-ranking adds business rules and diversity. Matrix factorisation is a classic candidate generator: once user and item factors exist, the best candidates for a user are the items with the largest dot products, which approximate-nearest-neighbour search can find quickly. The learned factors are also reused as features — user and item embeddings — by the ranking model. That is why the method survives in systems whose final ranking is done by much larger models: it is cheap, it captures collaborative signal well, and its output is a vector space.

What the interviewer is checking

That you fit observed entries only (not an SVD of a filled matrix); that you include biases and regularisation and can say why; that the SGD update uses old values and the right signs; that you can derive the ALS step as ridge regression; that you evaluate on held-out ratings against sensible baselines; and that you know how implicit feedback changes the objective and how ALS stays affordable on it.
body:
1. The problem as it is usually asked

"Given (user, item, rating) triples, implement matrix factorisation with biases, trained with SGD and with ALS. Evaluate on held-out ratings. Discuss regularisation and how you would handle implicit feedback." Clarify: explicit ratings (real-valued here); number of factors k (3 here, the true rank of the synthetic data); an 80/20 random split of the observed ratings; RMSE as the metric; λ chosen per method. Outline: hand examples, data generator and SGD, ALS and the implicit variant, tests.

2. The maths in plain words

Predict each rating as the overall average, plus how much this user tends to rate above or below average, plus how much this item tends to be rated above or below average, plus the dot product of the user's and the item's factor vectors. Choose all these numbers to make predictions close to the observed ratings, while penalising large values so they generalise.

SGD goes through the observed ratings in random order. For each, compute the error (actual minus predicted). If positive, the prediction was too low, so raise the user's and item's biases a little, move the user's factors a little in the direction of the item's factors, and the item's towards the user's — each step shrunk slightly towards zero by the regularisation.

ALS notices that if all item factors and item biases were known, each user's parameters would be an ordinary ridge regression: the "features" are the factor vectors of the items the user rated (plus a constant for the bias), and the "targets" are the ratings minus the global mean and the item biases. Ridge regression has a closed-form solution, so solve it for every user; then swap roles and solve for every item; repeat.

3. The equations

model:      r̂_ui = μ + b_u + b_i + p_uᵀ q_i                          p_u, q_i ∈ ℝᵏ
objective:  min Σ_(u,i)∈observed (r_ui − r̂_ui)² + λ(‖p_u‖² + ‖q_i‖² + b_u² + b_i²)
SGD:        e = r_ui − r̂_ui
            b_u ← b_u + γ(e − λ b_u)          b_i ← b_i + γ(e − λ b_i)
            p_u ← p_u + γ(e q_i − λ p_u)      q_i ← q_i + γ(e p_u_old − λ q_i)
ALS (user): X_u = [q_i, 1] for items i rated by u      y_u = r_ui − μ − b_i
            [p_u; b_u] = (X_uᵀ X_u + λ I)⁻¹ X_uᵀ y_u              (then the same for items)
implicit:   p_ui = 1[r_ui > 0],   c_ui = 1 + α r_ui
            min Σ_all (u,i) c_ui (p_ui − x_uᵀ y_i)² + λ(Σ‖x_u‖² + Σ‖y_i‖²)
            x_u = (YᵀY + Yᵀ(Cᵘ − I)Y + λI)⁻¹ Yᵀ Cᵘ p(u)            (Cᵘ − I non-zero on n_u items)
metric:     RMSE = √(mean over held-out (r − r̂)²)

4. A worked example by hand

Biases. Koren et al.'s example: the average rating over all movies is μ = 3.7; Titanic is rated 0.5 above average; Joe rates 0.3 below average. Baseline estimate for Joe on Titanic: 3.7 + 0.5 − 0.3 = 3.9, before any interaction term.

One SGD step. k = 1, μ = 3, bu = bi = 0, pu = 0.5, qi = 0.4, observed r = 4, learning rate γ = 0.1, λ = 0.1.

  • Prediction 3 + 0 + 0 + 0.5 × 0.4 = 3.2; error e = 0.8.
  • Biases: bu = 0 + 0.1(0.8 − 0) = 0.08, bi = 0.08.
  • Factors, both from the old values: pu = 0.5 + 0.1(0.8 × 0.4 − 0.1 × 0.5) = 0.5 + 0.027 = 0.527; qi = 0.4 + 0.1(0.8 × 0.5 − 0.1 × 0.4) = 0.4 + 0.036 = 0.436.
  • New prediction 3 + 0.16 + 0.527 × 0.436 = 3.390: the error fell from 0.8 to 0.61 in one step.

One ALS solve. A user rated two items whose (fixed) factors are q1 = 1 and q2 = 2 (k = 1, no bias to keep it short), with targets r − μ − bi of 1 and 3, and λ = 1. Ridge: p = (q1² + q2² + λ)⁻¹(q1·1 + q2·3) = (1 + 4 + 1)⁻¹(1 + 6) = 7/6 ≈ 1.167. Without regularisation it would be 7/5 = 1.4; λ shrinks it towards zero.

import numpy as np

# Hand-worked numbers. Baseline predictor from the paper's example: mu + b_i + b_u.
assert round(3.7 + 0.5 + (-0.3), 1) == 3.9                     # Joe rating Titanic

# One SGD step on one rating, k = 1: mu = 3, b_u = b_i = 0, p_u = 0.5, q_i = 0.4, r = 4.
mu, bu, bi, pu, qi, r, g, lam = 3.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.5, 0.4, 4.0, 0.1, 0.1
pred = mu + bu + bi + pu * qi                                  # 3.2
e = r - pred                                                   # 0.8
bu, bi = bu + g * (e - lam * bu), bi + g * (e - lam * bi)      # 0.08 each
pu, qi = pu + g * (e * qi - lam * pu), qi + g * (e * pu - lam * qi)   # both from the OLD values
assert np.isclose(e, 0.8) and np.allclose([bu, bi, pu, qi], [0.08, 0.08, 0.527, 0.436])
assert np.isclose(mu + bu + bi + pu * qi, 3.389772)            # error falls from 0.8 to 0.61

# One ALS user update by hand: item factors fixed (k = 1), targets are r - mu - b_i.
Q_u = np.array([[1.0], [2.0]]); y = np.array([1.0, 3.0]); lam_als = 1.0
p_new = np.linalg.solve(Q_u.T @ Q_u + lam_als * np.eye(1), Q_u.T @ y)
assert np.isclose(p_new[0], 7 / 6)                             # (1*1 + 2*3) / (1 + 4 + 1)

5. The naive implementation: data and SGD

make_ratings creates 80 users and 60 items with true rank-3 factors, user and item biases and a mean of 3.5, observes 30% of cells at random and adds noise of standard deviation 0.3 — so the best achievable test RMSE is about 0.3, and we know the right k. sgd_epoch is the textbook loop: visit observed ratings in random order, compute the error, apply the four updates, copying pu first so qi is updated with the old value. It is "naive" in the sense of one rating at a time in Python, which is exactly how the method is usually written; vectorising SGD changes the algorithm.

def make_ratings(n_users=80, n_items=60, k=3, density=0.3, noise=0.3, seed=0):
    """Synthetic explicit ratings: mu + user bias + item bias + rank-k interaction + noise,
    observed for a random 30% of (user, item) cells."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    P, Q = r.normal(scale=0.7, size=(n_users, k)), r.normal(scale=0.7, size=(n_items, k))
    bu, bi = r.normal(scale=0.4, size=n_users), r.normal(scale=0.4, size=n_items)
    full = 3.5 + bu[:, None] + bi[None, :] + P @ Q.T
    mask = r.random((n_users, n_items)) < density
    users, items = np.nonzero(mask)
    ratings = full[users, items] + r.normal(scale=noise, size=len(users))
    return users, items, ratings, n_users, n_items

def rmse(u, i, r, model):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean((r - predict(model, u, i)) ** 2)))

def predict(m, u, i):
    return m["mu"] + m["bu"][u] + m["bi"][i] + (m["P"][u] * m["Q"][i]).sum(axis=-1)

def init_model(nu, ni, k, mu, seed=1):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    return {"mu": mu, "bu": np.zeros(nu), "bi": np.zeros(ni),
            "P": r.normal(scale=0.1, size=(nu, k)), "Q": r.normal(scale=0.1, size=(ni, k))}

def sgd_epoch(m, users, items, ratings, lr=0.02, lam=0.05, rng=None):
    """Funk-style SGD, one rating at a time, in a random order (the Koren et al. update rules)."""
    order = rng.permutation(len(ratings)) if rng is not None else range(len(ratings))
    for t in order:
        u, i, r = users[t], items[t], ratings[t]
        e = r - (m["mu"] + m["bu"][u] + m["bi"][i] + m["P"][u] @ m["Q"][i])
        m["bu"][u] += lr * (e - lam * m["bu"][u])
        m["bi"][i] += lr * (e - lam * m["bi"][i])
        pu = m["P"][u].copy()
        m["P"][u] += lr * (e * m["Q"][i] - lam * pu)
        m["Q"][i] += lr * (e * pu - lam * m["Q"][i])

6. ALS and the implicit variant

als_sweep does one user half-step and one item half-step. For each user it gathers the indices of their ratings (via a sort and searchsorted so each user's slice is found in O(1) after one O(n log n) sort), builds a design matrix of the rated items' factors plus a column of ones for the bias, forms the targets r − μ − bi, and solves the (k + 1) × (k + 1) ridge system with np.linalg.solve (never an explicit inverse). Items are handled symmetrically. Every solve is independent of the others in its half-step — the property that makes ALS parallel. objective computes the full regularised loss so tests can confirm it never increases.

implicit_user_factor implements the Hu-Koren-Volinsky user step for one user over all items: preferences are 1 for touched items and 0 otherwise, confidences 1 + α·count. Instead of forming the n × n diagonal Cu, it computes YᵀY (shared by every user) and adds Yᵀ(Cu − I)Y using only the nu touched rows; the right-hand side YᵀCup(u) likewise only involves touched items, because p is zero elsewhere.

def als_sweep(m, users, items, ratings, lam=1.0):
    """One ALS sweep with biases. Fix items: each user's [p_u, b_u] is a ridge regression on the items
    they rated, targets r - mu - b_i. Then fix users and solve each item the same way."""
    k = m["P"].shape[1]
    for side in ("user", "item"):
        own, other = (users, items) if side == "user" else (items, users)
        F_other = m["Q"] if side == "user" else m["P"]
        b_other = m["bi"] if side == "user" else m["bu"]
        n_own = m["P"].shape[0] if side == "user" else m["Q"].shape[0]
        order = np.argsort(own, kind="stable")
        bounds = np.searchsorted(own[order], np.arange(n_own + 1))
        for a in range(n_own):
            idx = order[bounds[a]:bounds[a + 1]]
            if len(idx) == 0:
                continue
            X = np.hstack([F_other[other[idx]], np.ones((len(idx), 1))])      # (n_a, k + 1)
            y = ratings[idx] - m["mu"] - b_other[other[idx]]
            w = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X + lam * np.eye(k + 1), X.T @ y)       # closed-form ridge
            if side == "user":
                m["P"][a], m["bu"][a] = w[:k], w[k]
            else:
                m["Q"][a], m["bi"][a] = w[:k], w[k]

def objective(m, users, items, ratings, lam):
    e = ratings - predict(m, users, items)
    return float((e ** 2).sum() + lam * ((m["P"] ** 2).sum() + (m["Q"] ** 2).sum()
                                         + (m["bu"] ** 2).sum() + (m["bi"] ** 2).sum()))

def implicit_user_factor(Y, counts_u, alpha=40.0, lam=0.1):
    """Implicit-feedback ALS for one user (Hu, Koren & Volinsky): preference p = 1[count > 0],
    confidence c = 1 + alpha * count, over ALL items. Uses Y^T C Y = Y^T Y + Y^T (C - I) Y, so only
    the items the user touched cost anything beyond the shared Y^T Y."""
    nz = np.nonzero(counts_u)[0]
    YtY = Y.T @ Y
    Ynz, c = Y[nz], 1.0 + alpha * counts_u[nz]
    A = YtY + (Ynz.T * (c - 1.0)) @ Ynz + lam * np.eye(Y.shape[1])
    b = (Ynz.T * c) @ np.ones(len(nz))                      # Y^T C p, and p = 1 only where count > 0
    return np.linalg.solve(A, b)

7. Testing it

Six checks on 1,441 observed ratings split 80/20 (1,152 train, 289 test). (1) Predicting the training mean gives a test RMSE of 1.104; ALS with zero factors (biases only) gives 0.937. (2) SGD with biases and k = 3 for 60 epochs (γ = 0.02, λ = 0.05) reaches 0.509. (3) ALS with λ = 2 decreases the regularised objective at every one of 15 sweeps and reaches 0.511 — within a few thousandths of SGD on this data. (4) With k = 20 and λ = 0.001, ALS drives training RMSE to 0.001 while test RMSE rises to 1.118, worse than the global mean: the model memorised the training ratings. (5) For a user who touched 3 of 30 items, the YᵀY shortcut gives exactly the same factor vector as solving the full weighted ridge problem with the 30 × 30 confidence matrix. (6) PyTorch autograd on the per-rating loss ½e² + ½λ(‖p‖² + ‖q‖² + bu² + bi²) gives gradients whose negatives are exactly the SGD update directions.

users, items, ratings, nu, ni = make_ratings()
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)

tr = (users[~test], items[~test], ratings[~test]); te = (users[test], items[test], ratings[test])
mu = float(tr[2].mean())

# 1. Baselines: global mean, then mean plus user and item biases (from an ALS with k = 0 factors).

rmse_mean = rmse(*te, base)
bias_only = {k_: (v.copy() if isinstance(v, np.ndarray) else v) for k_, v in base.items()}
for _ in range(10):

8. Numerical and practical traps

Updating qi with the new pu: a subtle inconsistency; copy first. Learning rate: too large and SGD diverges on users or items with many ratings; decay it over epochs. Zero initialisation of factors: with p = q = 0, the factor gradients are e·0 = 0 and the factors never move; initialise small random values. Forgetting to subtract μ: the factors then waste capacity on the mean. Solving with inv: use solve for stability. Data leakage: compute μ and any normalisation on the training split only.

9. Edge cases worth naming

Users or items with no training ratings: ALS skips them, leaving initial values; predict with μ (+ the other side's bias). A user with one rating: the ridge solve is still well defined because of λ. Ratings on a bounded scale: clip predictions to the scale for evaluation. Duplicate (user, item) pairs: keep the latest or average before training. Very popular items: dominate SGD updates; per-item learning rates or ALS help.

10. Complexity

SGD: O(N·k) per epoch for N observed ratings. ALS: for each user, building XᵀX costs O(nu·k²) and solving O(k³), so a sweep is O(N·k² + (users + items)·k³) — linear in data for small k, and parallel across users and items. Implicit ALS with the YᵀY trick: O(f²·N + f³·users) for the user half-step, as Hu et al. state, instead of O(f²·n) per user. Memory: (users + items)·(k + 1) parameters.

11. Talking through the design

Write the model with biases and the loss on observed entries with λ, give the SGD update and the ALS ridge step, compare them (learning rate versus closed form, sequential versus parallel, sparse explicit versus dense implicit), evaluate on held-out data against the mean and bias baselines, show what regularisation prevents, and describe implicit feedback with confidence weights and the YᵀY trick. Close with cold start and why RMSE is not the whole story.
deep:
Why fitting only the observed entries is the key move

Early approaches imputed the missing ratings (with zeros or averages) and decomposed the completed matrix with SVD. Two problems follow. Computationally, the completed matrix is dense and enormous. Statistically, the imputed values dominate, because they vastly outnumber real ratings, so the factorisation mostly fits guesses. Fitting only the observed cells with regularisation — what Koren et al. describe as modelling directly the observed ratings while avoiding overfitting through a regularised model — avoids both. It also makes the problem non-convex (the product p·q is bilinear), which is why the choice of optimiser matters and why regularisation and initialisation influence the solution found.

The probabilistic view

The regularised squared loss is the negative log posterior of a simple probabilistic model: ratings are Gaussian around μ + bu + bi + pu·qi, and all parameters have zero-mean Gaussian priors. λ is the ratio of the noise variance to the prior variance. This is Salakhutdinov and Mnih's probabilistic matrix factorisation, which Koren et al. cite as a probabilistic foundation for regularisation. It explains why larger k needs larger λ (more parameters, each needs a tighter prior to avoid fitting noise), and it opens Bayesian variants that average over factors instead of picking one point estimate.

ALS as block coordinate descent

ALS is block coordinate descent on the bilinear objective: holding one block fixed makes the problem in the other block a sum of independent ridge regressions, each solved exactly. Exact minimisation over a block can only lower (or keep) the objective, which is why the lesson's test of monotone decrease is a real correctness check — a bug in the design matrix or the targets usually breaks it. ALS converges to a stationary point, not necessarily the global minimum, and typically needs only 10-20 sweeps (Hu et al. report about 10).

Implicit feedback: why all pairs, and how it stays cheap

With only positive signals, a model fitted on observed pairs could predict 1 everywhere and be perfect. Implicit models therefore treat every unobserved pair as a weak negative (preference 0 with confidence 1) and every observed pair as a positive with confidence growing with the amount of interaction (Hu et al. used c = 1 + α·r with α = 40, and also suggest c = 1 + α·log(1 + r/ε)). The objective now has users × items terms — billions — so SGD over it is impractical. ALS rescues it: each user's normal equations involve YᵀCuY, which splits into YᵀY (identical for everyone, computed once) plus a correction involving only the items the user touched. The work becomes linear in the number of interactions, the same as explicit ALS. The same paper notes that the solution can be rewritten as a weighted sum of item-item similarities, giving explanations ("recommended because you watched…").

Beyond the basic model

Koren et al. extend the model with implicit signals inside an explicit model (a user represented also by the normalised sum of factor vectors of items they interacted with, |N(u)|−1/2 Σ xi, which helps users with few ratings), user attributes, temporal dynamics (biases and user factors as functions of time, because tastes and item popularity drift), and confidence weights for explicit ratings. Modern systems often replace the dot-product model with neural two-tower models trained on implicit data with sampled negatives, but the bias terms, the regularisation logic and the treatment of implicit feedback carry over directly.

Initialisation and symmetry

The factor model is symmetric under rotations: replacing pu by Rpu and qi by Rqi for any orthogonal R leaves every prediction unchanged, so individual factor dimensions have no fixed meaning and differ between training runs. Initialising at exactly zero is a saddle point where the factor gradients vanish; small random values break the symmetry and let both optimisers start moving. This is also why comparing factor vectors across separately trained models requires aligning them first.

Ranking versus rating prediction

The Netflix Prize measured RMSE on ratings, but a recommender shows a ranked list of items the user has not seen. Optimising squared error on observed ratings does not directly optimise that ranking, and missing ratings are not random — people rate what they chose to watch, so observed ratings skew positive. For production, evaluate with ranking metrics on held-out interactions over the full catalogue (or carefully sampled candidates), and consider objectives such as implicit ALS or pairwise ranking losses that train on the decision the system actually makes.
prod:
Where it runs

Matrix factorisation — especially implicit-feedback ALS — remains a standard component of recommender systems: as a candidate generator producing a few hundred items per user from millions, as a source of user and item embeddings for downstream ranking models, and as a strong baseline that newer models must beat. Distributed ALS implementations (for example in Spark MLlib) scale it to billions of interactions by solving users and items in parallel.

Failure modes and symptoms

Popularity bias. Symptom: everyone gets the same popular items. Cause: biases and factors dominated by popular items, implicit confidence too high for heavy items. Fix: tune α and λ, down-weight popular items, add diversity in re-ranking.

Cold start. Symptom: new users get generic recommendations, new items are never shown. Cause: no factors. Fix: fold-in with one ALS step after a few interactions, side information, exploration slots for new items.

Overfitting. Symptom: offline training metrics excellent, online engagement flat. Cause: λ too small or k too large; leakage between train and evaluation (random splits that put a user's future in training). Fix: time-based splits, validation-tuned λ.

Stale factors. Symptom: recommendations ignore recent behaviour. Cause: factors retrained infrequently. Fix: frequent retraining, fold-in updates for users between full retrains.

Feedback loops. Symptom: the system keeps recommending what it recommended. Cause: implicit training data are produced by the recommender's own exposure. Fix: log exposures, weight or correct for position and exposure, reserve exploration traffic.

What to monitor and tune

Held-out RMSE (explicit) or recall@k and NDCG (implicit) with time-based splits; catalogue coverage and the share of recommendations going to the top 1% of items; performance for new and light users separately; training objective per sweep (it must fall monotonically for ALS). Tune k, λ, α (implicit), the number of sweeps or epochs and learning-rate schedules.

A cost estimate

Implicit ALS on 10 million users, 1 million items and 1 billion interactions with f = 100: each user half-step costs about f²·N = 104 × 109 = 1013 operations to accumulate the corrections plus f³·users = 106 × 107 = 1013 for the solves; the item half-step is similar. Around 4 × 1013 operations per sweep and ten sweeps per training run — minutes to an hour on a modest cluster. Storing the factors takes 11 million × 100 × 4 bytes ≈ 4.4 GB.

The reference for this problem

Koren, Bell and Volinsky (IEEE Computer, 2009) give the regularised objective over the known ratings, the SGD updates qi ← qi + γ(euipu − λqi) and pu ← pu + γ(euiqi − λpu), describe ALS as rotating between fixing the q's and solving least squares for the p's and vice versa — favourable when parallelising and for implicit data — add biases with the Joe/Titanic example, and discuss implicit feedback and confidence. Hu, Koren and Volinsky (ICDM 2008) define pui = 1[rui > 0], cui = 1 + αrui with α = 40, the all-pairs weighted objective, and the YᵀCuY = YᵀY + Yᵀ(Cu − I)Y speed-up that makes each sweep linear in the data.
myths: Matrix factorisation is SVD of the rating matrix.

SVD needs a complete matrix, and a rating matrix is mostly missing — typically over 99% in real systems. Filling the gaps with zeros or means and decomposing treats guesses as data. Matrix factorisation for recommendations fits factors to the observed entries only, with regularisation, by SGD or ALS. It is SVD-like in spirit, not SVD.
The latent factors are what matters; biases are a detail.

Much of the variation in ratings is users who rate everything high or low and items that everyone likes or dislikes. In the lesson, adding just a user and an item bias to the global mean cuts test RMSE from 1.10 to 0.94; factors then take it to 0.51. Koren, Bell and Volinsky stress that accurate bias modelling is vital because biases capture much of the observed signal.
Lower training error means a better recommender.

With 20 factors and almost no regularisation, the model fits the training ratings to an RMSE of 0.001 and gets worse than predicting the mean on held-out ratings (1.12). The factor model has enough parameters to memorise; λ, tuned on held-out data, is what makes it generalise.
ALS and SGD find the same solution.

They minimise the same objective but are different optimisers of a non-convex problem: SGD takes small noisy steps and needs a learning rate; ALS alternates exact ridge-regression solves and decreases the objective every sweep. On the lesson's data they reach nearly the same test RMSE (0.509 and 0.511), but on real data they can land in different places, and ALS is preferred when the data are dense or the work must be parallel.
Implicit feedback is just ratings of 1.

A click, a play or a purchase is evidence of preference with varying confidence, and the absence of one is weak evidence of anything. Hu, Koren and Volinsky model a binary preference with a confidence 1 + α·r that grows with the amount of interaction, and fit over all user-item pairs, including the unobserved ones — which needs a special ALS trick to be affordable.

recap: The prediction is r̂_ui = μ + b_u + b_i + p_u·q_i: global mean, user bias, item bias and a dot product of k latent factors.
Training minimises squared error on the observed ratings plus λ times the squared norms of factors and biases.
SGD visits ratings one at a time: e = r − r̂, then each bias moves by γ(e − λb) and each factor by γ(e·other − λ·self), using the old values.
ALS fixes item factors, which makes each user's factors (and bias) a ridge regression with a closed form, then swaps roles; the objective never increases.
ALS parallelises across users and across items, and handles dense implicit data; SGD is simple and fast on sparse explicit data.
Evaluation uses RMSE on held-out ratings, compared against the global mean and the bias-only baseline.
Without regularisation and with many factors the model memorises the training ratings and fails on held-out ones.
Implicit feedback uses preference p = 1[r > 0] with confidence c = 1 + α·r over all user-item pairs.
Implicit ALS stays linear in the number of interactions by computing YᵀY once and adding only the interacted items' correction per user.
Factors and biases are learned from data alone, so cold-start users and items need side information or fallbacks.
glossary: Alternating least squares: fix one set of factors, solve the other exactly by least squares, and alternate.
A per-user or per-item offset capturing a tendency to rate high or low, independent of interactions.
Making recommendations for users or items with little or no interaction history.
A weight c_ui = 1 + α·r_ui expressing how sure the model is about an observed or unobserved preference.
Normalised discounted cumulative gain: a ranking metric that rewards relevant items more the higher they appear in the list.
Ratings users give deliberately, such as stars.
Preferences inferred from behaviour such as views, clicks, plays or purchases.
A learned dimension of the user and item vectors whose dot product predicts the interaction.
Approximating the user-item matrix as the product of a user-factor matrix and an item-factor matrix, fitted to observed entries.
A penalty on squared parameter norms that keeps factors small to avoid overfitting.
Least squares with an L2 penalty, solved by (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy.
Singular value decomposition: the exact low-rank factorisation of a complete matrix.
Root mean squared error between predicted and actual ratings.
Stochastic gradient descent: updating parameters after each training example (here, each rating).
The fraction of the user-item matrix with no observed interaction.

(a) A user has rated three items whose fixed factors (k = 2) are q1 = [1, 0], q2 = [0, 1], q3 = [1, 1], with targets r − μ − bi of 1, 2 and 2. Solve for pu with λ = 1 and no user bias. Answer 
Qd = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]]); yd = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 2.0])
pd_ = np.linalg.solve(Qd.T @ Qd + np.eye(2), Qd.T @ yd)
assert np.allclose(pd_, [0.625, 1.125])
naive = 50e6 * 64 ** 2 * 200_000                                  # f^2 n per user

The determinant is 3·3 − 1·1 = 8, so p = (1/8)[[3, −1], [−1, 3]]·[3, 4] = (1/8)[5, 9] = [0.625, 1.125]. Without λ the unregularised least-squares answer would be [2/3, 5/3]; the penalty shrinks both components. With the trick: f²·N + f³·m = 4,096 × 2 × 109 + 262,144 × 5 × 107 ≈ 8.2 × 1012 + 1.3 × 1013 ≈ 2.1 × 1013, about 1,900 times less — the difference between impossible and routine.

Write the biased matrix factorisation model and its loss.

r̂_ui = μ + b_u + b_i + p_uᵀq_i. Minimise Σ over observed (u, i) of (r_ui − r̂_ui)² + λ(‖p_u‖² + ‖q_i‖² + b_u² + b_i²). μ is the global mean; b_u and b_i capture user and item tendencies; p_u and q_i are k-dimensional latent factors.
E
Why not compute the SVD of the rating matrix?

Because most entries are missing, and SVD is defined for a complete matrix. Imputing missing values distorts the data and is expensive. Matrix factorisation fits only the observed entries with regularisation, which Koren et al. describe as modelling observed ratings directly while avoiding overfitting through a regularised model.
E
What are the baselines you compare against?

The global mean (predict μ for everything) and the bias-only model μ + b_u + b_i. In the lesson they give test RMSE 1.104 and 0.937; the factor model reaches 0.509. A factor model that does not clearly beat the bias baseline is learning little beyond popularity and user generosity.
M
Write the SGD update for one rating and work an example.

e = r − r̂; b_u ← b_u + γ(e − λb_u); b_i ← b_i + γ(e − λb_i); p_u ← p_u + γ(e·q_i − λp_u); q_i ← q_i + γ(e·p_u − λq_i), using the old p_u in the last line. With μ = 3, zero biases, p_u = 0.5, q_i = 0.4, r = 4, γ = λ = 0.1: r̂ = 3.2, e = 0.8; biases become 0.08; p_u = 0.5 + 0.1(0.32 − 0.05) = 0.527; q_i = 0.4 + 0.1(0.40 − 0.04) = 0.436; the new prediction is 3.390.
Follow-up: Why use the old p_u when updating q_i? — Both updates are the gradient at the same point; using the new p_u would mix two points and is a different (though usually harmless) algorithm.
M
How does ALS work?

With item factors fixed, the loss is quadratic in each user's parameters separately: user u's [p_u, b_u] is a ridge regression on the items u rated, with features [q_i, 1] and targets r_ui − μ − b_i, solved in closed form by (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy. Do that for every user, then fix users and solve every item the same way. Each half-step solves its subproblem exactly, so the objective never increases.
M
SGD or ALS?

SGD is simple, memory-light and fast on sparse explicit ratings, but needs a learning rate and schedule. ALS needs no learning rate, decreases the objective monotonically, and parallelises naturally — every user's solve is independent given the items — and it is the practical choice for implicit feedback, where the objective covers all user-item pairs and SGD would have to visit billions of terms. Koren et al. name exactly these two cases as favouring ALS.
M
How do you pick k and λ?

On held-out ratings: sweep λ (and k) and choose the lowest validation RMSE (or ranking metric). Larger k needs larger λ. The lesson shows the failure without it: k = 20 and λ ≈ 0 give train RMSE 0.001 and test 1.118, worse than predicting the mean.
M
Why are biases so important?

Ratings are dominated by systematic effects: some users rate everything generously, some items are rated highly by everyone. Without explicit biases, the factors must spend capacity encoding those offsets. Koren et al.'s example: overall mean 3.7, Titanic rated 0.5 above average, Joe rates 0.3 below average, so the baseline estimate for Joe and Titanic is 3.9 before any interaction term.
H
Explain implicit-feedback ALS and its speed-up.

Hu, Koren and Volinsky turn raw counts r_ui into a preference p_ui = 1 if r_ui > 0 else 0 and a confidence c_ui = 1 + α·r_ui (α = 40 in their experiments), and minimise Σ over ALL (u, i) of c_ui(p_ui − x_uᵀy_i)² + λ(‖x‖² + ‖y‖²). Each user's solve is x_u = (YᵀC^uY + λI)⁻¹YᵀC^u p(u), which naively costs O(f²n) per user. Writing YᵀC^uY = YᵀY + Yᵀ(C^u − I)Y, with YᵀY computed once and C^u − I non-zero only on the n_u items the user touched, makes each solve O(f²n_u + f³) and the whole sweep linear in the number of interactions.
Follow-up: Why include the unobserved pairs at all? — Without them every prediction could be 1 and the loss would be zero; the zeros with low confidence teach the model what users did not choose.
H
How do you recommend for a brand-new user?

Matrix factorisation has no factors for them. Options: popularity or bias-only recommendations until data arrive; fold-in — once the user has a few interactions, solve their factor with one ALS step against the fixed item factors (cheap and exact); side information — represent users by attributes or by the sum of the items they touched (Koren et al.'s |N(u)|^−0.5 Σ x_i term); or a separate content-based model blended in.
H
RMSE improved but the recommendations did not. Why?

RMSE on ratings rewards predicting all ratings accurately, including for items users would never be shown; recommendation quality depends on ranking the top few items correctly among everything, including unrated ones. Missing ratings are also not missing at random — users rate what they chose to watch. Evaluate with ranking metrics (recall@k, NDCG) on held-out interactions, sampled or full-catalogue, and consider objectives built for ranking or implicit data.
H
How does ALS scale to a billion interactions?

Each sweep is embarrassingly parallel: partition users across workers, broadcast or shard the item factors, solve each user's small k × k system independently, then do the same for items. Communication is the factor matrices (users × k and items × k), not the ratings. With implicit data, the YᵀY trick keeps work linear in interactions. This is why ALS is the matrix factorisation in distributed frameworks such as Spark MLlib.
